passages.title: The clear Book opens Moses' story
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are the doorway into Sūrah al-Qasas: three separate letters, a declaration that what follows belongs to a Book that makes things plain, and then Allah's announcement that He Himself recites to His Prophet ﷺ part of the news of Mūsā and Fir'awn. What binds them together is a single claim about *how* this story arrives: as revelation, recited by Allah, delivered "in truth," and aimed at a particular audience — "a people who believe."

## The moment this sūrah was given

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens its commentary with a piece of context that changes how the whole sūrah reads: **Sūrah al-Qasas is the very last among the Makkan sūrahs.** It was revealed between Makkah and Juhfah (Rabigh) — that is, during the migration itself.

Maʿārif relates that it is mentioned in some narrations that during the journey from Makkah to Madīnah, when the Prophet ﷺ had reached near Juhfah or Rabigh, Jibra'īl (peace be upon him) came to him and asked whether he was feeling homesick, as he was leaving the place where he was born and where he had spent his whole life. The Prophet ﷺ replied that he was. Jibra'īl then recited this sūrah to him and gave him the good tiding that ultimately Makkah would come under his control — the promise that appears near the sūrah's close:

> *"Surely the One who has enjoined the Qurʼān upon you will surely bring you back to the place of return."* (28:85)

(Note that Maʿārif introduces this as something "mentioned in some narrations" without naming a collection, so we receive it as it is given — as reported context, not as an authenticated hadith with a named source.)

Hold that scene in mind while you read ayah 3. A man who has just been asked, in effect, *do you miss your home?* — and answered yes — is then given a recitation about Mūsā and Fir'awn. The choice of story is itself part of the consolation.

Maʿārif also notes something about the sūrah just before this one, which closed by naming Allah as *"the Lord of this city"* (27:91). The majority of the commentators, Maʿārif says, have taken "the city" here to be Makkah; since Allah is the Lord of all the worlds and the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the particular mention of Makkah is to show its revered splendour and its honour in the sight of Allah. So the sūrah revealed to a man on the road out of that honoured city carries, at its far end, the promise of his return to it.

## Ayah 1: Ṭā Sīn Mīm

The sūrah opens with three letters recited singly. On their meaning, Ibn Kathīr is brief here — he simply says that the significance of the separate letters has already been discussed, rather than unpacking it again at this point. That restraint is itself instructive: where the sources do not press for a meaning, we do not manufacture one.

What Ibn Kathīr does record here is a small scene from the generation that received the Qurʼān. He reports that **Imam Ahmad bin Hanbal**, may Allah have mercy on him, recorded that Ma'diykarib said: "We came to 'Abdullāh and asked him to recite to us Ṭā Sīn Mīm, the two hundred. He said, 'I do not know it; you should go to someone who learned it from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — Khabbāb bin Al-Aratt.' So we went to Khabbāb bin Al-Aratt and he recited it to us, may Allah be pleased with him."

Two things are worth pausing over. First, a Companion is asked for a sūrah and answers plainly, *I do not know it* — and then points the questioners to the man who learned it from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. There is no embarrassment in the gap and no attempt to fill it from himself. Second, this shows how the Qurʼān actually travelled: from the Prophet ﷺ to a named man, and from him to those who came asking. The very ayah that follows calls this "the manifest Book" — and here we see the human chain by which it was carried.

(Note that this is a report about the Companions, not a saying of the Prophet ﷺ himself.)

## Ayah 2: "These are the ayat of the manifest Book"

Ibn Kathīr's gloss is compact and worth taking slowly. *These are the Ayat of the manifest Book* means, he says, **"the Book which is clear and makes plain the true reality of things, and tells us about what happened and what will happen."**

Two claims sit inside that one sentence. The Book is clear *in itself* — and it *makes other things plain*. It does not merely add information to the world; in Ibn Kathīr's phrase, it makes plain "the true reality of things," showing you what is actually the case beneath appearances.

And it reaches in both directions in time — "what happened and what will happen." A man leaving Makkah is handed a Book that reports the past truly and tells of what is to come. What follows immediately, the news of Mūsā, belongs to the first; the promise of 28:85 belongs to the second.

## Ayah 3: "We recite to you some of the news of Mūsā and Fir'awn, in truth"

Every word here is doing work.

**"We recite to you."** Allah does not say *listen to this story* or *here is what happened*. He says *natlū* — We recite. The Prophet ﷺ is not the author or the researcher of this account; he is its recipient.

**"Some of the news."** The translations render *min naba'* as "some of the news" (Ibn Kathīr) and "part of the story." That partial quality is real, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws it out across the whole Qurʼān: the story of Sayyidnā Mūsā (peace be upon him) is related extensively, at places briefly and at others in detail. In Sūrah al-Kahf we are given the part in which he encountered al-Khadir (peace be upon him); in Sūrah Tāhā other parts are related in some detail; some details are related in Sūrah an-Naml; and now in al-Qasas they are being reiterated.

Maʿārif also maps what is coming: the sūrah begins with the story of Sayyidnā Mūsā first briefly and then in detail; the first half contains his episodes with the Pharaoh, and towards the end of the sūrah comes his episode with Qārūn. And Maʿārif tells us frankly why its own commentary here will be brief — at *"And We tested you with a great ordeal"* (20:40) in Sūrah Tāhā, Imam Nasā'ī and some other commentators penned down the entire story, and the writer of Maʿārif followed suit, setting out the whole story there by quoting Ibn Kathīr. The related issues and rulings, Maʿārif says, have been discussed in detail under Sūrahs al-Kahf and Tāhā, and for any question of an issue or ruling it would be apt to look them up there. So in al-Qasas the commentary is restricted to a brief explanation of the wording of these verses.

**"In truth" — bi-l-haqq.** Ibn Kathīr connects this to Allah's words, *"We relate unto you the best of stories"* (12:3), and explains what such reciting means: **'We tell you about things as they really were, as if you are there and are seeing them yourself.'** That is a remarkable standard. The claim is not only that the account is free of error, but that it places the listener inside the event.

**"For a people who believe."** This is the audience the recitation names. The report is given, and it is those who believe who are named as the ones it is for.

## What these ayat open onto

Having announced the recitation, the passage turns at once to Fir'awn — and the note Ibn Kathīr sounds there is the one these three opening ayat are preparing you for. Fir'awn, fearing that a boy would appear among the Children of Israel who would be the cause of his destruction and the downfall of his kingdom, **took precautions against that happening** by ordering that all boys born to the Children of Israel should be killed — "but this precaution did not protect him against the divine decree, because when the term of Allah comes, it cannot be delayed, and for each and every matter there is a decree from Allah."

That is the news being recited "in truth," and it is worth carrying no further than the sources take it here: a man with every instrument of power calculated carefully against a decree he could not calculate against.

## Living it

**Receive knowledge the way Khabbāb passed it on.** The report Ibn Kathīr records shows a Companion refusing to answer beyond what he had, and sending the questioners to someone who learned it from the Prophet ﷺ. That is the posture: say "I do not know" without shame, and go to the one who actually took it from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

**Read the Qurʼān as a Book that makes things plain, not only a book to be recited.** If Ibn Kathīr is right that it "makes plain the true reality of things," then the test of your reading is whether it changes how you see what is actually in front of you.

**Take the timing to heart.** These ayat were given, by the account Maʿārif relates, on the migration road — with the promise of return attached at the far end of the same sūrah (28:85). The consolation and the promise arrive together.

**And notice what the passage asks of you.** It does not ask you to calculate like Fir'awn, whose precautions did not protect him against the divine decree. It asks you to listen — *We recite to you* — and to be among "a people who believe," which is the audience the ayah itself names.

passages.title: Pharaoh's tyranny and Allah's counter-plan
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat set up the whole sūrah: ayah 4 photographs Pharaoh's tyranny at its height, and ayat 5 and 6 answer it with what Allah had already decided to do. What binds them together is a single contrast — one man's plan against Allah's plan — and the Qur'an places them side by side so that the outcome is announced before the story has even begun.

## Where and when this sūrah came down

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Sūrah al-Qasas is the very last of the Makkan sūrahs, revealed between Makkah and Juhfah (Rabigh) during the migration itself. It records that in some narrations, when the Prophet ﷺ reached near Juhfah or Rabigh on the journey from Makkah to Madinah, Jibrīl (peace be upon him) came and asked whether he was feeling homesick, since he was leaving the place where he was born and had spent his whole life. The Prophet ﷺ replied that he was. Then Jibrīl recited this sūrah to him and gave him the glad tiding that Makkah would in the end fall to him and come under his control — the promise in ayah 85: *"Surely the One who has enjoined the Qur'an upon you will surely bring you back to the place of return."*

Hold that setting in mind and ayat 4–6 change colour completely. A man is being driven out of his own city by a hostile power, and among the first things he is given is a story about the most powerful tyrant and the most helpless community — and how that ended. The consolation is not a vague "be patient". It is a precedent.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also maps the sūrah for us: it opens with the story of Mūsā (peace be upon him), first briefly and then in detail — the first half covering his episodes with Pharaoh, and the closing portion his episode with Qārūn. The story of Mūsā is spread across the Qur'an: his encounter with al-Khadir (peace be upon him) in Sūrah al-Kahf, other parts in some detail in Sūrah Ṭā-Hā, further details in Sūrah an-Naml, and now reiterated here. Because the full narrative and its related issues and rulings were treated under Sūrah al-Kahf and Sūrah Ṭā-Hā — where Allah says *"And We tested you with a great ordeal"* (20:40), and where Imām Nasā'ī and some other commentators set down the entire story — the commentary here confines itself to a brief explanation of the wording of these verses.

## An early note on reciting this sūrah

Ibn Kathīr opens with a report recorded by Imām Aḥmad bin Ḥanbal, may Allah have mercy on him, from Maʿdīkarib, who said: "We came to ʿAbdullāh and asked him to recite to us *Ṭā Sīn Mīm*, the two hundred. He said, 'I do not know it; you should go to someone who learned it from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — Khabbāb bin al-Aratt.' So we went to Khabbāb bin al-Aratt and he recited it to us, may Allah be pleased with him."

There is a quiet lesson in that exchange before we even reach the text: a Companion of that rank declining to recite what he had not taken directly, and sending the questioners instead to the man who had learned it from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Knowledge here is not guessed at; it is traced back to its source, or else honestly declined.

## "The manifest Book" and news told "in truth"

The passage is introduced in ayat 2–3. *"These are the Ayat of the manifest Book"* means, Ibn Kathīr says, the Book which is clear and which makes plain the true reality of things, and which tells us about what happened and what will happen. Then *"We recite to you some of the news of Mūsā and Pharaoh in truth."* Ibn Kathīr links this to *"We relate unto you the best of stories"* (12:3), and explains the sense as: **'We tell you about things as they really were, as if you are there and are seeing them yourself.'**

That is worth pausing on. What follows is not a moral fable dressed as history. It is Allah's own account of what actually happened — and it is selective (*"some of the news"*), given for a purpose, to *"a people who believe."*

## Ayah 4: the anatomy of a tyrant

Ayah 4 builds Pharaoh's tyranny in stages, and each stage is a different kind of wrong.

**"Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land."** Ibn Kathīr's gloss is compact: **he was an arrogant oppressor and tyrant.** That is the root posture out of which everything else in the ayah grows.

**"and made its people into Shiyaʿ."** Ibn Kathīr explains: he made them into different classes, each of which he used to do whatever he wanted of the affairs of his state. Notice that this is described before the killing is mentioned — the population is first sorted into groups, each assigned its function in the machinery of his rule.

**"weakening a group among them."** Ibn Kathīr identifies them: the Children of Israel — who, he says, **at that time were the best of people**, even though this tyrant king overpowered them. Take in the moral geometry of that sentence: the group at the bottom of Pharaoh's ranking was, in the sight of Allah, the best of the people of that age.

Ibn Kathīr fills in the daily reality: Pharaoh used them for the most menial work and forced them to hard labour night and day, for himself and for his people.

**"killing their sons, and letting their females live."** Ibn Kathīr gives two motives running together: **to humiliate them**, and **because he feared that there might appear among them the boy who would be the cause of his destruction and the downfall of his kingdom.** So Pharaoh took precautions against that happening, ordering that all boys born to the Children of Israel should be killed.

Then Ibn Kathīr states the hinge of the whole passage: **this precaution did not protect him against the divine decree, because when the term of Allah comes it cannot be delayed, and for each and every matter there is a decree from Allah.**

**"Verily, he was of the mischief-makers"** — the ayah's closing verdict. Whatever Pharaoh called his programme, Allah files it under corruption in the earth.

## Ayat 5–6: the counter-plan

Now the camera turns. Ayah 5 reads, in the renderings before us, *"And We wished to do a favour to those who were weak in the land"* / *"And We intended to favour those who were held as weak in the land."* The very group Pharaoh's policy had pressed down — described in ayah 4 as the ones he was "weakening" — is in ayah 5 the object of Allah's intended favour. They are identified by their oppression, and that is precisely where Allah's kindness lands.

Then four things are promised, and they escalate:

1. **"and to make them leaders"** (Ibn Kathīr's rendering: "rulers") — the ones who were worked as labour become the ones others follow.
2. **"and to make them the inheritors"** — they receive what the tyrant had. Ibn Kathīr cites the fulfilment: *"And We made the people who were considered weak…"* through *"…they erected"* (7:137), and *"Thus, and We caused the Children of Israel to inherit them"* (26:59).
3. **"And to establish them in the land"** (ayah 6) — not a brief reversal but a settled footing, real ground under their feet.
4. **"and We let Pharaoh and Hāmān and their armies receive from them that which they feared"** — or, in the other rendering before us, *"to make Pharaoh and Hāmān and their armies see what they were fearing."*

That fourth item is the sharpest. The very thing Pharaoh had built an entire apparatus of watching and killing to prevent, Allah promises will come to him from the very people he was crushing — and that he will see it happen.

Ibn Kathīr closes the point: Pharaoh hoped that by his strength and power he would be saved from Mūsā, but that did not help him in the slightest. Despite his great power as a king he could not oppose the decree of Allah, which can never be overcome. On the contrary, Allah's ruling was carried out, for **it had been written and decreed from past eternity that Pharaoh would meet his doom at the hands of Mūsā.**

## The irony Allah wrote into the plot

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out how completely the counter-plan overturned Pharaoh's: the plan of Pharaoh was not equal to that of the divine decree — it turned out completely ineffective, and he and his entire court were made fools of.

Trace the sequence. On the basis of the dream and its interpretation, that an Israelite boy was the one from whom Pharaoh's life was at risk, hundreds of newborn Israelite boys were put to death at birth. And then Allah made **that very boy grow up in Pharaoh's own house.** Not only that: for the solace of the boy's mother, it was arranged in a most astonishing manner that he be sent back to her to nurse. And on top of that, Pharaoh was made to pay a service charge for the nursing — according to some narrations, one dinar a day.

So the cruelty he had perpetrated to quell the risk was of no avail to him at all, because that very danger was ultimately reared in his own home and finally erupted like lava. The dream came true, and he saw it happening with his own eyes. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says this is exactly what ayah 6 is describing — *"and to make Pharaoh and Hāmān and their armies see what they were fearing."*

Consider what that means about the phrase *"We wished to do a favour."* Allah's intention did not merely overrule Pharaoh's plan from outside; the very measures Pharaoh took became the road along which his ruin travelled. The boy he feared was raised, protected and funded inside his own household.

**A small point of fiqh in passing.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that since this nursing payment was taken from a disbeliever with his own consent, there is no confusion about its being lawful.

## Living it

**Read the two plans against each other.** Ayah 4 is what a tyrant can do: elevate himself, sort a society into classes, crush a group, kill children. Ayat 5 and 6 are what Allah does about it — and He states His intention in the same breath as the atrocity, not after it. The Qur'an does not deny the horror; it simply refuses to let it be the last word.

**Do not read your circumstances as a verdict on your worth.** The people Pharaoh had pressed to the bottom were, in Ibn Kathīr's words, the best of people at that time. Where you stand in someone else's ranking is not where you stand with Allah.

**And do not read a tyrant's confidence as strength.** Pharaoh had a warning, a standing order and an army, and he still could not stop what had been decreed. As Ibn Kathīr puts it, when the term of Allah comes it cannot be delayed. That is a warning to anyone who thinks their arrangements can outmanoeuvre Allah, and a mercy to anyone with no arrangements left at all.

**Finally, remember who first heard this.** A Prophet ﷺ leaving his home under threat, given a story whose ending was already written — and, with it, the promise of ayah 85 that he would be brought back. The believer who is at the bottom today can hear ayah 5 as an address, not only as history: *"And We intended to favour those who were held as weak in the land."*

passages.title: The infant Moses returned to his mother
passages.tafsir:
**The promise, and the keeping of it.** These seven ayat are one story with one shape: Allah tells a terrified mother to place her newborn in the river, promises to give him back, and then gives him back. Ayah 7 is the promise; ayah 13 is its fulfilment. Everything in between is the route Allah chose to get from the one to the other — and that route ran directly through the palace of the man who was killing Israelite infants.

One phrase holds the passage together at its two ends. In ayah 9 the wife of Fir'awn looks at the rescued baby and calls him *qurratu ʿayn* — "a comfort of the eye" — for herself and her husband. In ayah 13 Allah says He returned the child to his mother *kay taqarra ʿaynuhā*, "that her eye might be comforted." The palace laid claim to him with that phrase; the ayah gives the phrase back to the woman it truly belonged to.

## The Egypt this child was born into

Ibn Kathir relates the background that makes ayah 7 land. Fir'awn's slaughter of the Israelite males had been so thorough that the Copts themselves grew alarmed — not out of mercy, but out of self-interest. They said to Fir'awn that if this continued, and the old men died and the young men were killed, the women would not be able to do the work the men were doing, and the Copts would end up having to do it themselves. So Fir'awn issued orders that the boys should be killed one year and left alone the following year. Harun, peace be upon him, was born in a year when the boys were not killed. Musa, peace be upon him, was born in a year when the boys were being killed.

The machinery was meticulous. Fir'awn had people entrusted with the task. Midwives went around checking on the women, and if they noticed a woman was pregnant they wrote her name down. When her time came, no one was allowed to attend her except Coptic women. If the baby was a girl, they left her alone and went away. If it was a boy, the killers came in with their sharp knives and killed the child, then went away — "may Allah curse them," says Ibn Kathir.

Two mercies come before the ayah even begins. First, when Musa's mother was carrying him, she did not show any signs of pregnancy as other women did, and none of the midwives noticed. Second, once she gave birth to a boy she became very distressed and did not know what to do with him — she was extremely scared for him, Ibn Kathir says, *because she loved him very much.* And no one ever saw Musa, peace be upon him, but they loved him; the blessed ones were those who loved him both as a natural feeling and because he was a Prophet. Ibn Kathir cites here the ayah Allah later spoke to Musa directly: **"And I endued you with love from Me"** (Ta Ha 20:39).

## Ayah 7: what kind of "revelation" this was

**"And We inspired the mother of Musa."** Maarif ul Quran is careful here: the word *waḥy* ("inspiration") is used in this ayah in its literal meaning. It does **not** mean the *waḥy* that is peculiar to prophets — the formal revelation Allah sends to His Messengers. Maarif ul Quran notes that it has already explained this point under Surah Ta Ha. What Musa's mother received was guidance cast into her heart and mind at the moment she was most worried and confused; it did not make her a prophetess.

Look at what she is actually told. It comes as a sequence of commands, prohibitions, and promises:

- **"Suckle him"** — an ordinary instruction. Feed your baby. Do the normal thing, for now.
- **"But when you fear for him, then cast him into the river"** — note the condition. She is not told to throw him in immediately, but *when the fear comes*.
- **"And fear not, nor grieve"** — two separate prohibitions, one after the other. Allah forbids her both.
- **"Verily, We shall bring him back to you, and shall make him one of the Messengers"** — two promises, one small and one enormous. She will get her baby back; and this baby will be a Messenger of Allah.

Ibn Kathir describes what she then did. Her house was on the banks of the Nile, so she took a box and made it into a cradle, and started to nurse her child there. When someone she was afraid of came to the house, she would put him in that box and put it in the river — and she would tie it with a rope. Then one day someone she was afraid of came, she put the child in the box and put it in the river, but **she forgot to tie it.** The water carried him away.

Sit with that. The moment the whole story turns on is a forgotten knot. The mother had a system, and the system failed. Allah's promise did not.

## Ayah 8: picked up as an enemy

The water carried the box past the house of Fir'awn, where some servant women picked it up and took it to Fir'awn's wife. They did not know what was inside, and they were afraid they would be in trouble if they opened it without her. When the box was opened, they saw a child with the most beautiful features. Allah filled her heart with love for him when she saw him — this was, Ibn Kathir says, because she was blessed, and because Allah wanted to honour her and to cause her husband's doom.

Then comes one of the most arresting lines in the Qur'an: **"Then the household of Fir'awn picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a cause of grief."** Notice how the ayah words it. The outcome is stated in the language of purpose — as *what he was picked up for* — though nothing in the account suggests that acquiring an enemy was on anyone's mind that morning. Ibn Kathir's comment on the closing words of ayah 9, **"and they perceived not,"** speaks directly to this: they did not know what Allah planned for them when they picked him up, by His great wisdom and definitive proof. What looked to them like a happy discovery was, in the knowledge of Allah, already the beginning of their end.

The ayah then names them — **"Verily, Fir'awn, Haman and their armies were sinners"** — a reminder that the tenderness in the palace nursery does not soften the verdict on the regime.

## Ayah 9: Asiyah speaks, and Fir'awn answers

When Fir'awn saw the child he wanted to kill him, fearing that he was one of the Children of Israel. It was his wife — Ibn Kathir names her **Asiyah bint Muzahim** — who came to the child's defence and did it by endearing him to Fir'awn: **"A comfort of the eye for me and for you. Kill him not."**

Fir'awn's reply, as Ibn Kathir records it, is one of the great ironies of the Qur'anic narratives. He said: *"For you he may be, but not for me."* And Ibn Kathir comments: this was indeed the case — Allah guided her because of him, and destroyed Fir'awn at his hands. On that reading, Fir'awn's own sentence came true, word for word, against him.

Her two reasons deserve attention:

- **"Perhaps he may be of benefit to us."** Ibn Kathir: this is indeed what happened in her case, for Allah guided her through him and caused her to dwell in Paradise because of him. She was hoping for some usefulness; she received Paradise.
- **"Or we may adopt him as a son."** She wanted to take him and adopt him as a son, Ibn Kathir explains, because she had no children from Fir'awn. It was through that circumstance — a household without a child of its own — that Allah placed a Messenger in safety and brought her to guidance.

## Ayah 10: a heart emptied out

**"And the heart of the mother of Musa became empty."** The Arabic is *fu'ād... fārigh*. Ibn Kathir reports the interpretation of a long line of early authorities — Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Sa'id bin Jubayr, Abu 'Ubaydah, Ad-Dahhak, Al-Hasan Al-Basri, Qatadah and others — that when her child was lost in the river she could not think of any matter in this world except Musa. Her heart was not empty of feeling; it was emptied of everything *but* him.

**"She was very near to disclose his case."** Because of the intensity of her grief, Ibn Kathir explains, she almost told people that she had lost a son — which, in that city, in that year, would have been a death sentence for the child and quite possibly for her. She *would* have disclosed her situation, he says, had Allah not given her strength and patience.

**"Had We not strengthened her heart."** Notice the sequence: Allah promised her in ayah 7, but that did not mean she felt calm. She was on the edge of breaking. What Allah gave her was not the removal of the pain but the strength and patience to hold under it — **"so that she might remain as one of the believers."** Faith, in this ayah, is not the absence of anguish; it is what Allah gives the heart so the anguish does not overcome it.

## Ayah 11: the sister who watched without watching

**"And she said to his sister: 'Follow him.'"** Ibn Kathir explains that she told her daughter, who was older and was of an age to understand things. The command *quṣṣīhi* means: follow his traces and look for information about him, try to find out about him around the city. And she went out to do that.

Then: **"So she watched him from a far place."** The phrase *ʿan junub* drew careful comment from the early scholars. Ibn 'Abbas said it means "off to the side." Mujahid said it means she looked from afar. Qatadah gave the most vivid reading of all: **"She started to look at him as if she was not really interested."**

That is the craft of a girl keeping her brother alive. She is watching him with her whole soul and arranging her face to say she is not. **"While they perceived not"** — the palace, with its midwives and its registers and its knives, is outmanoeuvred by a child pretending to be bored.

## Ayah 12: the nurses he would not take

Once Musa, peace be upon him, had settled into the house of Fir'awn, after the king's wife had begun to love him and had asked Fir'awn not to kill him, they brought him the wet nurses who were to be found in their household — and he did not accept any of them, refusing to take milk from them. So they took him out to the marketplace, hoping to find a woman who would be suitable to nurse him. When his sister saw him in their arms she recognised him, but she did not give any indication, nor did they suspect her.

**"And We had already forbidden foster suckling mothers for him."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is exact: because of Musa's honoured status with Allah, it was forbidden by divine decree. It was decreed that no one should nurse him except his own mother, and Allah caused this to be the means of reuniting him with his mother, so that she could nurse him and feel safe after having felt such fear. Look at what Allah used as the instrument of the promise made in ayah 7 — not an army, not a sign in the sky, but **a baby's refusal to feed.** And note *min qablu*, "already": the arrangement was in place before the confusion in the marketplace ever arose. The way out was prepared before the difficulty was felt.

Then the sister steps forward: **"Shall I direct you to a household who will rear him for you, and look after him in a good manner?"** Ibn 'Abbas relates that this nearly undid her. They had some doubts about her, so they seized her and asked: *How do you know these people will be sincere and will care for him?* She answered — with astonishing composure — that they would be sincere and would care for him **because they want the king to be happy and because they hope for some reward.** She gave them a motive they could believe, in their own currency. So they let her go.

Safe from their harm, they took her to their house and brought the baby to his mother. She gave him her breast and he accepted it. They rejoiced and sent the glad tidings to the wife of Fir'awn, who called for Musa's mother, treating her kindly and rewarding her generously — not realising she was his real mother, only that the baby had accepted her breast. Then Asiyah asked her to stay and nurse the baby there, but she refused, saying she had a husband and children and could not stay, though she would gladly nurse him in her own home. The wife of Fir'awn agreed, paid her a regular salary, gave her extra gifts and clothing, and treated her kindly.

So the mother came back with her child, happy that after a time of fear Allah had granted her security, prestige, and ongoing provision. And Ibn Kathir adds the detail that turns the whole episode into consolation: **there was only a short time between the distress and the way out — a day and a night, or thereabouts, and Allah knows best.**

## Ayah 13: the promise kept, and what she understood

**"So We restored him to his mother, that her eye might be comforted, and that she might not grieve."** Ibn Kathir ties both clauses back to the child: her eye comforted *by him*, her grief lifted *for him*. Read ayah 13 next to ayah 7 and you find the two prohibitions answered one by one — she was told "fear not, nor grieve," and here the fear ends in safety and the grief ends in her son at her breast.

**"And that she might know that the promise of Allah is true."** Ibn Kathir draws out the meaning: Allah had promised her to return him to her and to make him one of the Messengers. When he was returned to her, she realised that he was one of the Messengers. So, Ibn Kathir says, **as she brought him up she treated him both as a child, with kindness, and as a Messenger, with respect.** She was rearing a prophet of Allah in her own house, on a salary paid by Fir'awn's household.

**"But most of them know not."** Ibn Kathir explains: they do not know the wisdom of Allah in His actions and their good consequences, for which He is to be praised in this world and the Hereafter. For a thing may happen that people do not like, but its consequences are good. He cites Allah's own words: **"and it may be that you dislike a thing which is good for you, and that you like a thing which is bad for you"** (al-Baqarah 2:216), and **"it may be that you dislike a thing and Allah brings through it a great deal of good"** (an-Nisa' 4:19).

## Living it

Ibn Kathir pauses in the middle of this narrative to say something that reads like a summary of the whole passage: glory be to the One in whose hands are all things — what He wills happens and what He does not will does not happen; and He is the One who grants those who fear Him a way out from every worry and distress.

Three things this passage asks of a believer:

- **Do the frightening thing you have been shown to do.** She was told to put her child into the water — the very element of danger — and told in the same breath not to fear and not to grieve. Obedience did not wait for the fear to pass.
- **Expect the rescue to arrive by the strangest road.** Not away from Fir'awn's palace, but into it. Not by hiding the child, but by releasing him. Not by force, but by a nursing refusal and a sister's careful glance.
- **Do not judge an event by how it feels while it is happening.** Ayah 13 ends by telling us most people do not know — and the mother herself, in ayah 10, could not think of anything in the world but her lost son, right up until he was placed back in her arms. The distance between her worst hour and her best was about a day and a night.

passages.title: Moses kills the Egyptian and repents
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat carry Musa (peace be upon him) from the strength of his young manhood into the crisis that would drive him out of Egypt altogether: a man grown to full strength, a blow struck in defence of a fellow Israelite, a death he never intended, and — immediately — the turn back to his Lord in confession, forgiveness and a lifelong vow. What holds the passage together is that single movement from **power** (ayah 14) to **a wrong use of power** (ayah 15) to **repentance** (ayah 16) and finally to **a promise about how power will be used from now on** (ayah 17).

## Ayah 14: the man he became

"And when he reached full strength and maturity, We gave him wisdom and knowledge."

**أَشُدَّ (ashudd)** literally means to attain the peak of one's strength or intensity. A person develops gradually from the weakness of youth up to the strength of adulthood, and a time comes when he has attained all the strength and vigour he could achieve. That point in life is *ashudd*. Ma'arif ul Qur'an notes that it falls at different ages in different parts of the world and for different peoples — climate, the character of the land, and race all affect it; some attain it early, others take time. 'Abd ibn Humayd reported that Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid placed *ashudd* at the thirty-third year of life: the age of perfection, or the age of discernment, when the development of the body stops after reaching its peak. **وَاسْتَوَىٰ (istawa)** — "and became perfect" — is then the period of hold that follows, lasting until forty, after which decline and weakness set in (Ruh, Qurtubi).

So the Qur'an is not being vague here. It is telling us that when Musa acted in the next ayah, he was a man at the height of his physical strength.

**حُكْمًا وَعِلْمًا (hukman wa 'ilman).** Mujahid said that *hukm* here means prophethood; Ma'arif ul Qur'an takes the word the same way, with *'ilm* referring to knowledge of the divine injunctions. The gift is twofold: the office, and the understanding that fills it.

**"And thus do We reward the doers of good."** Ibn Kathir draws out what this sentence is quietly doing. Allah goes on to describe how Musa reached the status decreed for him — prophethood, and being spoken to by Allah — and Ibn Kathir says this came as a direct consequence of the killing of the Copt, since that was the reason he left Egypt and went to Madyan. The worst moment of his life is the road to the highest station of his life. That is not an excuse for the act; it is a statement about how Allah runs the affairs of those He has chosen.

## Ayah 15: the city, the hour, the blow

**"And he entered the city…"** Most commentators take "the city" to be the main city of Egypt (Ma'arif ul Qur'an). The words "he entered" indicate that Musa had gone away somewhere outside it. Ma'arif ul Qur'an reports a narration quoted by Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Zayd that fills the gap: when Musa had started speaking to people about the true religion, Pharaoh turned against him and wanted to kill him — but on the appeal of Pharaoh's wife, Sayyidah 'Asiyah, Pharaoh restrained himself and commanded him to go into exile instead. Musa then shifted to a hiding place and would come to the city occasionally, in hiding. This reading is supported, Ma'arif notes, by the words **مِن شِيعَتِهِ** ("of his group") in this very ayah: some people had accepted his preaching and were known as his disciples.

Note the honest difference here. Ibn Kathir's presentation places prophethood after this episode, as its eventual consequence; the narration of Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Zayd cited by Ma'arif ul Qur'an has Musa already announcing his prophethood before it. Both are transmitted from early authorities.

**عَلَىٰ حِينِ غَفْلَةٍ — "at a time of unawareness of its people."** What hour was that? Ibn Kathir gives two chains, both back to Ibn 'Abbas: Ibn Jurayj narrated from 'Ata' al-Khurasani, "That was between Maghrib and 'Isha'"; Ibn al-Munkadir narrated from 'Ata' ibn Yasar, "That was in the middle of the day" — which was also the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah, as-Suddi and Qatadah. Ma'arif ul Qur'an says most commentators take it as the afternoon, when people generally take a siesta (Qurtubi). Either way, the picture is the same: a time when people normally sleep, and a man moving through the city in hiding.

**"And he found there two men fighting."** Ibn Kathir explains *yaqtatilan* as hitting one another and struggling with one another. One was **of his party**, meaning an Israelite; the other **of his foes**, meaning a Copt — this was the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, as-Suddi and Muhammad ibn Ishaq. The Israelite asked Musa for help, and Musa, Ibn Kathir notes, took advantage of the fact that people were not paying attention.

**فَوَكَزَهُ مُوسَىٰ فَقَضَىٰ عَلَيْهِ.** Ibn Kathir records Mujahid's gloss on *wakaza*: "This means he punched him with his fist." Ma'arif ul Qur'an says *wakaza* means to box. And **قَضَىٰ عَلَيْهِ**: the expression *qada 'alayhi* is used when someone is totally finished, so here it means that he killed him (Mazhari). One blow, struck to free the Israelite from the man's grip, and a life was over.

**"This is of Shaytan's doing; verily he is a plain misleading enemy."** Musa does not begin with self-defence. His first words name the hand behind what has happened.

## Ayah 16: why a prophet called this a sin

"He said: My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me. Then He forgave him. Verily, He is the Oft-Forgiving, the Most Merciful."

This is where the commentary goes deepest, because a real difficulty stands here. Ma'arif ul Qur'an states it plainly: Musa (peace be upon him) regarded the killing of the Copt as a sin **despite the fact that it had happened without any intention on his part**, because it was in conflict with his status of prophethood and below its dignity — and so he begged Allah's pardon, which was duly granted.

**The objection.** In the language of the law, this Copt was a *harbi* — an unbelieving combatant, neither a *dhimmi* (a non-Muslim citizen of an Islamic state) nor under any covenant with Musa. On the face of it, his killing was permissible, even preferable: he was harming a Muslim unjustly, and he was killed in the process while Musa was trying to save that man's life. So why did Musa regard it as his own wrong and as an act of Shaytan?

**The answer: the covenant that is never written down.** Ma'arif ul Qur'an answers that covenants of peace are of two kinds. Some are written or spoken in express words. Others come into effect through the consistent practice of the parties, which amounts to an implied agreement and is as good as a written covenant; violating that kind is likewise prohibited in Islam. If in a non-Islamic state Muslims and non-Muslims live in harmony without conflict, and any pillage or fighting between them would be regarded as treachery, then this consistent practice of co-existence is itself an implied agreement for peaceful living, and its violation is not allowed.

**The proof from the Sunnah.** Ma'arif ul Qur'an grounds this in a lengthy hadith of Sayyiduna Mughirah ibn Shu'bah reported by Imam Bukhari in the chapter entitled *Kitab ash-Shurut* (the Book of Conditions). Mughirah had good relations with a group of unbelievers before the advent of Islam; later he killed them and took possession of all their wealth. He then went to the Prophet ﷺ, submitted to Islam, and presented that wealth to him. The Prophet ﷺ said to him: "As far as your embracing Islam is concerned, I accept it, but I have nothing to do with this wealth." Abu Dawud has quoted the hadith with the wording: "As for wealth, we have no concern with it." The wealth had been taken by breach of trust and was treachery, and so he ﷺ had no desire for it. Hafiz Ibn Hajar observed in his commentary that this hadith lays down the principle that seizing the wealth of unbelievers during peacetime is not permissible — for the simple reason that people living together in a city or township, or working together, regard themselves as secure from one another, and the agreement established through their practice is like a trust which every person must honour, Muslim or not. The property of unbelievers permitted to Muslims is only what is acquired during a war with them. Qastalani observed the same in his commentary on Bukhari: the wealth of the idolaters may be taken as spoils in a state of war, but taking it is not lawful in a state of security; a person living and socialising with them such that each is safe from the other may not shed their blood or seize their wealth — that would be treachery and forbidden — unless the peace established through practice is openly renounced.

**Putting it together.** Ma'arif ul Qur'an sums up: had the Copt been killed with preconceived resolve while this implied peace stood, it would not have been lawful. But Musa had no intention of killing him. He only hit him with his bare hands to save the Israelite from his grip. In the normal course such a blow should not have been fatal, yet the man died by it. Musa then realised that a lighter blow would also have done the job; and realising that the harder blow was not needed, he repented and invoked Allah's mercy.

**A second view.** Ma'arif ul Qur'an also reports (from Ruh) that some commentators observed that although the killing of the Copt was permissible, prophets take extra care in special cases even with permissible acts and avoid them unless they receive a cue from Allah. On this occasion Musa did not wait for that permission and acted on his own; and so, in view of his status as a prophet, he maintained that it was a sin on his part and invoked Allah's pardon. Both explanations are transmitted; the Qur'an gives us Musa's verdict on himself, not a legal file.

**How this teaching reached us.** Ma'arif ul Qur'an carries a personal note here. Its author records that this principle of the implied covenant was explained to him by Sayyidi Maulana Ashraf Thanivi (may Allah have mercy on him) while he was writing the commentary on Surah al-Qasas in *Ahkamul-Qur'an*, the Arabic commentary written under Maulana Thanivi's supervision. It was the last scholarly benefit he received from him: that work was completed on 2 Rajab 1362 AH, after which Maulana Thanivi's sickness intensified, and on 16 Rajab 1362 he passed away. *Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un.*

**Read the du'a again.** "My Lord, I have wronged myself" — not *I wronged him*, and not a word of blame for the Israelite who called him in, nor for the Copt who started it. He owns the whole thing as damage done to his own soul. There is no bargaining and no listing of circumstances — only confession and a request. And the response comes inside the same ayah: **فَغَفَرَ لَهُ**, "Then He forgave him," followed by the reason it happened — *Verily, He is the Oft-Forgiving, the Most Merciful*. The forgiveness rests on who Allah is.

## Ayah 17: the vow that comes out of gratitude

"He said: My Lord, for that with which You have favoured me, I will nevermore be a helper of the criminals."

Ibn Kathir explains "for that with which You have favoured me" as what Allah had given him of prestige, power and blessings; and "a helper of the criminals" as those who disbelieve in Allah and go against His commands.

Two things are worth noticing. First, this is **an act of gratitude, not of guilt**. Ma'arif ul Qur'an points out that when Allah pardoned this slip, Musa said in gratitude to Allah that he would never again help a criminal — the natural reply of a servant who has just been forgiven is to bind his own future.

Second, it is **specific**. Ibn 'Abbas, explaining this ayah, held that the word for criminals, *mujrimin*, stands here for the unbelievers; Qatadah interpreted it in almost the same way. On the basis of these commentaries, Ma'arif ul Qur'an observes that the Israelite whom Musa had defended was in fact not a Muslim — Musa helped him considering that he was an oppressed person. And the second incident of the quarrel that follows proved that this man was quarrelsome; so in declaring him a criminal, Musa vowed not to help such a person again.

## Living it

Ma'arif ul Qur'an draws two rulings from this one saying of Musa (peace be upon him), and they belong together:

- **Even if an oppressed person is a sinner or an unbeliever, he should be helped.** Musa's intervention in ayah 15 is not what he repents of. Being wronged is itself a claim on you.
- **It is not permitted to help any criminal or oppressor.** Scholars have argued on the basis of this ayah that working in the employment of cruel rulers is also not permitted, since such people would be regarded as their associates; Ma'arif ul Qur'an notes that many citations from the righteous *salaf* have been quoted in support of this argument (Ruh ul-Ma'ani). Support for oppressors or unbelievers may take different forms, and the detailed rulings on each are laid down in the books of *fiqh*; Ma'arif ul Qur'an's author adds that he has dealt with the subject at greater length in his Arabic book *Ahkamul-Qur'an*, and directs interested scholars there.

There is a third lesson the passage teaches by its shape rather than by a ruling. A man of great strength, acting from a good motive, struck harder than was needed and a man died. He did not manage the story or minimise it. He said *this is of Shaytan's doing*, then *I have wronged myself, so forgive me*, and then bound himself for the future. Confession, forgiveness, changed conduct — three ayat, in that order. And in Ibn Kathir's reading, the very road out of that failure was the road to Madyan, to prophethood, and to being spoken to by Allah.

passages.title: Warned of the plot, Moses flees Egypt
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat carry Musa (peace be upon him) from the morning after the killing of the Copt to the moment he slips out of Egypt as a hunted man. What holds them together is a single phrase that opens the passage and closes it: **khā'ifan yataraqqab** — "fearful, watching out." In ayah 18 he is fearful and watchful *inside* the city; in ayah 21 he is fearful and watchful *leaving* it. Everything between those two occurrences is the story of how the secret came out and how Allah got him out alive.

## Ayah 18: the morning after

Ibn Kathir sets the scene with a single clause: "when Musa killed that Coptic." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that this was a brawl Musa had involved himself in on the side of an Israelite, and that Allah pardoned that slip of Musa (peace be upon him).

Ayah 18 picks up the next morning. Ibn Kathir explains **fī al-madīnati khā'ifan** — "he became afraid in the city" — as fear "of the consequences of his action," and **yataraqqab** — usually translated "looking about" or "watching out" — as "turning around and watching out, waiting for the consequences of his action to befall him."

Sit with that second gloss. Waiting for consequences is a particular kind of fear: not dread of the unknown, but the alertness of someone expecting something specific. A prophet of Allah is shown to us in this state, and the Qur'an does not soften it.

Then, says Ibn Kathir, "he went out and about, and saw the man who sought his help the day before, fighting with another Coptic." The very same Israelite. Same man, a new fight, a new opponent. And when Musa passes by, the man calls for his help again.

## The vow of ayah 17, and what the second fight proved

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads ayah 18 in the light of what Musa had just said in ayah 17: **"O my Lord, since You have favoured me, I will never be a supporter to the sinners."** When Allah pardoned this slip of Musa (peace be upon him), he said in gratitude that he would never again help a criminal.

The commentary then makes a sharp observation: the second quarrel *proved* the point. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says this second incident "had proved that the Israelite in whose defence Musa (peace be upon him) had involved himself in the brawl was quarrelsome. Therefore, by declaring him a criminal he vowed not to help such a person again."

On the identity of the "criminals" (*al-mujrimīn*) in that vow, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that **Ibn ʿAbbās** (may Allah be pleased with him) held that the word here stands for the disbelievers, and that **Qatādah** interpreted it in almost the same way. On the basis of those two early readings, the commentary offers a careful inference — it says "it seems" — that the Israelite Musa had defended "was not a Muslim, but he helped him considering that he was an oppressed person."

Notice what that means. On this reading, Musa did not step in because the man shared his faith. He stepped in because the man was being wronged.

## Two rulings drawn from one sentence

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says that this single saying of Musa (peace be upon him) has established rulings on two distinct issues:

**One — the oppressed are to be helped even when they are sinners or disbelievers.** Wrongdoing is wrong regardless of who is on the receiving end. The victim's faith and character are not a filter through which his right to protection must pass.

**Two — it is not permitted to help any criminal or oppressor.** This is the flip side, and it is where the ruling bites. Being the one who is *wronged* earns support; being the one doing the *wronging* forfeits it.

From this second ruling, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, scholars have argued that **working in the employment of cruel rulers is also not permitted**, since such employees "would be regarded as their associates," and it notes that many citations from the righteous *salaf* (the early generations) have been quoted in support of this — attributing the discussion to *Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī*. The commentary is careful to add that supporting oppressors or disbelievers "may take different forms," and that the rulings for those different forms are laid out in detail in the books of *fiqh* (Islamic jurisprudence); the author refers readers to his own Arabic work *Aḥkām ul-Qurʼān* for fuller treatment.

That caution matters. The principle is clear; its application to a particular job, contract, or situation is a detailed legal question, not something to settle from a paragraph.

## "Verily, you are a plain misleader"

So when the Israelite cries for help a second time, Musa says: **innaka la-ghawiyyun mubīn** — "Verily, you are a plain misleader!" Ibn Kathir glosses it: "you obviously lead people astray and are very evil."

The word *mubīn* — "plain," "manifest" — matches Ibn Kathir's "obviously." This is not a suspicion Musa is voicing; on Ibn Kathir's reading it is something out in the open.

## Ayah 19: the secret escapes

And yet — this is the moving detail — Musa *still* moves to act. Ibn Kathir: "Then Musa intended to attack that Coptic." The ayah calls that Copt **alladhī huwa ʿaduwwun lahumā**, "the one who was an enemy to both of them." Musa rebukes the Israelite and still turns toward the man who is an enemy to them both.

What happens next is a small masterpiece of unintended consequence. The Israelite, says Ibn Kathir, "because of his own cowardice and weakness, thought that Musa wanted to hit *him* because of what he had said." So he blurts out in self-defence:

**"O Musa! Is it your intention to kill me as you killed a man yesterday? Your aim is nothing but to become a tyrant in the land, and not to be one of those who do right."**

Read that again with Ibn Kathir's next line beside it: "Nobody except him and Musa, peace be upon him, knew about it." The killing was a secret between two people. One of those two people has just shouted it in the street — while accusing the man who had stepped in for him twice of wanting to be a tyrant rather than one of the righteous.

"But when the other Coptic heard this," Ibn Kathir continues, "he took the news to Firʿawn's gate and told him about it. So Firʿawn came to know of it, and he became very angry and resolved to kill Musa, so he sent people after him to bring him to him."

A panicked sentence from a frightened man reaches Firʿawn's gate, and Firʿawn sends men after Musa. The passage is quietly honest about how fragile human plans are: the secret was not uncovered by a spy or an investigation, but by the tongue of the very person Musa had defended.

## Ayah 20: the man from the farthest end of the city

Now the counterweight. **"And there came a man, rushing from the farthest end of the city."**

Ibn Kathir pauses on the word **rajul**, "a man." Why is he described that way? Because "he had the courage to take a different route, a shorter route than those who were sent after Musa, so he reached Musa first." On Ibn Kathir's reading, then, the description points to courage — and courage spent on someone else's rescue. He is unnamed, he appears for one ayah, and his warning is what gets a prophet out.

Two things about him deserve notice. He came **from the farthest end of the city** — the whole width of it lay between him and Musa. And he came **running**.

His message is precise:

- **"Verily, the chiefs are taking counsel together about you"** — *yaʾtamirūna bika*, which Ibn Kathir explains as "they are consulting with one another about you." The *malaʾ* — the Arabic word rendered here as "the chiefs," the leading men around Firʿawn. This is not a rumour on the street; it is a consultation at the top.
- **"to kill you, so escape"** — and Ibn Kathir specifies what "escape" means here: "from this land." Not hide, not lie low. Leave.
- **"Truly, I am one of the good advisers to you."** He tells Musa why he should be believed. In a city where a man had just carried news straight to Firʿawn's gate, someone who runs the other way — to warn rather than to report — has to say plainly which side he is on.

## Ayah 21: out of Egypt, with nothing

**"So he escaped from there, looking about in a state of fear"** — Ibn Kathir again: "meaning, turning around and watching." The same phrase as ayah 18, now carried out of the city gates.

And Ibn Kathir adds a line about the cost of that departure that is easy to skim past: "he left Egypt on his own. He was not used to being alone, because before that he had been living a life of luxury and ease, in a position of leadership."

That is the whole reversal in one sentence. Accustomed to comfort and standing, Musa walks out alone — with men sent after him.

What he has instead is a sentence: **"My Lord! Save me from the people who are wrongdoers!"** — *Rabbi najjinī min al-qawmi al-ẓālimīn*. Ibn Kathir identifies exactly who is meant: "from Firʿawn and his chiefs."

Note the shape of this *duʿāʾ* — the Arabic word for supplication, the act of calling on Allah and asking Him. Musa does not ask for a route, a companion, a plan, or revenge. He asks to be *saved* from a named danger, and he opens with **Rabbi** — "my Lord" — the address of someone who has nothing left but a relationship.

Ibn Kathir then reports, with appropriate reserve: "It was mentioned that Allah sent to him an angel riding a horse, who showed him the way. And Allah knows best." That closing phrase is the scholar's own signal — the report is passed on, not asserted as certain. It is a good habit to imitate when we speak about matters we have only received.

## What this passage asks of us

**Help the wronged because he is wronged.** On the reading Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws from Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatādah, the man Musa defended was not a Muslim; Musa helped him "considering that he was an oppressed person." And when that same man was found brawling a second time, Musa called him a plain misleader and — as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it — declared him a criminal he would not support again. The commentary turns this into a plain rule: the oppressed is helped even if he is a sinner or a disbeliever, and no criminal or oppressor is to be helped at all.

**Weigh who you lend your strength to.** The ruling reported from *Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī* — that entering the employment of tyrannical rulers makes one their associate — is the passage's uncomfortable edge. Support for the oppressor takes many forms, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sends the reader to the books of *fiqh* rather than to a slogan. The habit to build is the question itself: whose hand am I strengthening?

**Fear and faith are not opposites.** Ayah 18 and ayah 21 both leave Musa "fearful, watching out," and the Qur'an records it plainly. A prophet felt the danger fully, took the practical step the warner urged — he left the land — and prayed as he went. Reliance on Allah did not replace caution or effort; it accompanied them.

**Be the man from the farthest end of the city.** Someone had to cross a city and take the shorter, riskier road. He gets one ayah, no name, and the honour of being called simply *a man*.

**And when everything is gone, you still have "Rabbi."** Stripped of the comfort and leadership he was used to, with Firʿawn's men behind him, Musa had a single word to open with. Ibn Kathir, commenting on what follows, says Musa then turned towards Madyan saying "It may be that my Lord guides me to the right way" — and that "Allah did indeed do that, for He guided him to the straight path in this world and the Hereafter, and caused him to be guided and to guide others."

passages.title: Moses reaches Midian and waters the flock
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat follow Musa (peace be upon him) out of Egypt as a hunted fugitive and set him down at a well in a foreign town — where the first thing he does, before eating, before resting, before asking anyone for anything, is help two strangers with their sheep. What holds the passage together is a single movement of the heart: a man with nothing turns to his Lord (ayah 22), notices someone else's difficulty before his own (ayah 23), serves them without being asked and without asking for payment (ayah 24), and only then quietly lays his own need before Allah.

## Backdrop: a man alone on the road

Ibn Kathir sets the scene in a line. When a man told Musa how Fir'awn and his chiefs were conspiring against him, he left Egypt on his own — and Ibn Kathir draws attention to how hard that must have been: he was not used to being alone, because before that he had been living a life of luxury and ease, in a position of leadership.

That is the state in which our passage opens.

## "It may be that my Lord will guide me" (ayah 22)

**وَلَمَّا تَوَجَّهَ تِلْقَاءَ مَدْيَنَ** — "and when he went towards Madyan."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān supplies the geography. Madyan was a city in Sham — the large territory now consisting of Syria, Jordan, Lebanon and Palestine — named after Madyan, the son of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). Crucially, it lay outside the empire of the Pharaoh, and it was eight days' journey from Egypt. Perhaps, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, Musa decided to head for Madyan because it was a habitation of the descendants of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and he too was of that progeny: a fugitive heading, however faintly, towards kin.

He set out in a condition with neither provisions for the journey nor baggage — and he did not know the route. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that scholars have observed the only food he had during this journey was the leaves of trees, and that Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said this was the first trial and test of Musa (peace be upon him).

**On fear and trust.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a point worth pausing over. It describes Musa as taken over by the natural fright of the pursuing army of the Pharaoh — and adds that this fright "was not in conflict either with the prophethood or with trust in Allah." He runs, and while running he prays; the tafsir sees no contradiction between the two.

Of his turning towards Madyan Ibn Kathir says: he took a smooth and easy route, and he rejoiced because of that. A small mercy inside a large fear, and he noticed it.

Then comes the sentence that gives the ayah its flavour: **عَسَىٰ رَبِّي أَن يَهْدِيَنِي سَوَاءَ السَّبِيلِ**. Ibn Kathir renders it, "It may be that my Lord guides me to the right way"; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, "I hope my Lord will guide me to the straight path." Either way, Musa does not announce that he knows where he is going, nor does he frame it as a demand. He says, in effect: *I have no map, but I have a Lord.* And he says **rabbī** — "my Lord" — a man with nothing else to his name.

Ibn Kathir glosses **sawāʼ al-sabīl** as "the most straight route." Musa asked for a road through the desert; and Ibn Kathir then lifts the answer far above the desert: "And Allah did indeed do that, for He guided him to the straight path in this world and the Hereafter, and caused him to be guided and to guide others." The man who did not know which way to walk was made a guide for others. That is what it looks like when Allah answers a prayer more generously than it was asked. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same in its own words: in that state of helplessness he turned to Allah with this prayer, and Allah accepted it.

## At the well of Madyan (ayah 23)

**وَلَمَّا وَرَدَ مَاءَ مَدْيَنَ** — "and when he arrived at the water of Madyan." Ibn Kathir explains: he reached Madyan and went to drink from its water, for it had a well where shepherds used to water their flocks. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same — "the water of Madyan" refers to the well from where the people of that place used to make their animals drink.

The scene is drawn in two halves. First, **أُمَّةً مِّنَ النَّاسِ يَسْقُونَ** — a whole group of people watering. Then, set apart from them, **امْرَأَتَيْنِ تَذُودَانِ** — two women *keeping back*. Ibn Kathir: they were stopping their sheep from drinking with the sheep of those shepherds, lest some harm come to them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: he saw two girls stopping their goats from going to the water, so that they did not get mixed up with other goats.

And the little phrase **مِن دُونِهِمُ** — "besides them," aloof from them — tells you their whole position: two women waiting at the edge of a crowded place, unable to get near. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it plainly: they had brought their goats for drinking water, but they were unable to find room because of the rush of people.

Ibn Kathir records Musa's reaction in one line: when he saw them, he felt sorry for them and took pity on them. He is hunted, unfed and far from home — and his first instinct is compassion for someone else.

**مَا خَطْبُكُمَا** — "What is the matter with you?" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the word *khatb* means "matter," and unpacks the question as: what is it that makes you stop your goats from coming to the well to drink like the other goats? Ibn Kathir gives the same sense: why do you not water your flocks with these people?

Their answer is two short sentences, and the second explains the first. **لَا نَسْقِي حَتَّىٰ يُصْدِرَ الرِّعَاءُ** — "we cannot water until the shepherds take (their flocks)," that is, as Ibn Kathir puts it, we cannot water our flocks until they finish; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that in order to avoid mixing with the men-folk they used to make their goats wait until the men had left the place after watering their animals. Then: **وَأَبُونَا شَيْخٌ كَبِيرٌ** — "and our father is a very old man." Ibn Kathir catches the force of it exactly: this means, *this is what has driven us to what you see.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it as an answer to the unspoken question of whether there was no male member of the family to do this job: their father was very old and could not perform it, and that is why they were doing it.

### Four points Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws from this scene

1. **It was the practice of the prophets to help the weak.** Musa saw that two girls had brought their goats for water but could find no room because of the rush of people, so he asked them about their problem.
2. **There is no harm in talking to stranger women, if no mischief is involved.** Musa's question and their reply are recorded in the Qur'an itself.
3. **The spirit of modesty preceded the ruling of hijab.** This incident happened when hijab was not enjoined — a situation that continued even into the early days of Islam, since hijab was enjoined in Madinah after the Hijrah. Yet the underlying spirit of hijab, the natural instinct of modesty and bashfulness, was there even in those days: because of it these two preferred hardship over getting mixed with the men-folk.
4. **It was not considered desirable for women even in those days to go out and perform such duties,** which is why they put forward the justification that their father was very old and weak.

## The stone, the shade, and the prayer (ayah 24)

**فَسَقَىٰ لَهُمَا** — "so he watered (their flocks) for them." Two words. No negotiation, no conditions, no mention of a fee. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: Musa took pity on the girls, drew water from the well and satiated their goats.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then reports, citing Qurtubi, that it is related in some narrations that the shepherds, after watering their cattle, used to place a very heavy stone over the mouth of the well to make it unusable, so that these girls would have only the leftover water for their herd. The stone was so heavy that ten men together could move it — and Musa removed it all by himself and drew the water. Perhaps for this reason, Qurtubi suggests, one of the two girls later reported to her father that Musa was very strong. (This is a narration passed on in the tafsir, offered as a possible explanation, not a matter of creed.)

Then: **ثُمَّ تَوَلَّىٰ إِلَى الظِّلِّ** — "then he turned back to shade." Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and As-Suddi (may Allah be pleased with them) said: "He sat beneath a tree."

Look at the sequence. He does not follow the women. He does not stand there waiting to be thanked. He does the work and withdraws. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān tells us the state he withdrew in: he had not had any food for the last seven days.

**رَّبِّ إِنِّي لِمَا أَنزَلْتَ إِلَيَّ مِنْ خَيْرٍ فَقِيرٌ** — "My Lord! Truly, I am in need of whatever good that You bestow on me."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says he came under the shade of a tree and prayed to Allah, describing his condition and need "in an exquisite manner" — and the phrase is well chosen. Notice what the sentence does *not* contain: no specific demand, no list, no bargaining over the service he has just rendered. He states his condition — *I am faqīr*, in need — and leaves the rest with Allah. He does not tell his Lord what to send; he only says that whatever good comes down, he is in need of it. And he says **rabbī** again, exactly as he did on the road in ayah 22.

**What is the "good" (khayr) he is asking for?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, again citing Qurtubi, notes that the word *khayr* is used in different senses: sometimes for wealth, as in "he leaves some wealth" (2:180); sometimes for strength, as in "are they better, or the people of Tubbaʿ?" (44:37); and here, in this ayah, for food. A man who had not eaten for seven days, sitting under a tree, asking for something to eat — in language so restrained that you could read past the hunger entirely.

Ibn Kathir preserves one further detail, from 'Ata' bin As-Sa'ib: when Musa said these words, **the women heard him.** He had addressed his need to his Lord, not to them — and yet those words did not stay private.

## Living it

- **Pray while you run.** Musa is frightened, unfed and without a route, and treats none of that as an obstacle to turning to Allah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit that his natural fright was in no conflict with prophethood or with trust in Allah. Move, and say with him: *it may be that my Lord will guide me.*
- **Ask small, and let Allah answer large.** He asked for a road; Ibn Kathir says Allah guided him to the straight path in this world and the Hereafter, and caused him to be guided and to guide others. Never shrink a request because your situation feels small.
- **Notice the person at the edge.** There was a crowd at that well, and two women who could find no room in the rush of it. A stranger with nothing arrived and saw them, and felt pity. Helping the weak, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, was the practice of the prophets.
- **Serve, then step back.** فَسَقَىٰ لَهُمَا ثُمَّ تَوَلَّىٰ — he watered for them, then withdrew. No fee, no lingering, no waiting for gratitude. He took his need straight to Allah rather than presenting it to the people he had just helped.

passages.title: The invitation, the hire, and the marriage
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat carry Musa (peace be upon him) from being a stranger who had just fled his country to being a man with work, a household and a wife. The bundle's own heading for the passage names its three movements: the invitation, the hire, and the marriage. The thread running through all of them is **character recognised and rewarded**: what Musa did at the well is reported to the girls' father, and it is answered with an invitation, a job offer, and a proposal of marriage.

## The scene the ayat assume

Ibn Kathir fills in what the Qur'an leaves out. When the two women came back quickly with the sheep, their father was surprised that they had returned so soon. He asked them what had happened, and they told him what Musa (peace be upon him) had done. So he sent one of them to call him to meet her father. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same background and adds the reason for the summons: in keeping with Qur'anic practice the story has been summarised here, and the father thought he should make up for the favour Musa had done his daughters.

**Who was the father?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is candid that the commentators hold different views on this, but notes (citing Qurtubi) that the Qur'anic verses allude to his being Shuʿayb (peace be upon him), on the evidence of 7:85. Ibn Kathir simply calls him "this old man" and, later, Musa's "father-in-law". It is honest to hold the identification the way the sources hold it — as what the wording alludes to, rather than as an explicitly stated fact.

## Ayah 25: how a woman speaks to a stranger

The ayah describes her approach with a single phrase: *tamshī ʿalā istiḥyāʾ* — "walking bashfully", "walking shyly", "walking with shyness" in the renderings the commentators use.

Ibn Kathir explains the phrase to mean **she was walking like a free woman**, and reports from the Commander of the Faithful ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him): "She was covering herself from them with the folds of her garment." He then gives the fuller narration: Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from ʿAmr bin Maymun that ʿUmar said, "She came walking shyly, putting her garment over her face. She was not one of those audacious women who come and go as they please." Ibn Kathir adds that this chain of narrators is *Sahih*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the implication that is easy to miss: **hijab had not been enjoined by then**, and yet good women would not talk to men freely. She had come with a need, so she spoke with shyness. Some commentators give the detail of that shyness — that as she spoke she had raised her sleeve up to her face.

Then look at what she actually says: **"My father is calling you, so that he may reward you for having watered our flocks for us."** Ibn Kathir calls this an example of good manners — *she did not invite him directly, lest he have some suspicious thoughts about her.* Rather she said: "My father is inviting you so that he may reward you for watering our sheep," that is, give you some payment for it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same observation from the other side: it was possible for her to have invited him on her own, but she did not; she conveyed her father's message instead, because it was against modesty for a girl to invite a stranger home. The summons is her father's, and the reason given is payment owed.

There is a thread in the Arabic here too. She speaks of *ajr mā saqayta* — the **wage** for what he watered. The same root then runs through the passage: *istaʾjirhu* (hire him) in ayah 26, *taʾjuranī* (you serve me for hire) in ayah 27. What begins as an offer of payment for watering a flock becomes, by the end of the passage, eight years of employment — ten if he chose — and a marriage.

## "Fear not — you have escaped the wrongdoing people"

When Musa arrived, he **narrated the story** — which Ibn Kathir explains to mean that he told the old man about his story and why he had to leave his country. The reply is: *"Do not fear. You have escaped from the people who are wrongdoers."*

Ibn Kathir renders the sense as: *calm down and relax, for you have left their kingdom and they have no authority in our land.* It is a plain, practical reassurance: the reach of those he fled stops at this border. The old man begins with the man's safety.

## Ayah 26: the two words that decide everything

Then one of the daughters speaks — Ibn Kathir notes that it was said she was the one who had walked behind Musa (peace be upon him). She says: **"O my father, hire him! Verily, the best of men for you to hire is the strong, the trustworthy."** Ibn Kathir explains *istaʾjirhu* concretely: hire him as a shepherd to look after the sheep.

Her two words are *al-qawiyy* (the strong) and *al-amīn* (the trustworthy) — **capability and integrity**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that she is naming the two qualities required in a servant, and that she had seen both in him: his strength when he removed the stone from the mouth of the well, and his integrity when he made her walk behind him.

**How did she know?** Ibn Kathir reports from ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbas, Shurayh al-Qadi, Abu Malik, Qatadah, Muhammad bin Ishaq and others that when she said this, her father asked her, "What do you know about that?" She answered: "He lifted a rock which could only be lifted by ten men, and when I came back with him, I walked ahead of him, but he said to me: walk behind me, and if I get confused about the route, throw a pebble so that I will know which way to go."

That answer is the whole of her case. **Strength** she saw at the well. **Trustworthiness** she saw on the road home — he arranged the walk so that she was behind him, and solved the problem of directions with a thrown pebble. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the narrations relate exactly this, that the objective was that he could not cast his eye on her, and that perhaps for this reason she told her father he was trustworthy.

**The praise of her discernment.** ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud said: "The people who had the most discernment were three: Abu Bakr's intuition about ʿUmar; the companion of Yusuf when he said, *Make his stay comfortable*; and the companion of Musa, when she said: *O my father, hire him! Verily, the best of men for you to hire is the strong, the trustworthy.*" One of the three is this young woman.

**Living it.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān turns this straight onto us. In the present set-up of employment, great emphasis is laid at interview on scrutinising a candidate's degrees and experience, but no attention is paid to ascertaining his integrity and trustworthiness; as a result there is neither efficiency nor honesty of purpose in the offices, while bribery and nepotism are so common that there seems to be no law in operation. If people could pay heed to this Qur'anic verse, it says, many problems would be solved automatically. Both qualities are asked for, not one.

## Ayah 27: the proposal

Ibn Kathir summarises the arrangement: this old man asked Musa to take care of his flocks, and then he would marry one of his two daughters to him. On the terms — *"eight years; but if you complete ten years, it will be a favour from you"* — Ibn Kathir explains: on the condition that you tend my flocks for eight years, and if you want to give me two extra years, that is up to you, but if you do not want to, eight years is enough. And on *"I intend not to place you under a difficulty"*: 'I do not want to put pressure on you or cause you any inconvenience or argue with you.' He closes with *"If Allah wills, you will find me one of the righteous"* — a promise of good conduct immediately handed back to Allah's will.

Several things in this ayah repay attention.

**A father may take the initiative.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that Shuʿayb (peace be upon him) made the proposal of marriage of his daughter on his own. This shows that a girl's guardian need not wait for the proposal to come from the boy's side; if a suitable good match is available, the guardian may take the lead, for this has been the practice of the prophets. It cites (from Qurtubi) the example of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), who offered his daughter Hafsah (may Allah be pleased with her) in marriage to Abu Bakr and to ʿUthman (may Allah be pleased with them) when she became a widow.

**Why "one of these two daughters of mine"?** Shuʿayb (peace be upon him) did not select one girl or the other; he kept it unspecified.
