Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that this was **not the formal nikah** — which requires offer and acceptance in the presence of two witnesses — but only a discussion to obtain Musa's consent to work for eight years in exchange for marriage to one of the girls. Musa agreed to the proposal and was married to one of them. The Holy Qur'an does not describe every detail of a story when the context makes it obvious, so it cannot be doubted here on the grounds that no bride was pinpointed and no witnesses mentioned. (Ruh, Bayan ul Qurʼan.)

**Was the service the mahr?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states that the eight years of service and employment was regarded as the *mahr* (the dower) of the marriage — and it is careful here, because scholars have different points of view on whether service rendered to one's wife can be taken as a valid mahr. Imam Abu Hanifah ruled in his *Zahir al-Riwayah* that service rendered for one's wife cannot be considered a valid mahr. In a later ruling by the scholars it is elaborated that although it is against the honour and dignity of a husband to serve his wife in lieu of mahr, any duty performed **outside** the house — such as grazing cattle or trading — can be made a substitute for it, provided a time frame is agreed beforehand, as in the case of Musa, where the parties had agreed beforehand on an eight-year period of service; the reason being that the husband's remuneration payable by his wife is then treated as mahr (Badaʾiʿ, from Nawadir Ibn Samaʿah). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also offers the plain resolution for the common reader: if it is not allowed in the Muhammadi law, it might have been permitted in the code of law followed by Shuʿayb (peace be upon him) — it is not uncommon to have minor differences in the laws brought by various prophets.

**But the mahr is the right of the wife.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the objection itself: the words *an taʾjuranī* ("that you serve **me**") prove that Shuʿayb had hired him, so the benefit of the service went to the father — how then could this be the wife's mahr? Two answers: it is quite probable that the herd was the property of the girls, so the benefit of the service went to the wife; or, if the goats belonged to the father and the wages were due from him, then those wages belonged to the daughter as her mahr — and it is lawful for a father to spend his daughter's money with her permission. It is quite obvious, it adds, that the whole deal was carried out with the consent of the girl.

**A ruling drawn from the wording.** From *unkiḥaka* ("I wish to marry you to…"), Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the father arranged the nikah, and that the jurists are unanimous that it should be done in this way: it is the father's duty and privilege to make arrangements for his daughter's marriage, and a girl should not arrange her own. Where they differ is whether a nikah a girl arranges for herself, under some need or pressure, is lawful — Imam Abu Hanifah ruled that it is. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, with integrity, that **this verse is silent on the issue**.

## Why Musa hired himself out

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that ʿAli bin Rabah al-Lakhmi said: "I heard ʿUtbah bin an-Nadar as-Sulami, the Companion of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, narrating that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *Musa, peace be upon him, hired himself out for the purpose of keeping chaste and to feed himself.*"

Two purposes, and no more: chastity and bread. A prophet of Allah tended another man's flocks for exactly that.

## Ayah 28: how Musa closes the deal

Musa's reply is short and precise: *"That is settled between me and you: whichever of the two terms I fulfil, there will be no injustice to me, and Allah is Surety over what we say."*

Ibn Kathir puts his words into plain speech: Musa said to his father-in-law, "The matter is as you say. You have hired me for eight years, and if I complete ten years, that is my choice, but if I do the lesser amount, I will still have fulfilled the covenant and met the conditions." On *"there will be no injustice to me"* he explains: there will be **no blame on me** — the complete term is permissible, but it is still regarded as something extra.

Ibn Kathir then gives two parallels for this pattern of a valid minimum with something extra above it. The first is the Qur'an's own: *"But whosoever hastens to leave in two days, there is no sin on him, and whosoever stays on, there is no sin on him"* (2:203). The second is what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Hamzah bin ʿAmr al-Aslami (may Allah be pleased with him), who used to fast a great deal and who asked him about fasting while travelling: *"If you wish, then fast, and if you wish, do not fast"* — even though it is better to fast, according to the evidence of other reports. The floor is settled clearly, and the extra is left free. Musa was not being grudging by naming the minimum; he was stating exactly what the covenant required.

**Which term did he serve?** Ibn Kathir says there is evidence indicating that Musa (peace be upon him) fulfilled the longer of the two terms. Al-Bukhari recorded that Saʿid bin Jubayr said: "A Jew from the people of Hirah asked me, 'Which of the two terms did Musa fulfil?' I said, 'I do not know until I go to the scholar of the Arabs and ask him.' So I went to Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him) and asked him. He said: 'He fulfilled the longer and better of them, for when a Messenger of Allah said he would do a thing, he did it.'"

That last line deserves to be sat with. Ibn ʿAbbas settled the question from the character of prophets: **when a Messenger of Allah says he will do a thing, he does it.**

**"And Allah is Surety over what we say."** Musa closes the agreement by placing Allah as Surety over the words the two of them had just exchanged.

## What the passage leaves with us

Read as one unit, ayat 25–28 are a portrait of decency in ordinary dealings. A woman who guards her manner of walking and the phrasing of her invitation, and who names capability and integrity together when she recommends a man for work. A man who arranges the walk home so that his eye cannot fall on her, and who lifted a stone at the well that ten men could barely lift. An old man who says "do not fear" before he says anything about terms, states his conditions plainly, does not wish to place the other party under difficulty, and says *in shāʾ Allah* about his own righteousness. And a hired man who confirms the minimum, keeps the extra voluntary, calls Allah as Surety — and then serves the longer term.

passages.title: The fire at the valley and two signs
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat carry Musa (peace be upon him) from the last day of a shepherd's contract in Madyan to the moment he is made a prophet. A man finishes his service, packs up his family and his flock, loses his way on a freezing night, goes looking for a flame to warm his wife and children — and is addressed by the Lord of all that exists. What holds ayat 29–32 together is that single arc: an ordinary journey interrupted by revelation, and a frightened man steadied by Allah and handed two signs to carry into the court of Fir'awn.

## Ayah 29: the term completed

The passage opens with the closing of a contract: **"Then, when Musa had fulfilled the term."** Ibn Kathir notes that this refers to the longer of the two terms that had been offered him — "and Allah knows best."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes up the question directly. Musa's agreement was eight years compulsory and two years optional; did he serve eight or ten? Sahih al-Bukhari has reported that when this very question was put to Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him), he answered: ten years. And he added the principle behind it — **prophets always fulfil their commitments, rather they do more than what they agree to.**

Maʿārif then draws the line forward to our own Prophet ﷺ, who was likewise in the habit of giving more than was due to the one having a right, and who advised his Ummah to be selfless and considerate in the matters of employment, wages, and business dealings.

Do not hurry past this. The man about to be given prophethood is first shown to us as a man who did not shave a day off his obligations to his employer. Before the miracle comes the character. If you owe someone labour, hours, money, or a promise, the prophetic pattern is not to meet the minimum but to exceed it.

## The cold night

Ibn Kathir preserves the human texture of what happened next. Musa missed his country and his relatives, so he resolved to visit them in secret, without Fir'awn and his people knowing. So he gathered up his family and the flocks which his father-in-law had given to him, and set out on **a cold, dark, rainy night.**

They stopped to camp. And whenever Musa tried to start a fire, he did not succeed. Ibn Kathir says he was surprised by this — and it was precisely while he was in this state that he **"saw a fire in the direction of At-Tur,"** burning from afar.

Look at what is being withheld and what is being given. The small fire he could produce with his own hands was denied him. The fire he could never have produced was already lit and waiting for him on the mountain. This is how Allah often works: the ordinary door is closed so that the extraordinary one can be walked through.

His words to his family are the words of a shepherd and a husband, not yet a prophet: **"Wait, I have seen a fire"** — meaning, as Ibn Kathir explains, *wait while I go there* — **"perhaps I may bring to you from there some information, or a burning firebrand that you may warm yourselves."**

Two requests, both entirely practical. *Some information* (khabar): Ibn Kathir explains this was **because they lost their way**, and a fire in the night means people, and people mean directions. *A burning firebrand* (jadhwah): so that they could get warm and find relief from the cold.

He went looking for directions and heat. He came back with prophethood. He asked for a coal; he was given the call of the Lord of all that exists.

## Ayah 30: called from the blessed place

**"So when he reached it, he was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed place, from the tree."**

Ibn Kathir maps the scene for us. The call came from the side of the valley that adjoined the mountain on his right, to the west. He supports this with a later ayah of this same surah: **"And you were not on the western side, when We made clear to Musa the commandment"** (28:44). Putting the two together, Ibn Kathir concludes that when Musa headed for the fire, he headed in the direction of the Qiblah with the western mountain on his right.

And the fire itself? Ibn Kathir says he found it **burning in a green bush** on the side of the mountain adjoining the valley — **and he stood there amazed at what he was seeing.**

Then, out of that fire and that tree, came the voice: **"O Musa! Verily, I am Allah, the Lord of all that exists!"**

Ibn Kathir unfolds the sentence: the One who is addressing you and speaking to you is the Lord of all that exists, the One who does what He wills, the One apart from whom there is no other god or lord, may He be exalted and sanctified — the One who **by His very nature, attributes, words and deeds is far above any resemblance to His creation**, may He be glorified.

That last clause is the doctrine that guards this whole scene. Allah truly spoke, and Musa truly heard. But the Speaker resembles nothing in His creation, and neither does His speech. We affirm what Allah has affirmed of Himself, without likening it to anything created and without explaining it away.

**Three surahs, one moment.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that this same subject appears in Surah Ta Ha, where the words are *"it is Me your Lord"* (20:12); in Surah An-Naml, where the call is *"Blessed is the one who is in the fire"* (27:8); and here in Al-Qasas as *"I am Allah, the Lord of the worlds"* (28:30). Although the wordings are slightly different, says Maʿārif, the meanings are almost the same — the incident is related in the words which suited to the situation being described. This is worth internalising for anyone who has ever worried that Qur'anic retellings "don't match": they are not competing transcripts. They are the same event related in the words that suited each setting.

**What exactly did Musa see?** Maʿārif is careful here. The refulgence Musa (peace be upon him) saw in the form of fire was only *mithālī* — in the form of an example — because it is impossible for a worldly being to see the actual refulgence of Allah. That is why Musa was told **"You will never see Me"** (7:143) in respect of actual refulgence. So the light in the bush was a sign granted to his eyes, not an unveiling of the Divine reality itself.

**Why "the blessed ground"?** Maʿārif draws a general principle from the phrase *fī al-buqʿah al-mubārakah*. The Holy Qur'an has termed Mount Tur blessed ground, and it is obvious that the reason for its being auspicious is the refulgence of Allah, which was manifested at that spot in the form of fire. From this Maʿārif concludes: **if something virtuous happens at a place, that particular spot also turns auspicious.** A stretch of ground has no holiness of its own; it acquires honour from what Allah caused to occur upon it.

## Ayah 31: the stick, and the fear

**"And throw your stick!"**

Ibn Kathir stresses the ordinariness of the object: *the stick that is in your hand*. He points to the exchange in Surah Ta Ha, where Allah asks, *"And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?"* and Musa answers, *"This is my stick, whereon I lean, and wherewith I beat down branches for my sheep, and wherein I find other uses"* (20:17–18). The meaning, says Ibn Kathir, is: **this stick, which you know so well.**

That familiarity is the point. The miracle is not performed with a special instrument brought down from heaven. It is performed with the worn, leaned-on, everyday tool of a shepherd's trade. What changes is not the wood; it is the command of Allah upon it.

Then: **"But when he saw it moving as if it were a snake, he turned in flight, and looked not back."** Ibn Kathir describes what Musa was actually looking at: it moved so quickly, **even though it was so big**, and its mouth was so huge, with its jaws snapping. It swallowed every rock it passed, and every rock that fell into its mouth fell with a sound like a rock falling into a valley. That combination of bulk and speed is what made it so appalling to watch.

**"He turned in flight, and looked not back."** Ibn Kathir's comment is beautifully unembarrassed: he did not turn around, **because it is human nature to flee from such a thing.** The Qur'an records the flight of a prophet without treating it as a defect. Fear of a charging snake is not weakness of faith; it is a body doing what bodies do. It matters that Allah preserved this detail — a believer who feels fear has not thereby failed.

And then the voice again: **"O Musa! Draw near, and fear not. Verily, you are of those who are secure."** Ibn Kathir says simply that Musa **came back to his original position.** The command was not "stop being afraid" as an abstract instruction; it was "draw near" paired with a guarantee — *you are of those who are secure*. Fear is answered not with rebuke but with security from Allah.

Notice also, from Ibn Kathir's earlier note, what Musa understood as he watched the stick transform: he **knew that the One who was speaking to him was the One who merely says to a thing, "Be!" and it is.** The miracle was, first of all, an argument addressed to Musa himself. Before he could carry proof to anyone else, he had to be given certainty.

## Ayah 32: the shining hand, and the cure for fear

**"Put your hand into the opening of your garment, it will come forth white without a disease."**

The word here is *jayb*, the opening of the garment. Ibn Kathir explains: when you put your hand in your garment and then draw it out, it will be shining white **as if it were a piece of the moon or a flash of lightning.** And the qualification *min ghayri sū'* — **"without a disease"** — means, in his words, with no trace of leukoderma. This is radiance, not sickness; a light, not a lesion. The distinction had to be explicit, because a hand suddenly turned white could otherwise be mistaken for the very thing it was not.

**"And draw your hand close to your side to be free from the fear."**

The early commentators the source names agree on the sense: **Mujahid said, "To be free from terror."** **Qatadah said, "To be free from fear."** Ibn Kathir explains that Musa was commanded, when he felt afraid of anything, to draw his hand close to his side to be free from the fear — and if he did that, whatever fear he felt would be gone.

Then Ibn Kathir offers a gentle extension, and he is careful to mark it as a possibility rather than a ruling: **perhaps** if a person does this, following the example of Musa, and puts his hand over his heart, his fear will disappear or be lessened, **if Allah wills** — "in Allah we place our trust."

Take it in the spirit he offers it: not a formula that compels a result, but a prophetic gesture worth imitating when the heart is pounding, with the outcome left entirely to Allah.

## The two proofs and their audience

**"These are two proofs from your Lord."**

Ibn Kathir identifies them exactly: the throwing down of his stick, whereupon it turned into a moving snake, and his putting his hand into his garment and bringing it forth white without a disease. The word is *burhān* — a clear, decisive proof. These two, he says, were **clear and definitive proofs of the power of the One who does as He chooses, and of the truth of the prophethood of the one at whose hands these miracles occurred.**

So the signs argue two things at once. First, about Allah: that His power is unrestricted, turning wood into a living creature and flesh into light. Second, about the messenger: that a man at whose hands such things occur is sent by that same power. A sign is never a spectacle for its own sake.

**"To Fir'awn and his chiefs."** *Al-mala'*, Ibn Kathir explains, means his leaders and prominent followers. The signs were aimed not only at the throne but at the whole ruling circle around it — the leadership that sustained the tyranny. Systems of oppression are never one man.

**"Verily, they are the people who are rebellious."** *Fāsiqīn*, says Ibn Kathir, means those who are disobedient towards Allah and who go against His commands and His religion. This closing clause is the justification for the whole mission: the confrontation Musa is being sent into is not a political quarrel, it is a response to a people who had broken out of obedience to their Lord.

## Holding the passage together

Read the four ayat as one movement and the shape is unmistakable. A man honours a contract to the last day and beyond it (ayah 29). A man loses his road in the dark and cannot even start a fire (ayah 29). A man is called by name by the Lord of all that exists, from a tree on a blessed stretch of ground (ayah 30). A man runs from a snake, and is called back and made secure (ayah 31). And a man who moments earlier was hoping for a firebrand to warm his family is sent, with two proofs in his own hand and body, to Fir'awn and his chiefs (ayah 32).

Between the lost traveller and the messenger to Fir'awn there is nothing but the word of Allah. That is the passage. As Ibn Kathir says of the moment the stick moved: Musa knew that the One speaking to him was the One who merely says to a thing, "Be!" and it is.

passages.title: Moses fears reprisal and asks for Aaron
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** Musa (peace be upon him) has just been called by his Lord and commanded to go to Fir'awn. These three ayat are his reply and Allah's answer to it: a man voicing two very human fears — that he will be killed, and that he will not be believed — asking for his brother as support, and being given more than he asked for. Ayat 33 and 34 are Musa's request; ayah 35 is Allah's response, and it answers both fears at once.

*A note on voices: below, anything introduced as coming from Ibn Kathir or from Maʿārif ul Qurʾān is theirs. Passages marked as reflection are my own drawing-out of what the commentators say, not part of their commentary.*

## The situation behind ayah 33

Ibn Kathir sets the scene plainly: **Allah commanded Musa to go to Fir'awn — the one he had run away from, and whose vengeance he feared.** That is the whole weight of ayah 33. The command sends him back toward the very power he had fled.

So he says: **"My Lord! I have indeed killed a man among them, and I fear that they will kill me."**

**"A man among them."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is a single identification and no more: **"meaning, that Coptic."** He does not narrate the incident here; he simply names who it was. What the ayah itself supplies is the pronoun *them* — the killing was among the people Musa is now being sent back to.

**"I fear that they will kill me."** Ibn Kathir glosses this with three words: **"when they see me."** That is, the danger begins at recognition. On this reading Musa is not imagining a long trial and a verdict; he expects the matter to be settled the moment he is identified. The fear is immediate and physical.

## Fear in a prophet's mouth — a reflection

*The following is my own reflection on the wording of the ayah, not something the commentators state.*

Notice what Musa does with the fear. He does not deny it, and he does not use it to excuse himself from the mission. He brings it to Allah. The ayah opens with **"Rabbi"** — *My Lord* — the word of a servant turning to the One who owns his affair. The command has been given and Musa is not disputing it; he is telling his Lord the truth about his own state and asking for what he needs to carry it out.

Feeling afraid of a real danger is not, in itself, a defect in faith. What Musa does with the fear is turn it into a *duʿāʾ* — a supplication, a request spoken directly to Allah.

## Ayah 34: "My brother Harun is more eloquent in speech than me"

The second fear is different in kind. In ayah 33 he fears for his life; in ayah 34 he fears for the message — **"Verily, I fear that they will deny me."**

Behind that fear lies something Ibn Kathir explains: **Musa, peace be upon him, had a speech defect** — Ibn Kathir gives its origin as this: when he had been given the choice between a date and a pearl, he mistakenly picked up a coal and placed it on his tongue, so that he found it difficult to speak clearly. Ibn Kathir then sets beside this ayah Musa's supplication from Sūrah Ṭā Hā: *"And loose the knot (the defect) from my tongue. That they understand my speech. And appoint for me a helper from my family, Harun, my brother. Increase my strength with him, and let him share my task"* (20:27–32).

So when Musa says his brother is **afṣaḥ** — more eloquent, more fluent in tongue — he is naming a limitation of his own and asking for a man whose strength covers exactly where he is weak.

**The key word: ridʾ.** Musa asks that Harun be sent with him *ridʾan*, rendered "as a helper." Ibn Kathir explains it as **a support to give strength to my cause and confirm what I say and convey from Allah.** Muhammad bin Ishaq, quoted by Ibn Kathir, reads the phrase *ridʾan yuṣaddiqunī* ("as a helper to confirm me") as meaning: **"to explain to them what I say, for he can understand me where they may not."** On that reading Harun is not merely a witness standing beside Musa; he is the one who makes Musa intelligible — a brother who knows his speech well enough to carry it across to those who do not.

**"Because the word of two carries more weight in people's minds than the word of one."** That is Ibn Kathir's own explanation of why Musa asks for a companion. And in the same passage he gives the deeper reason drawn from Sūrah Ṭā Hā: *give me someone to keep me company in this immense task* of prophethood and of conveying the Message **to this arrogant, tyrannical and stubborn king.** The burden is real. Musa asks not to carry it alone.

**A practical note from Maʿārif ul Qurʾān.** Commenting on *"He is more fluent in his tongue"* (28:34), Maʿārif ul Qurʾān draws out a lesson under the heading *A sermon should have a high degree of eloquence*: **this verse points out that a high degree of oratory and eloquence is desirable for sermons and preaching, and there is no harm if one takes training in that.**

## Ayah 35: what Allah answers

**"We will strengthen your arm through your brother, and give you both power, so they shall not be able to harm you, with Our Ayat; you two as well as those who follow you will be the victors."**

Read it against the two fears, and every clause lands on one of them.

**"We will strengthen your arm through your brother."** Ibn Kathir: **"We will add strength to your cause and give you help through your brother, who you have asked to be made a Prophet alongside you."** Note that the promise is stated in the future — *We **will** strengthen* — given before a single step has been taken.

The request was granted in full. Ibn Kathir places beside this ayah Allah's words to Musa elsewhere: *"You are granted your request, O Musa!"* (20:36), and *"And We granted him his brother Harun, (also) a Prophet, out of Our mercy"* (19:53). Musa asked for a helper; Allah made him a Prophet.

**"And We will give you both power (sulṭān)."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is precise: **overwhelming evidence.** The word rendered "power" here, on his reading, means proof so decisive it cannot be answered.

**"So they shall not be able to harm you, with Our Ayat."** *Ayat* here means the signs of Allah. Ibn Kathir: **"they will have no way or means of harming you because you are conveying the signs of Allah."** This is the direct answer to ayah 33. Musa said *I fear they will kill me*; Allah says they will have no way to harm him. And the reason Ibn Kathir gives is not Musa's own strength but what he is carrying — the protection is tied to conveying Allah's signs.

Ibn Kathir gathers other verses that say the same thing about those who carry revelation: *"O Messenger! Proclaim (the Message) which has been sent down to you from your Lord"* through to *"and Allah will protect you from mankind"* (5:67); and *"Those who convey the Message of Allah"* through to *"and sufficient is Allah as a Reckoner"* (33:39). He adds: **and sufficient is Allah as a Helper and Supporter.**

**"You two as well as those who follow you will be the victors."** Here the promise widens past the two brothers. Ibn Kathir notes that Allah told them the consequences **in this world and the next, for them and for those who followed them.** He cites the same pattern elsewhere: *"Allah has decreed: 'Verily, it is I and My Messengers who shall be the victorious.' Verily, Allah is All-Powerful, All-Mighty"* (58:21), and *"Verily, We will indeed make victorious Our Messengers and those who believe in this world's life"* (40:51).

So the man who a moment ago expected to be killed on sight is told he stands on the side of a decree already written.

## The greatest favour a brother ever did

Ibn Kathir records a remark from **one of the Salaf** — the early generations — that is easy to pass over and hard to forget once seen:

> There is no one who has ever done a greater favour to his brother than Musa did for Harun, may peace be upon them both, for he interceded for him until Allah made him a Prophet and Messenger with him to Fir'awn and his chiefs.

The same passage continues: **Allah said concerning Musa: "he was honourable before Allah"** (33:69).

Musa was in a fearful hour, standing before his Lord with a request — and part of what he asked for was that his brother be raised. Allah answered it.

## Living it

*What follows is applied reflection — my own, built on the material above.*

**Bring the fear to Allah, not instead of the task.** Musa says the frightening thing out loud — *I have killed a man among them; I fear they will kill me* — and in the same breath asks for what he needs to go anyway. Honesty about weakness and obedience to the command are not opposites.

**Ask for help; it is not a failure of trust.** A prophet asked for a companion, and Ibn Kathir's reason is plain: "the word of two carries more weight in people's minds than the word of one." If Musa asked for a brother at his side for a hard task, no one else is above needing one.

**Work on being understood.** Musa named his own difficulty in speech and asked for a remedy. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān takes the ayah as encouragement to seek a high degree of eloquence for preaching — and says plainly there is no harm in training for it.

**Lift the person next to you.** As one of the Salaf observed, Musa's request ended in his brother being made a Prophet and Messenger. When you are given a chance to ask, ask for someone else too.

**The protection is in the mission.** *"They shall not be able to harm you, with Our Ayat."* Ibn Kathir ties the safety to the work: they cannot be reached because they are conveying the signs of Allah. And the end of the story is announced before it begins: **you two as well as those who follow you will be the victors.**

passages.title: Called sorcery; Pharaoh claims to be god
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

Musa (peace be upon him) and Harun (peace be upon him) finally stand before Pharaoh's court and lay out the clear signs — and the court answers with a sneer and a slogan. Ayat 36–38 are one scene with three movements: the rejection (ayah 36), Musa's calm reply that hands the verdict over to Allah (ayah 37), and Pharaoh's counter-move, in which he stops arguing about the message and simply declares himself the only god his people have ever known (ayah 38). What holds the three together is a single contest: **who really knows?** The court appeals to what they heard from their fathers; Musa answers that his Lord knows best; Pharaoh answers that he knows of no god but himself — and then orders a tower built to go and check.

---

## The scene: two brothers, clear signs, and a court that already knew

Ibn Kathir sets the frame. Allah tells us how Musa (peace be upon him) and his brother Harun (peace be upon him) came before Pharaoh and his chiefs and "showed them the clear miracles and overwhelming proof that Allah had given them," proof meant to confirm exactly what the two of them had been saying: that Allah is One, and that His commandments are to be followed.

Notice what Ibn Kathir says next, because it is the hinge of the whole passage: "Fir'awn and his chiefs saw that with their own eyes and realized that it was certainly from Allah, but because of their disbelief and sin they resorted to stubbornness and false arguments. This was because they were too evil and arrogant to follow the truth."

So this is not a scene about a court that lacked evidence. It is a scene about a court that had the evidence, recognised it, and refused it anyway. The ayah calls what they were shown **āyāt bayyināt** — "Our clear signs," clear miracles, in Ibn Kathir's words. Whatever the objection about to be raised, it cannot be that the matter was unclear.

There is a quiet touch of mercy in the background here. A few ayat earlier (28:34) Musa had asked for Harun, saying "he is more fluent in his tongue" — *huwa afṣaḥu minnī lisānan*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a general principle from that line: a high degree of oratory and eloquence is desirable for sermons and preaching, and there is no harm if one takes training in it. And indeed the two brothers came to Pharaoh's court together, as Ibn Kathir describes. Still the message was called magic. Eloquence is worth seeking — but it was never the thing that would move a heart described as too arrogant to follow the truth.

---

## Ayah 36: two objections, and what each really means

The court's answer has two parts, and they are of different kinds.

**"This is nothing but invented magic"** — *mā hādhā illā siḥrun muftaran*. Ibn Kathir glosses this as "fabricated and made up." The accusation is doubly dismissive: first that the signs are sorcery rather than revelation, and second that even as sorcery they are a concoction. It is the language of men reaching for any label that will let them stop looking.

And Ibn Kathir tells us what lay behind the label: "They wanted to oppose him by means of their own tricks and their position and power, but this did not work." The charge of magic was not a considered verdict; it was the opening move of a strategy — meet the sign with their own tricks, and back the tricks with the throne. Ibn Kathir's closing clause is worth keeping in view: *this did not work.*

**"Never did we hear of this among our fathers of old"** — this is the second objection, and it is the more revealing one. What is the "this" they had never heard of? Ibn Kathir is precise: "They were referring [to] worshipping Allah Alone, with no partner or associate." Their argument, in his paraphrase, runs: *We have never seen anyone among our forefathers following this religion; we have only ever seen people associating other gods in worship with Allah.*

Sit with the shape of that argument. It concedes the point without noticing. They do not say Musa's claim is false; they say it is unfamiliar. Inherited practice becomes the measure of truth, and novelty becomes the disqualification. It is the oldest refusal in the world and the least examined: *our fathers did not do it, therefore it cannot be right.* The signs were before their eyes; the answer came from behind them.

---

## Ayah 37: Musa does not argue — he refers the case upward

Musa's reply is remarkable for what it does not do. He does not defend his credentials, does not restage the miracle, does not match insult with insult. He says: **"My Lord knows best him who came with guidance from Him, and whose will be the happy end in the Hereafter. Verily, the wrongdoers will not be successful."**

Ibn Kathir unpacks each clause.

**"My Lord knows best him who came with guidance from Him"** — meaning, says Ibn Kathir, "of me and you, and He will decide between me and you." Musa places himself and them on the same footing before a Judge who cannot be deceived by rhetoric. It is a direct answer to their pretended knowledge: you appeal to what you heard from your fathers; I appeal to the One who knows. And note the word Musa chooses in addressing Allah: **Rabbī**, *my Lord* — the very title Pharaoh is about to claim for himself.

**"and whose will be the happy end in the Hereafter"** — Ibn Kathir explains this as "who will be supported and will prevail." Musa moves the whole dispute onto the axis of the ending. A court, a throne, an army and a slogan can win an afternoon; they cannot settle who prevails in the end, and that is the only question Musa is willing to argue about.

**"Verily, the wrongdoers will not be successful"** — Ibn Kathir specifies that this "refers to the idolators who associate others in worship with Allah." This is worth pausing on, because in ordinary English "wrongdoers" suggests cruelty or theft. The wrong named here is idolatry itself — assigning to others what belongs to Allah alone. And the promise is flat and unconditional: such people will not succeed, however the court's afternoon appears to go.

---

## Ayah 38: the claim, and the tower

Ibn Kathir introduces this ayah with a sentence heavy with grief: "Allah tells us of Fir'awn's disbelief and wrongdoing, and how he falsely claimed divinity for his evil self, may Allah curse him."

**"O chiefs! I know not that you have a god other than me."** The address is to *al-malaʾ*, the chiefs — the inner circle whose assent holds the system together. Pharaoh does not engage Musa's evidence at all. He changes the question from *is this true?* to *who is in charge here?*

Ibn Kathir gathers the rest of the Qur'an around this line to show how the claim worked. Of Pharaoh Allah says elsewhere, "Thus he fooled his people, and they obeyed him" (43:54) — Ibn Kathir comments that "he called on his people to recognize his divinity, and they responded, because of their weak and foolish minds." In Sūrat al-Nāziʿāt: "Then he gathered his people and cried aloud, saying: 'I am your lord, most high.' So Allah seized him with punishment for his last and first transgression. Verily, in this is an instructive admonition for whosoever fears Allah" (79:23–26) — meaning, says Ibn Kathir, he brought his people together, called to them in a loud voice, and they responded obediently; so Allah took revenge on him and made him a lesson to others in this world and the Hereafter. And to Musa's face he had threatened, "If you choose a god other than me, I will certainly put you among the prisoners" (26:29).

Now note the exact wording of ayah 38: not *there is no god but me*, but **"I know not that you have a god other than me"** — *mā ʿalimtu*. He speaks in the register of knowledge, mirroring the court's claim in ayah 36 that they had never *heard* of such a thing, and standing directly opposite Musa's "**my Lord knows best**" in ayah 37. Three claims to knowledge in three ayat; only one of them rests on anything.

**"So kindle for me a fire, O Haman, upon the clay, and set up for me a Ṣarḥ, that I may look at the deity of Musa."** Ibn Kathir explains that Pharaoh commanded his minister and adviser Haman to bake bricks out of clay in order to build a *ṣarḥ* — "an exalted towering palace." He reads it alongside 40:36–37, where Pharaoh says: "O Haman! Build me a Ṣarḥ that I may arrive at the ways — the ways of the heavens, and I may look upon the deity of Musa, but verily, I think him to be a liar." The same passage adds the verdict: "Thus it was made fair seeming, in Fir'awn's eyes, the evil of his deeds, and he was hindered from the path; and the plot of Fir'awn led to nothing but loss and destruction."

Ibn Kathir states the purpose plainly: Pharaoh built this tower — "which was the highest structure ever seen on earth" — "because he wanted to show his people that Musa was lying when he claimed that there was a deity other than Fir'awn." The tower was propaganda in masonry. Its audience was his own people, not the heavens.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** fills in the human detail of the order. When Pharaoh planned this very tall palace, he asked Haman to get the bricks baked *properly* first, "because half baked bricks could not take the load of a tall building." Some have observed that Pharaoh was the first to have tough bricks baked for buildings, no one having used them before. And Maʿārif reports, citing Qurtubi, that historical narrations record Haman collecting fifty thousand masons for the palace, with skilled labour such as carpenters and blacksmiths besides; it was built so tall that there was no parallel to it in the world. When it was completed, Allah commanded Jibra'il (peace be upon him) to knock it down. He struck one blow, and it tumbled down in three pieces, killing thousands of Pharaoh's soldiers. (This is a historical narration transmitted by the commentators — not a text of the Qur'an — and is best taken as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presents it, on the authority of Qurtubi.)

There is something almost pitiable in the engineering. A man who claims to be a god has to worry whether his bricks are hard enough to carry the weight of his own ladder to the sky.

**"and verily, I think that he is one of the liars."** Ibn Kathir gives the sense: 'when he says that there is a lord other than me.' And then he makes a point of real precision: the issue was never whether Allah had sent Musa as a messenger, "because he did not acknowledge the existence of the Creator in the first place." The evidence is Pharaoh's own recorded words — "And what is the Lord of al-ʿĀlamīn?" (26:23), "If you choose a god other than me, I will certainly put you among the prisoners" (26:29), and this ayah, "O chiefs! I know not that you have a god other than me." Ibn Kathir notes that this was the view of **Ibn Jarir**. Pharaoh was not disputing a prophet's credentials; he was denying that there was any Lord above him at all.

Note too that he says *aẓunnuhu* — I *think*, I suppose. Even at the height of his defiance the tyrant's language betrays him: conjecture on his side, clear signs on the other.

---

## Where this is going

Ibn Kathir reads straight on into what follows, and the ending is worth knowing even in a sentence. Pharaoh and his armies "were arrogant in the land, without right, and they thought that they would never return to Us" (28:39) — meaning, he says, "they were arrogant oppressors who spread much mischief in the land, and they believed that there would be no Resurrection." Then: "We seized him and his armies, and We threw them all into the sea" (28:40) — Ibn Kathir: 'We drowned them in the sea in a single morning, and not one of them was left.' The tower reached for the sky; the end came from the water.

Musa's quiet sentence in ayah 37 — *whose will be the happy end* — turned out to be the only accurate forecast anyone made that day.

---

## Living it

**Recognise the two refusals.** "It's just magic" and "our fathers never did this" are still the two commonest ways truth gets waved off — one attacks the messenger's honesty, the other appeals to inherited habit. Neither engages the evidence. When you catch either one forming in your own mouth, ask what the clear sign in front of you actually is.

**Learn Musa's composure.** Insulted before the most powerful court on earth, he neither retaliated nor performed. He named his Lord, named the criterion — the ending, not the moment — and stopped. That is a usable model for anyone who has been mocked for their religion: state the truth, refer the verdict to Allah, and refuse to be dragged onto the mocker's ground.

**Watch for the small pharaoh.** Few claim divinity outright. But "I know of no authority above me" is a posture available to anyone with a little power over others — in a household, a workplace, a community. Ibn Kathir names what makes it possible: believing there will be no Resurrection, thinking one will never be returned to Allah (ayah 39). Keep that memory alive and the posture cannot take root.

**Take the sermon seriously.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's note on Musa's words about Harun stands: work on how you speak when you are speaking for the truth. Eloquence will not compel a closed heart — but seeking it is, as Maʿārif says, desirable, and there is no harm in training oneself in it.

passages.title: Arrogance, then seized and cast into the sea
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat close Fir'awn's story in this surah: a tyrant who falsely claimed divinity for himself, was arrogant along with his armies, assumed he would never be brought back to his Lord — and was then seized, thrown into the sea, and left with a curse in this world and disgrace in the next. What holds the passage together is a single chain of cause and consequence: arrogance and the denial of the Resurrection (ayah 39) lead to seizure and drowning (ayah 40), and beyond death to a role as leaders inviting to the Fire (ayah 41) and a curse that follows them into the Day of Resurrection (ayah 42). Ibn Kathir titles the whole section "The Arrogance of Fir'awn and His ultimate Destiny" — that is exactly the arc.

## What Fir'awn had just said

Ayah 39 lands with its full weight only if you hear the boast it answers. In the ayah immediately before, Fir'awn says: "O chiefs! I know not that you have a god other than me. So kindle for me (a fire), O Haman, to bake clay, and set up for me a Sarh in order that I may look at the deity of Musa; and verily, I think that he (Musa) is one of the liars."

Ibn Kathir explains that Fir'awn ordered his minister and adviser Haman to bake bricks so as to build a *Sarh* — an exalted, towering palace — and that this tower was the highest structure ever seen on earth. Fir'awn built it, Ibn Kathir says, because he wanted to show his people that Musa was lying when he claimed there was a deity other than Fir'awn. Ma'arif ul Qur'an adds the practical detail behind "kindle for me a fire on the clay": half-baked bricks could not take the load of so tall a building, so Haman was told to have them fired properly first. Citing Qurtubi, it relates that Haman gathered fifty thousand masons for the project besides other skilled labour, that the palace rose without parallel in the world, and that when it was complete Allah commanded Jibra'il (peace be upon him) to knock it down — one blow, and it fell in three pieces, killing thousands of Fir'awn's soldiers.

One clarification from Ibn Kathir is worth carrying forward. When Fir'awn says "I think he is one of the liars," what was he actually denying? Ibn Kathir says the meaning is: a liar "when he says that there is a lord other than me." The issue was not whether Allah had sent Musa, because Fir'awn did not acknowledge the existence of the Creator in the first place — as shown by his own words, "And what is the Lord of Al-'Alamin?" (26:23), and his threat, "If you choose a god other than me, I will certainly put you among the prisoners" (26:29). Ibn Kathir attributes this reading to Ibn Jarir.

Ibn Kathir also notes how the crowd was handled: "Thus he fooled his people, and they obeyed him" (43:54). He called them to recognise his divinity and they responded — because of their weak and foolish minds. And Allah reports the climactic performance: "Then he gathered (his people) and cried aloud, saying: 'I am your lord, most high.' So Allah seized him with punishment for his last and first transgression. Verily, in this is an instructive admonition for whosoever fears Allah" (79:23-26). Ibn Kathir's comment: Allah took revenge on him and made him a lesson to others in this world and the Hereafter.

That is the man ayah 39 now describes.

## Ayah 39: arrogance "without right", and the assumption underneath it

"And he and his armies were arrogant in the land, without right, and they thought that they would never return to Us."

Two things are worth slowing down on.

**First, "without right."** The qualifier delivers the verdict before the punishment arrives: there is no truth and no entitlement underneath this self-elevation — it is greatness asserted where none is owed. Ibn Kathir's summary is blunt: "they were arrogant oppressors who spread much mischief in the land." Notice too that it is not Fir'awn alone. The ayah names "he and his armies": arrogance in a ruler becomes a system when the people with the swords sign on to it.

**Second, the thought that made it possible.** "…and they thought that they would never return to Us." Ibn Kathir glosses this simply: "they believed that there would be no Resurrection." That is the engine of the whole passage. Once a man is convinced there is no coming back before his Lord, there is nothing left to restrain him: no reckoning to fear, no account to answer, no limit on what he may do to the weak. The Qur'an here diagnoses tyranny not merely as a political fault but as a belief problem. Whoever is genuinely certain he will stand before Allah cannot behave like Fir'awn; whoever is certain he will not, has already removed the only ceiling over his appetite.

And notice the direction of the wording: they thought they would never return **to Us**. The ayah states as fact the very thing they dismissed.

## Ayah 40: seized, and thrown into the sea

"So, We seized him and his armies, and We threw them all into the sea. So, behold what was the end of the wrongdoers."

Ibn Kathir leads into this with another ayah about a proud, ruined nation: "So, your Lord poured on them different kinds of severe torment. Verily, your Lord is Ever Watchful (over them)" (89:13-14). The tyrant assumed no one was keeping account. Someone was.

Then the reversal, and it lands in a single sentence. Ibn Kathir's comment on "We threw them all into the sea" is: "We drowned them in the sea in a single morning, and not one of them was left."

Consider the contrast the passage builds. Fifty thousand masons and the highest structure ever seen on earth; an army; a man who gathered a nation and cried aloud, "I am your lord, most high." One morning. Not one of them left. This is not a battle between rivals; it is a seizure and a disposal, and nothing in it is a struggle.

**"So, behold what was the end of the wrongdoers."** The passage now turns and speaks to us. It is an imperative — *look*. History is not being narrated as information; it is being held up as evidence. And the thing we are told to look at is not the height but the end. Fir'awn at his height looked unanswerable. Look at how it finished.

## Ayah 41: "leaders inviting to the Fire"

"And We made them leaders inviting to the Fire: and on the Day of Resurrection, they will not be helped."

Ma'arif ul Qur'an brings out the bitter irony: Allah had elevated Fir'awn's courtiers as leaders of their people, and these wrongdoers were busy inviting the people towards the Fire. Ibn Kathir explains the phrase as leadership "for those who followed them and took the same path as they did, rejecting the Messengers and denying the Creator." Their leadership did not end when they drowned; every later soul who takes the same road is walking a road they helped make.

**A discussion worth understanding.** Ma'arif ul Qur'an records that most commentators take "invitation to fire" as a metaphor — that by "fire" the allusion is to evil deeds that will result in burning in the fire of Jahannam. But it then reports the position of its author's respected teacher, Sayyidna Maulana Sayyid Muhammad Anwar Shah Kashmiri (may Allah have mercy on him): that the reward of the Hereafter is the deed itself. One's deeds in this world will change their forms, first in *barzakh* and then in *mahshar*. Righteous deeds will change into flowers and gardens and take the shape of the bounties of Paradise; evil deeds will turn into snakes and scorpions, ultimately manifesting themselves as the various types of torment.

On that reading, someone who invites another towards evil and disbelief in this world is in fact bidding him to go into the fire. These evils do not manifest themselves as fire in this world, yet in reality they are fire — so there is no metaphor in the ayah at all; it rests with its true meaning. Ma'arif ul Qur'an adds that if this course of argument is adopted, many ayat are freed from dependence on metaphor and become straightforward to read, and it offers as examples "And they will find what they did all there" (18:49) and "Whoever does good to the measure of a particle will see it" (99:7).

Both readings are transmitted; the difference is one of interpretation, and either way the warning is the same. But the second reading changes how a sin feels. It says the punishment is not an external penalty bolted on afterwards; it is the deed itself, finally shown for what it always was.

**"And on the Day of Resurrection, they will not be helped."** Ibn Kathir observes that their humiliation in this world is combined with and connected to their humiliation in the Hereafter, and quotes: "We have destroyed them. And there was none to help them" (47:13). The armies that made Fir'awn untouchable are the same armies that went into the sea with him. Power that cannot save you at the moment you need saving was never power.

## Ayah 42: a curse in this world, disfigurement in the next

"And We made a curse to follow them in this world, and on the Day of Resurrection, they will be among disgraced."

Ibn Kathir explains the first half: Allah decreed that they and their king Fir'awn should be cursed by the believers among His servants who follow His Messengers, just as in this world they were cursed by the Prophets and their followers. So the curse is not only a decree in the unseen; it is worked out through the tongues of the believers in every generation. Every time the story is recited, the verdict is renewed. Fir'awn wanted a name that would tower over the earth. He got one — and it is a byword for the worst thing a man can become.

Qatadah, as Ibn Kathir reports, said this ayah is like the ayah: "They were pursued by a curse in this (life) and on the Day of Resurrection. Evil indeed is the gift given" (11:99). Notice that last phrase: the curse is spoken of as though it were a present handed over. A tyrant's legacy is his own gift to himself.

**"Among disgraced" — al-Maqbuhin.** Ma'arif ul Qur'an opens this word up: *Maqbuhin* is the plural of *Maqbuh*, which means spoilt, damaged or disfigured. So the meaning of the ayah is that on the Day of Judgement their faces will be disfigured, turning black, and their eyes will turn blue. It is a punishment fitted to the crime. A man who spent his life engineering how he looked to other people — the palace, the gathered crowds, the proclamation — is exposed at last with a face that tells the truth about him in front of everyone.

## Living it

The passage is not really about ancient Egypt. It is a mirror, and Allah tells us plainly what to do with it: *"So, behold what was the end of the wrongdoers."*

**Arrogance is not a personality flaw here; it is the root sin.** Ayah 39 pairs it with "without right" and with the belief that there would be no Resurrection. Most of us will not claim divinity, but we make smaller versions of the same claim every time we behave as though we answer to no one — with an employee, a spouse, a child, anyone weaker than us who cannot push back. The cure the ayah points to is not merely a resolution to be humbler; it is to hold on to the certainty that we are returning to Him.

**Watch what your influence invites people towards.** Ayah 41 shows that leadership is amplified, not neutral: Allah had raised those men up as leaders of their people, and what they did with that position was call people towards the Fire. Anyone with followers, a platform, a household, or a younger sibling watching them is already leading someone somewhere.

**Do not envy anyone at their height.** Every impressive thing in this story — the highest structure ever seen on earth, the fifty thousand masons, the army, the obedient nation — is in the passage only to make one morning at the sea more devastating. Judge by the end, as the ayah tells you to.

**And take heart if you are on the weak side of a Fir'awn.** The seizure came from a Lord who is, as Ibn Kathir reminds us with 89:14, "Ever Watchful."</tafsir>

passages.title: You were not there — proof of revelation
passages.tafsir:
The long story of Musa has just ended. Now Allah turns from the story to the storyteller, and puts a question the Makkans could not answer: how does this unlettered man among you know any of this? Ayat 43–47 are a single argument — the Book given to Musa (43), three reminders that Muhammad ﷺ was not present at any of the scenes he has just described (44–46), and the reason Allah sent him anyway: mercy, warning, and the closing of every excuse (46–47).

## Ayah 43 — the Book that came after the great destructions

**"And indeed We gave Musa the Scripture — after We had destroyed the generations of old."** Ibn Kathir reads this as Allah recounting His blessings upon "His servant and Messenger Musa, the speaker" — the Tawrah revealed to him after Allah had destroyed Firʿawn and his chiefs.

Who are "the generations of old" (al-qurūn al-ūlā)? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies them as the peoples of Nuh, Hud, Salih and Lut, peace be upon them — nations destroyed before Musa's time because they denied the truth.

Ibn Kathir draws out something easy to miss in that little phrase **"after We had destroyed"**: it marks a turning point. After the revelation of the Tawrah, no nation would again be punished with an overwhelming calamity; instead the believers were now commanded to fight the enemies of Allah among the idolators. The age in which whole nations were seized in that way closed; the era of struggle in Allah's cause opened. Ibn Kathir cites the description of the earlier age: *"And Firʿawn, and those before him, and the cities overthrown committed sin. And they disobeyed their Lord's Messenger, so He seized them with a strong punishment"* (69:9–10).

**Basāʾir — sight for the heart.** Allah describes the Tawrah as *baṣāʾir li'l-nās wa hudan wa raḥmah* — "insights for people, and a guidance and a mercy." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *baṣāʾir* is the plural of *baṣīrah*, whose literal meaning is sagacity, insight and discernment. What is intended here, it says — quoting the commentary of Mazhari — is that light Allah bestows in the hearts of people, by which they find out the truth and discern the distinction between right and wrong. Not information, then, but perception.

Ibn Kathir unpacks the three words in order. *Baṣāʾir* — guidance from blindness and error. *Hudan* — a guidance to the truth. *Raḥmah* — a mercy, meaning it shows the way towards doing righteous deeds. And the closing purpose, *laʿallahum yatadhakkarūn*, "that they might remember," means that the people might be reminded by it and guided by it. Hold on to that word "remember"; it returns in ayah 46 about the people to whom the Prophet ﷺ was sent, tying the two revelations together.

## A question the scholars raised here: what about the Torah today?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on the phrase "insights **for people**" (li'l-nās). If "people" is taken to mean the people of Musa, the verse is quite clear — for them the Torah was the book of wisdom. But if the word is taken broadly, so as to include the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ, a difficulty arises: the Torah available to this Ummah is not the original one, and many changes have taken place in it. How could that be regarded as a book of wisdom for them — and would it mean that Muslims too should benefit from it?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers by recalling what it calls a well-known hadith — it does not name a collection for it, so neither will we — that Sayyidunā ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) once sought permission from the Prophet ﷺ to read the Torah, so that he could improve his knowledge and benefit from the injunctions contained in it. At this the Prophet ﷺ became angry and said that if Musa (peace be upon him) were alive, he too would have been required to follow him ﷺ. The essence of that retort, Maʿārif explains, is that ʿUmar should concentrate only on the teachings he already had; he was not required to look into the teachings of Torah or Injīl.

Two contextual points follow. First, it was a time when the revelation of the Qurʼān was still continuing, and in order to eliminate any possibility of hadith being mingled with the Qurʼānic text, the Prophet ﷺ had advised some of his Companions to stop writing even the hadith. In such a situation, reading a cancelled divine book was plainly not expedient. Second, it does not necessarily follow that reading the Torah and Injīl is banned for all times — on the contrary, reading and quoting by the Companions of the portions in which the coming of the Prophet ﷺ was predicted is well established, Sayyidunā ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām and Kaʿb al-Aḥbār being quite well known for this, and other Companions did not raise a finger against it.

**The bottom line Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws:** it is allowed to benefit from the unaltered part of these books, which no doubt contains wisdom — but only those can draw benefit who can distinguish the altered from the unaltered parts, and they are the expert scholars. A common man should avoid such an exercise, lest he get entangled in a quandary. And the same ruling applies to all books that are a mixture of right and wrong. That is a strikingly practical principle for a reader today: some material is not sinful in itself, yet is beyond the safe reach of someone without the tools to sift it.

## Ayat 44–46 — three scenes, and "you were not there"

Ibn Kathir titles this section **"Proof of the Prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ."** The argument is simple and devastating. Allah points out the proof of his prophethood in this: he told others about matters of the past, and spoke about them as if he were hearing and seeing them for himself. Yet, as Ibn Kathir stresses, he was an illiterate man who could not read books, and he grew up among a people who knew nothing of such things. There is no natural channel by which this knowledge could have reached him. Only one explanation remains: Allah revealed it.

Ibn Kathir shows this is Allah's recurring signature after narrating hidden history. After the account of Maryam: *"You were not with them, when they cast lots with their pens as to which of them should be charged with the care of Maryam; nor were you with them when they disputed"* (3:44) — meaning, you were not present then, but Allah has revealed this to you. After the account of Nuh and his people, how Allah saved him and drowned them: *"This is of the news of the Unseen which We reveal unto you; neither you nor your people knew it before this. So be patient. Surely the good end is for those who have taqwā"* (11:49) — taqwā being the mindfulness of Allah that makes a person guard himself against Allah's displeasure. And at the end of that same sūrah: *"That is some of the news of the towns which We relate unto you"* (11:100). And here, Ibn Kathir says, after telling the story of Musa from beginning to end and how Allah began His revelation to him and spoke with him, Allah says:

**Scene one — the western side (ayah 44).** *"And you were not on the western side of the Mount, when We made clear to Musa the commandment."* Ibn Kathir explains: you — O Muhammad — were not on the western side of the mountain, where Allah spoke to Musa from the tree which was to the east of it, in the valley. The Qurʼān gives the geography with the precision of an eyewitness: which side of the mountain, which side the tree stood on — and then says, and you were not there.

**"And you were not among the witnesses."** Ibn Kathir adds the purpose: you were not a witness to that event, but Allah has revealed this to you, so that it may be evidence and proof of events which happened centuries ago — for people have forgotten the evidence that Allah established against them and what was revealed to the earlier Prophets. Notice the double work the passage does. The revelation both proves the Prophet ﷺ true and restores to humanity a record it had lost.

**Scene two — Madyan (ayah 45).** Between the denials Allah inserts the reason the record needed restoring: *"But We created generations, and long were the ages that passed over them."* Generation after generation, the ages stretching out — and, as Ibn Kathir noted a line earlier, people had forgotten what Allah had established among them. Then: *"And you were not a dweller among the people of Madyan, reciting Our Ayat to them."* The word rendered "a dweller" is *thāwiyan*. Ibn Kathir's gloss: you were not living among the people of Madyan reciting Our verses to them, when you started to tell about Our Prophet Shuʿayb and what he said to his people and how they responded.

**"But it is We Who kept sending."** Ibn Kathir: but We revealed that to you, and sent you to mankind as a Messenger. The denial is never left bare; each "you were not" is answered by a "but We".

**Scene three — the side of aṭ-Ṭūr (ayah 46).** *"And you were not at the side of aṭ-Ṭūr when We called."* Ibn Kathir reports that Qatādah said this refers to Musa — and Ibn Kathir comments that this, and Allah knows best, is like the earlier statement in ayah 44, except that here Allah puts it in a different and more specific way, by describing it as **a call**. The passage moves from "We made clear the commandment" to "We called": from what was communicated to the act of communicating. He gathers the parallels: *"And when your Lord called Musa"* (26:10); *"When his Lord called him in the sacred valley of Ṭuwā"* (79:16); *"And We called him from the right side of aṭ-Ṭūr, and made him draw near to Us for a talk with him"* (19:52).

This is why Ibn Kathir opened the passage by naming Musa "the speaker" — and why he introduced these ayat by saying that Allah began His revelation to Musa and spoke with him. The verses are left to stand as Allah has spoken them.

## The turn: mercy, and a people with no warner

Everything so far has been negation. Ayah 46 pivots on a single word: *wa lākin* — **"But as a mercy from your Lord."** Ibn Kathir renders the sense: you were not a witness to any of those things, but Allah has revealed them to you and told you about them as a mercy from Him to you and to His servants, by sending you to them. The Prophet's ﷺ absence from those scenes is not a deficiency to be explained away. It is the very thing that makes his knowledge a gift, and his being sent a mercy that reaches everyone he is sent to.

**"To give warning to a people to whom no warner had come before you, in order that they may remember or receive admonition."** Ibn Kathir: so that they may be guided by that which you bring from Allah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān asks who "a people" refers to, and answers: the Arabs, who are the progeny of Sayyidunā Ismāʿīl (peace be upon him). No prophet was sent to this people after Ismāʿīl until the Prophet ﷺ was sent — the same subject, it notes, that will follow in Sūrah Yāsīn.

But does that conflict with *"There is no community but there has come a warner among them"* (35:24)? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says no: what the present verse means is that there was no prophet in this particular people **for a long time** after Ismāʿīl — and after the arrival of the Prophet ﷺ that void was filled up. Read that way, the two verses answer to each other rather than collide.

## Ayah 47 — the excuse that will never be made

*"And if We had not sent you — in case a calamity should seize them for what their hands have sent forth, they would have said: 'Our Lord! Why did You not send us a Messenger? We would then have followed Your Ayat and would have been among the believers.'"*

Ibn Kathir gives the sense: We have sent you to them to establish proof against them, and to give them no excuse when the punishment of Allah comes to them because of their disbelief — lest they offer the excuse that no Messenger or warner came to them.

Notice how the ayah works. It sets up the objection the disbelievers *would* have raised, in their own imagined words, complete with the promise they would have made — *"we would then have followed Your Ayat and would have been among the believers."* Allah quotes the excuse before it can be spoken, and by sending the Messenger, makes it unsayable. This is the mercy of ayah 46 shown from its other side: revelation arrives before judgement, so that no one stands on that Day with a legitimate grievance.

Ibn Kathir gathers the Qurʼān's other statements of the same principle, after Allah revealed His blessed Book the Qurʼān. *"Lest you should say: 'The Book was sent down only to two sects before us, and for our part, we were in fact unaware of what they studied.' Or lest you should say: 'If only the Book had been sent down to us, we would surely have been better guided than they.' So now has come unto you a clear proof from your Lord, and a guidance and a mercy"* (6:156–157). *"Messengers as bearers of good news as well as warning, in order that mankind should have no plea against Allah after the Messengers"* (4:165). *"O People of the Scripture! Now has come to you Our Messenger making things clear unto you, after a break in the series of Messengers, lest you say: 'There came unto us no bringer of glad tidings and no warner'"* (5:19). And there are many similar ayat, Ibn Kathir notes — this is one of the Qurʼān's steady themes.

## Living it

**Take the Qurʼān's history as evidence, not decoration.** Ibn Kathir's argument is meant to be felt: an illiterate man, among a people who knew nothing of such things, describing which side of a mountain a tree stood on. When you read a story in the Qurʼān, part of what you are reading is the proof that it came from Allah.

**Handle mixed sources the way the scholars said to.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's ruling on the altered scriptures is stated as a general principle: the same applies to all books that are a mixture of right and wrong. Such material is safe ground only for those who can distinguish the two — and distinguishing right from wrong is precisely what Maʿārif defines *baṣīrah* as.

**Recognise what has been closed off to you.** Ayah 47 removes an excuse. Allah sent the Messenger so that no one could plead that no warner reached them. The flip side of a mercy that arrives in time is a responsibility that cannot be handed back.

**Ask for baṣīrah, not just information.** The Tawrah was given as *baṣāʾir* — that light Allah places in hearts, by which people find out the truth and tell right from wrong — and both ayah 43 and ayah 46 end on the same hope: *laʿallahum yatadhakkarūn*, that they may remember, that they may receive admonition. Revelation is given so that something dormant in a person wakes up. The reading is not finished until that happens.

passages.title: Demanding signs like those of Moses
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat record an objection the Quraysh raised against the Prophet ﷺ — "why wasn't he given what Musa was given?" — and Allah's answer to it. What holds them together is a single argument: the objection is not a sincere request for evidence but an excuse, and Allah exposes it by pointing to history (ayah 48), by issuing a challenge no one takes up (ayah 49), and by naming what is actually driving the refusal (ayah 50).

## The excuse that Allah closed off

Ibn Kathir sets the scene. Allah tells us that if people were to be punished before proof was established against them, they would use the excuse that no Messenger came to them. So the Messenger came. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes on ayah 46 — "so that you warn a people to whom no warner has come before" — that "a people" here means the Arabs, the progeny of Sayyidnā Ismāʿīl (peace be upon him), to whom no prophet was sent after Ismāʿīl until the Holy Prophet ﷺ was sent.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to add that this verse is not in conflict with the other verse, "There is no community, but there has come a warner among them" (35:24). What 28:46 means is that there was no prophet in *this* people for a long time after Ismāʿīl — and after the arrival of the Holy Prophet ﷺ that void was filled up.

So the excuse was closed. Proof had arrived. And ayah 48 shows what happened next: **"But when the truth came to them from Us, they said, 'Why is he not given the like of what was given to Musa?'"** Ibn Kathir describes the spirit in which that was said — it came "in their stubbornness, disbelief, ignorance and misguided thinking." The demand looks like a demand for evidence. It functions as a replacement excuse.

## What they were asking for

To feel the objection you have to know what "the like of what was given to Musa" meant to them. Ibn Kathir spells it out: the staff; the hand; the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood; the destruction of crops and fruits, which made things difficult for the enemies of Allah; the parting of the sea; the clouds shading the Children of Israel in the wilderness; the manna and quails — "and other clear signs and definitive proof," miracles which Allah wrought at the hands of Musa as evidence and proof against Firʿawn, his chiefs, and the Children of Israel.

That is an enormous catalogue of visible, physical, undeniable wonders. And that is exactly the trap in the question. The Quraysh were saying: give us *that* kind of proof and we will believe.

## The historical answer: it never worked

Allah's reply in the same ayah is devastatingly simple — **"Did they not disbelieve in that which was given to Musa of old?"** Ibn Kathir paraphrases it as a question put to all of mankind: did not mankind disbelieve in those mighty signs which were given to Musa?

They did. Ibn Kathir points out that all of it had no effect on Firʿawn and his chiefs; on the contrary, they denied Musa and his brother Harun: **"Have you come to us to turn us away from what we found our fathers following, and that you two may have greatness in the land? We are not going to believe you two!"** (10:78) — and the outcome: **"So they denied them both and became of those who were destroyed."** (23:48)

This is the heart of the passage. The signs were not lacking; the willingness was. Notice too what Firʿawn's objection rests on: what "we found our fathers following," and suspicion of the messengers' motives. Not evidence — inheritance and ego. A man who will not believe does not need a bigger miracle. He needs a different heart. Ibn Kathir titles this section plainly: the rebellious do not believe in miracles.

## "Two kinds of magic, each helping the other"

Then the ayah quotes what the deniers said: **"Two kinds of magic, each helping the other!" And they said, "Verily, in both we are disbelievers."** The Arabic is *siḥrāni taẓāharā*, and Ibn Kathir glosses "each helping the other" as "cooperating or working one with the other" — backing each other up. The follow-up, *innā bi-kullin kāfirūn*, means, as Ibn Kathir puts it, "we disbelieve in each of them" — a blanket rejection of both. And he adds a note here: "Because of the close relationship between Musa and Harun, mention of one includes the other."

**But which two are being called "magic"?** The commentators differ, and Ibn Kathir reports both views rather than settling one.

**First view: Musa and Harun.** Mujahid bin Jabr said the Jews told Quraysh to say this to Muhammad ﷺ — so the phrase refers to Musa and Harun, may the peace and blessings of Allah be upon them both, and *taẓāharā* means "working together and supporting one another." Ibn Kathir notes that Saʿid bin Jubayr and Abu Razin also held that "two kinds of magic" referred to Musa and Harun, and he comments: "This is a good suggestion. And Allah knows best." On this reading, the accusation is a slur against two brothers said to be propping each other up.

**Second view: the Tawrah and the Qur'an.** ʿAli bin Abi Talhah and Al-ʿAwfi reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that the two "magics" are the two Books. The reason given for this reading is what Allah says next: the reply is "Then bring a Book from Allah, which is a better guide **than these two**." If the answer speaks of two Books, the accusation was about two Books.

That detail is worth pausing on. The whole identification turns on the small phrase "than these two" in the very next ayah. This is how classical tafsir works: a few letters at the end of a word decide whose reputation is being defended.

## The Tawrah and the Qur'an together

Taking the second reading, Ibn Kathir observes that Allah often mentions the Tawrah and the Qur'an together:

- "Say: 'Who then sent down the Book which Musa brought, a light and a guidance to mankind...'" leading to "And this is a blessed Book which We have sent down" (6:91–92).
- "Then We gave Musa the Book, to complete (Our favour) upon those who would do right" (6:154), followed by "And this is a blessed Book which We have sent down, so follow it and have Taqwa of Allah, that you may receive mercy" (6:155). (*Taqwa* is mindfulness of Allah — living with awareness that Allah sees you.)
- Even the jinn who heard the Qur'an described it this way: "Verily, we have heard a Book sent down after Musa, confirming what came before it" (46:30).

Ibn Kathir then states the judgement: those who are possessed of insight know instinctively that among the many Books Allah has sent down to His Prophets, there is no Book more perfect, more eloquent or more noble than the Book He revealed to Muhammad ﷺ, which is the Qur'an; and next to it in status and greatness is the Book Allah revealed to Musa bin ʿImran, of which Allah says, "Verily, We did send down the Tawrah, therein was guidance and light, by which the Prophets, who submitted themselves to Allah's will, judged for the Jews. And the rabbis and the priests, for to them was entrusted the protection of Allah's Book, and they were witnesses thereto" (5:44). The Injil, he adds, was revealed as a continuation and complement of the Tawrah, and to permit some of the things that had been forbidden to the Children of Israel.

The point is not incidental. The people mocking these two Books as "magic" were mocking the two greatest bodies of guidance Allah ever sent down.

## Ayah 49: the challenge

**"Say: 'Then bring a Book from Allah, which is a better guide than these two, that I may follow it, if you are truthful.'"**

Look at the shape of the reply. The Prophet ﷺ is not told to argue about miracles; he is told to raise the stakes and hand them the burden. You reject both Books? Fine — produce something better and *I* will follow it. The offer is genuine in form and impossible in fact.

"If you are truthful" is the sting. Ibn Kathir explains it as: truthful "in your efforts to refute the truth with false arguments." That is, if your rejection were really about the evidence not being good enough, you would be able to name what "good enough" looks like. Bring it forward.

And this is why the standard of judgement in the ayah is *guidance* — "a better guide" — not spectacle. A staff turning into a serpent settles an argument for a moment; a Book that guides settles a life. The Quraysh asked for wonders; Allah answered on the ground of guidance, which is what a Book is actually for.

## Ayah 50: naming the real cause

**"So if they fail to respond to you, then know that they only follow their own desires."**

Ibn Kathir explains "if they answer you not" as: if they do not respond to what you tell them, and do not follow the truth. Their failure to answer is itself the verdict.

"They only follow their own desires" — Ibn Kathir's gloss on this is stark: it means "with no basis or evidence." That is the diagnosis of the whole passage. The demand for Musa-like signs was never about the strength of the evidence. It was appetite wearing the costume of argument.

Then the ayah puts a question that answers itself: **"And who is more astray than one who follows his own desires, without guidance from Allah?"** Ibn Kathir explains "without guidance from Allah" as: with no guidance taken from the Book of Allah. So the two options are exhaustive. Either a man's life is steered by what Allah revealed, or it is steered by what he happens to want — and there is no third rail. The comparative "more astray" implies there is no deeper form of lostness available: you have taken the very faculty meant to be led, and made it the leader.

And the passage closes: **"Verily, Allah guides not the wrongdoing people."** In its context this describes those who have already turned away after the truth reached them, produced no answer to the challenge, and followed their own desires instead — the wrongdoers.

The ayah immediately after (51) reveals the mercy still running underneath the rebuke: "And indeed now We have conveyed the Word to them, in order that they may remember." Mujahid said this means "We have explained the Word to them," and As-Suddi said something similar; Qatadah said Allah is saying that He has told them what He did in the past and what He will do in the future — and Mujahid and others said that "conveyed the Word to them" means to Quraysh. Even while condemning the excuse, Allah kept delivering the message, in the hope they would take heed.

## Living it

**Be honest about what would actually change your mind.** The Quraysh asked for signs like Musa's, and the answer came back that those very signs had already been disbelieved. If someone keeps raising the bar for evidence, the bar was never the problem. It is worth asking yourself the same question about a command you find inconvenient: am I unconvinced, or unwilling?
