**Weigh guidance, not spectacle.** Ayah 49 makes "a better guide" the measure of a revelation. The judgement Ibn Kathir records about the Qur'an — that no Book Allah sent down is more perfect, eloquent or noble — is a claim to be tested by living with it, not merely admired from a distance.

**Watch the two masters.** Ayah 50 leaves exactly two possibilities: guidance taken from the Book of Allah, or one's own desires. Every ruling you set aside because it does not suit you is a small transfer of authority from the first to the second. The remedy the ayat point to is the one in the next breath — the Word has been conveyed and explained "in order that they may remember." Guidance is available; remembering is our part.

passages.title: Scripture-people who believe and are doubly rewarded
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat turn from the stubbornness of those who reject the truth to a very different kind of listener: people who already had a Scripture, recognised the Qur'an when they heard it, and accepted it — and whom Allah then describes, in four short strokes, as models of character. What holds the passage together is a single contrast: Allah has delivered His Word continuously (ayah 51), and the question is only who receives it. Quraysh, who had just dismissed what came to them as "two kinds of magic," did not. Certain People of the Book did — and ayat 52–55 tell us both what they said and how they lived.

## The setting, briefly

Ibn Kathir reads ayah 51 as the close of an argument that begins a few ayat earlier. Allah had said that if people were punished before proof reached them, they could plead that no Messenger had come. But when the truth did come through Muhammad ﷺ, they answered with stubbornness: *"Why is he not given the like of what was given to Musa?"* (ayah 48).

Ibn Kathir's reply is the hinge. He lists what Musa was in fact given — and Allah knows best — the staff, the hand, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the ruin of crops and fruits, the parting of the sea, the cloud that shaded the Children of Israel, the manna and the quails. Then comes the point that dismantles the whole request: **all of that was given, and it changed nothing.** Fir'awn and his chiefs still denied Musa and Harun (10:78), and *"they denied them both and became of those who were destroyed"* (23:48). Hence Allah's own answer within ayah 48: *Did they not disbelieve in that which was given to Musa of old?*

As for the taunt *"two kinds of magic, each helping the other"* (siḥrāni taẓāharā — the verb means cooperating, backing one another up), Ibn Kathir records two readings without forcing a choice. Mujahid bin Jabr said the Jews told Quraysh to say this, and that it refers to **Musa and Harun**; Sa'id bin Jubayr and Abu Razin held the same, and Ibn Kathir calls it "a good suggestion." Alternatively, 'Ali bin Abi Talhah and Al-'Awfi reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it means **the Tawrah and the Qur'an** — supported, Ibn Kathir notes, by the challenge in the very next ayah: *Say: "Then bring a Book from Allah, which is a better guide than these two, that I may follow it"* (ayah 49). And if they will not answer that challenge, ayah 50 states the verdict: *they only follow their own lusts* — with no basis or evidence, says Ibn Kathir; *without guidance from Allah* meaning with no guidance taken from the Book of Allah.

That is the audience. Now the ayah about the Word itself.

## Ayah 51: a Word conveyed one after the other

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that **waṣṣalnā** comes from *tawṣīl*, whose literal sense is **to strengthen a rope by adding more strands to its strands**. The image is rope-making: strand joined to strand until it will bear weight. That is what Allah has done with guidance — He has *maintained its continuity*, message joined to message, which is why certain subjects of admonition recur throughout the Qur'an: the repetition is what makes them effective.

The early authorities Ibn Kathir cites fill this out from different angles. **Mujahid**: "We have explained the Word to them," and As-Suddi said something similar. **Qatadah**: "He has told them what He did in the past and what He will do in the future." Mujahid and others say *"to them"* here means **to Quraysh**. And the purpose is stated plainly: *la'allahum yatadhakkarūn* — in order that they may remember.

**Living it.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a rule for anyone who calls others to good out of this one word. A defining trait of the prophets' preaching was that they conveyed the truth *continuously*. Rejection and denial did not deter them at all. If someone did not listen the first time, they said it a second time; if not then, a third; and so on, without any sign of exhaustion. No preacher and no well-wisher has the power to change a heart — but what the prophets could do was keep making the effort without becoming disheartened. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same principle applies today, and that those who preach should take serious note of it.

## Ayat 52–53: the ones who recognised it

*Those to whom We gave the Scripture before it, they believe in it. And when it is recited to them, they say: "We believe in it. Verily, it is the truth from our Lord. Indeed even before it we have been from Muslims."*

Ibn Kathir says this is Allah telling us that **the pious scholars among the People of the Book believe in the Qur'an**, and he strings together the parallel ayat: 2:121, on those who recite the Book as it should be recited; 3:199, on those among them who believe *"humbling themselves before Allah"*; 17:107–108, on those given knowledge who *"fall down on their faces in humble prostration"* when it is recited; and 5:82–83, on those nearest in love to the believers, who pray, *"so write us down among the witnesses."*

**The occasion.** Sa'id bin Jubayr said these ayat were revealed concerning **seventy priests sent by An-Najashi**, the ruler of Ethiopia. When they came to the Prophet ﷺ he recited to them *Ya Sin. By the Qur'an, full of wisdom* (36:1–2) until he completed the Surah. **They began to weep, and they embraced Islam** — and these ayat were revealed concerning them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān preserves related reports. Sayyidna Ibn 'Abbas reported that **forty courtiers of Najashi** came to Madinah while the Prophet ﷺ was occupied with the Battle of Khaybar; they joined the fighting, some were wounded, none were killed. Noticing the economic hardship the Companions were living in, they told the Prophet ﷺ that they were, by Allah's grace, quite wealthy, and sought his permission to bring some of it on their next visit — and on that occasion ayat 52–54 were revealed (Marduya, Tabrani, Mazhari). Sayyidna Sa'id Ibn Jubair also narrated that when Sayyidna Ja'far went to Habshah before the hijrah to Madinah and presented the teachings of Islam in Najashi's court, Najashi and many of his courtiers — people of the Book — submitted to Islam, as Allah had put faith in their hearts (Mazhari).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's framing of the ayah is that it speaks of those People of the Book who, **on the strength of the prophecies given in the Torah and the Injil, already had faith in the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ and in the revelation of the Qur'an before either had come** — so when he ﷺ announced his prophethood, they accepted.

## "We were Muslims even before this"

Their words in ayah 53 raise a real question, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats it carefully. Ibn Kathir's plain reading is: *even before the Qur'an came we were Muslims* — that is, we believed in One Allah and were sincerely responding to Allah's commands.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the two possibilities:

1. If **muslim** is taken in its **literal** sense — submissive, obedient — the meaning is clear: the faith they had in the Qur'an and the Prophet ﷺ through their own Books is being described with the words *islam* and *muslim* in that root sense of submission.
2. If **Muslim** is taken in the sense in which it is the **appellation of the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ**, then the ayah would signify that "Islam" and "Muslim" are not restricted to this Ummah but are common to the Ummahs of all the prophets.

Against the second, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that some ayat suggest these are special names for this Ummah — such as the assertion of Sayyidna Ibrahim recorded in the Qur'an, *"He named you as Muslims"* (22:78). **'Allamah Suyuti** favoured that line of argument and wrote a book on the subject in support of his contention; he explained our ayah to mean *"we were ready and prepared to accept Islam even before."*

Mufti Muhammad Shafi' then reconciles the two: looked at deeply, there is no conflict. Islam can be the common attribute of the religion of all the prophets in its literal sense, and at the same time a special appellation of the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ. He gives the analogy of *Siddiq* and *Faruq*: exclusive to Abu Bakr and 'Umar within this Ummah, yet as descriptive words applicable to anyone else who falls within their attributive meaning.

## Ayah 54: why the reward is doubled

*These will be given their reward twice over, because they are patient, and repel evil with good, and spend out of what We have provided for them.*

Ibn Kathir: this is for those who have this characteristic — **they believed in the first Book and then in the second**. And *because they are patient* means patience **in their adherence to the truth**, "for taking such a thing upon oneself is not easy for people."

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir reports that it was recorded in the Sahih, from 'Amir Ash-Sha'bi from Abu Burdah, that Abu Musa Al-Ash'ari (may Allah be pleased with him) said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"There are three who will be given their reward twice: a man among the People of the Book who believed in his Prophet then believed in me; a slave who fulfils his duty towards Allah and towards his master; and a man who has a slave woman and educates her and teaches her good manners, then he frees her and marries her."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān refers to the same teaching as a hadith of Sahih al-Bukhari.

Ibn Kathir also records that **Imam Ahmad** reported from Abu Umamah: "On the day of the Conquest of Makkah I was walking alongside the Messenger of Allah ﷺ as he was riding, and he said some very beautiful words, including: *'Whoever among the people of the two Books becomes Muslim, he will have his reward twice, and he has the same rights and duties as we do. Whoever among the idolators becomes Muslim will have one reward, and he has the same rights and duties as we do.'*" The second half of each clause is worth noticing: in both cases, *the same rights and duties as we do*.

**A subtle point on the wording.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pairs this ayah with the promise made to the wives of the Prophet ﷺ: *"whoever from among you stands in obedience to Allah and His Messenger and does righteous deeds, We will give her, her reward twice"* (33:31). Then it asks the obvious question: *why* is the reward doubled?

One possible cause is that each of these people has done **two** good deeds — believing in one's own prophet and then in the Prophet ﷺ; loving and obeying him ﷺ both as prophet and as husband; freeing a slave woman and then marrying her. But Mufti Muhammad Shafi' raises an objection to that: two rewards for two deeds applies to everybody according to the norms of justice — so where is the distinction? Allah has declared, *"I do not let go to waste the labour of a worker from you"* (3:195), so every single good deed is already rewarded.

His own answer, which he says he has set out fully in his *Ahkam ul-Qur'an* under Surah Al-Qasas, rests on the exact wording. Had the meaning been "two rewards," the appropriate word would have been *ajrayn* (two rewards). Instead the Qur'an says **ajrahum marratayn** — *their reward twice*. In that phrasing is a clear hint that **all their good deeds will be written twice**: two rewards for a single prayer, two for a single charity, two for each good deed such as fasting or performing Hajj.

As for *why* these particular people were chosen for so extraordinary a reward, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the straight answer first: **it is Allah's prerogative** to declare any deed preferable or superior to others and to enhance its reward, and no one has the right to question why He increased the reward of one act and not another. It is possible that the rank of these deeds is simply higher in His sight. Some prominent scholars have given as the reason that these things require **excessive effort and hardship** — an explanation Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls probable, taking *bimā ṣabarū*, "because they observed patience," at the end of the ayah as evidence for it. And Allah knows best.

## Repelling evil with good

Ibn Kathir's gloss on *yadra'ūna bil-ḥasanati as-sayyi'ah* is short and clear: **they do not respond to evil in kind; rather they forgive and overlook.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that scholars explained "good" and "evil" here in more than one way:

- **Good deed = obedience, evil = sin.** Every good deed wipes out the sin. The Prophet ﷺ told Sayyidna Mu'adh Ibn Jabal to perform a good deed after an evil deed, and it will wipe out the evil. On this reading, the ayah is praising these people because whenever they commit a wrong by mistake, they wipe it out by doing some good.
- **Good = knowledge and serenity, evil = ignorance and negligence.** On this reading, they respond to the ignorant acts of others with serenity and forbearance, not with a similar ignorance.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes that there is no contradiction between these: the words *ḥasanah* and *sayyi'ah* encompass all of it. And it draws **two important pieces of advice**: first, if someone commits a sin, the best remedy is to look for some good to do, since the virtuous deed becomes expiation for it. Second, if a person is wronged, he is within his right to take revenge provided he does not exceed the wrong done to him — **but it is much better to return cruelty with kindness and evil with virtue**. That is nobility of character of a high degree, with innumerable benefits in this world and the Hereafter, as another ayah says in very clear words: *"Repel with that which is fairer, and behold, he between whom and you there is enmity shall be as if he were a loyal friend"* (41:34).

The third quality, *and spend out of what We have provided for them*, Ibn Kathir explains as: out of the **lawful** provision Allah has given them, they spend on their families and relatives as they are required to do, and they pay Zakah and give voluntary charity.

## Ayah 55: walking away with dignity

*And when they hear evil vain talk, they withdraw from it and say: "To us our deeds, and to you your deeds. Peace be to you. We seek not the way of the ignorant."*

**Laghw** here is idle, worthless talk. Ibn Kathir says that withdrawing from it means **they do not mix with the people who indulge in such talk** — rather they do as Allah describes elsewhere: *"and if they pass by some evil vain talk, they pass by it with dignity"* (25:72).

Then the picture sharpens. If some foolish person speaks to them in a foolish manner and says something to which it does not befit them to respond, they turn away and **do not respond in kind with ugly speech. They never say anything but good words.** Their line is drawn without insult: *to us our deeds, and to you your deeds* — meaning, as Ibn Kathir puts it, we do not seek the way of the ignorant and we do not like it.

**A precise point about the "salām."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the good quality here: when these people hear something stupid from an ignorant foe, they simply say *salam* instead of giving a reply, and do not entangle themselves with the ignorant. It quotes **Imam Jassas**: there are two kinds of salam. One is for **salutation**, as Muslims greet one another. The other is for *musālamah* — adopting a peaceful attitude — and *mutārakah*, avoiding debate: it conveys to one's adversary that one does not wish to take note of his stupidity. **Here the second meaning is intended.** So this is not warmth being offered to a provocateur; it is a dignified declining to be drawn in.

## What the passage leaves us with

Read as one unit, ayat 51–55 set two responses to the same continuously conveyed Word side by side. One group answered with taunts and a demand for signs like Musa's — signs which, as Ibn Kathir points out, had already been given once and refused. The other group wept when they heard it, believed, and said *it is the truth from our Lord.* And Allah does not stop at their creed; He describes their **conduct**: patience in adhering to the truth, repelling evil with good, spending from lawful provision on family, Zakah and voluntary charity, and turning away from vain talk with a *salām* rather than a retort.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's two pieces of advice are the practical residue of all this: when you fall into a sin, go looking for a good deed to wipe it out; and when you are wronged, though justice permits you an equal response, it is far better to return the cruelty with kindness — for then, as Allah promises, the one between whom and you there was enmity may become as a loyal friend (41:34).

passages.title: Guidance is Allah's; the sanctuary excuse
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat place a limit and then remove an excuse. In ayah 56 Allah tells His Messenger ﷺ that he cannot put faith into another person, however dearly he loves him: guidance, in its deepest sense, belongs to Allah alone. In ayah 57 we hear the Makkans refusing that guidance with a very practical-sounding fear — *we would be snatched away from our land* — and Allah answers by pointing at the ground under their feet. What holds the passage together is a single question: who actually gives what a person is afraid of losing? Faith, safety, food, provision — none of it is in the hands of the one who fears, nor even in the hands of the Prophet ﷺ who loves him. It is all with Allah.

## "You surely cannot guide whoever you like"

Ibn Kathir renders Allah's address to His Messenger ﷺ plainly: *the matter does not rest with you; all that you have to do is convey the Message, and Allah will guide whom He wills, and His is the ultimate wisdom.* He sets the ayah beside two others of the same family — "Not upon you is their guidance, but Allah guides whom He wills" (2:272), and "And most of mankind will not believe even if you desire it eagerly" (12:103) — and notes that our ayah is more specific still.

**Two meanings of *hidāyah*.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the key word carefully, because a careless reading turns this ayah into a contradiction. *Hidāyah*, guidance, is used for several meanings. One meaning is **to show the path** — which does not necessarily mean that the one shown it will reach his destination. Another meaning is **to make a person reach his destination**. In the first sense, Maʿārif says, it is obvious that the Holy Prophet ﷺ and all the prophets before him *were* guides, and that imparting guidance was within their control, since it was the obligation of their duty — for if they had no control over it, how could they have fulfilled that obligation at all? So the denial in this ayah must belong to the second sense: it was not his duty or obligation to put faith into someone's heart and so make him a Muslim through his teaching and preaching. That is in the control of Allah alone.

This distinction is worth holding onto. It does not shrink the Prophet's ﷺ role; it defines it exactly. Conveying the message, teaching, preaching, showing the path — all of that was his. The final placing of faith inside a heart was not, and was never meant to be.

**"Whoever you like."** The limit is drawn precisely at the point of love, which is exactly where a person feels most entitled to expect a result. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes this explicit: it was the Prophet's ﷺ great desire that his uncle Abu Talib should accept the faith, and it was because of that desire that he was told it was not within his control to put faith in anybody's heart.

## The deathbed of Abu Talib

Ibn Kathir reports that it is recorded in the Two Sahihs that this ayah was revealed concerning **Abu Talib**, the paternal uncle of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān likewise cites Sahih Muslim for the same occasion.

Ibn Kathir describes the relationship with real precision: Abu Talib used to protect the Prophet ﷺ, support him and stand by him, and he loved him dearly — **but this love was a natural love, born of kinship, not a love born of the fact that he was the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.** That single sentence is the hinge of the whole story. Blood-loyalty is not faith. A man can shield the Prophet ﷺ and still not accept what the Prophet ﷺ came with.

The narration comes through Az-Zuhri, who said: Sa'id bin Al-Musayyib narrated to me that his father, Al-Musayyib bin Hazan Al-Makhzumi, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

> When Abu Talib was dying, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to him and found Abu Jahl bin Hisham and 'Abdullah bin Abi Umayyah bin Al-Mughirah with him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"O my uncle, say *La ilaha illallah* — a word which I may use as evidence in your favour before Allah."** Abu Jahl bin Hisham and 'Abdullah bin Abi Umayyah said: "O Abu Talib, will you leave the religion of 'Abdul-Muttalib?" The Messenger of Allah kept urging him to say *La ilaha illallah*, and they kept saying, "Will you leave the religion of 'Abdul-Muttalib?" — until, at the very end, he said that he was on the religion of 'Abdul-Muttalib, and he refused to say *La ilaha illallah*.

Ibn Kathir notes this was recorded by Al-Bukhari and Muslim from the hadith of Az-Zuhri.

Notice what the dying man was actually asked for: one sentence. And notice what was set against it — not an argument, but a question repeated at his bedside about the religion of 'Abdul-Muttalib. That is what he held to at the end.

The Prophet ﷺ then said, **"By Allah, I shall certainly seek forgiveness for you unless I am told not to."** Ibn Kathir records that Allah then revealed, "It is not proper for the Prophet and those who believe to ask Allah's forgiveness for the idolaters, even though they be of kin" (9:113) — and concerning Abu Talib was revealed our ayah, "Verily, you guide not whom you like, but Allah guides whom He wills."

Ibn Kathir closes the account with restraint: when Abu Talib was on his deathbed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called him to faith and to enter Islam, *but the decree overtook him and he remained a follower of disbelief, and Allah's is the complete wisdom.*

**A note of adab.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes *Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī*: one should abstain from discussing or passing judgment unnecessarily on the question of whether Abu Talib accepted faith, because this may hurt the feelings of the Holy Prophet ﷺ, given his natural love for his uncle. That is a striking piece of etiquette — the sources tell us what happened, and then tell us not to make a debating topic out of another man's ending. *And Allah, glorified and exalted, knows best.*

## "And He knows best those who are guided"

The ayah does not end with the limit; it ends with Allah's knowledge. Ibn Kathir explains: **Allah knows best who deserves to be guided and who deserves to be misguided.** The believer is therefore left in a settled place rather than a bitter one. We do not know who will end where, and we are not asked to know. Affirm Allah's will and His knowledge as they are stated here, without imagining them as some human deciding-and-finding-out, and without emptying them of meaning.

## Ayah 57: the excuse of the frightened

Now the scene shifts from a deathbed to a negotiation. "And they say: 'If we follow the guidance with you, we would be snatched away from our land.'"

Ibn Kathir tells us this is the excuse given by some of the disbelievers for not following true guidance, and spells out the fear behind the words: *we are afraid that if we follow the message of guidance that you have brought, and go against the pagan Arab tribes around us, they will seek to do us harm and wage war against us, and they may snatch us away from wherever we may be.* They are not picturing a debate; they are picturing being torn out of their land.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds who said it: it reports, citing Nasai and others, that **Harith Ibn 'Uthman** and other disbelievers of Makkah put this forward as one of their reasons for not accepting faith — and, importantly, **they believed that his teachings were based on truth.** Their objection was never that the message was false. Their objection was the cost: that the entire people of Arabia would turn against them, and they would be driven out of their land.

That is a recognisable species of refusal. It is not intellectual at all. It is calculation dressed up as caution — *I know it is true, but I cannot afford it.*

## Allah's answer: look at the ground you are standing on

"Have We not established for them a secure sanctuary, to which are brought fruits of all kinds, a provision from Ourselves?"

Ibn Kathir is blunt: **the excuse they give is a lie and is false**, because Allah has put them in a secure city and a venerated sanctuary which has been safe from the time it was built. Then comes his pointed question: how could this sanctuary be safe for them while they believed in disbelief and *shirk* — associating others with Allah — and then somehow *not* be safe for them once they became Muslims and followed the truth?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in what that safety actually looked like on the ground. Allah had already made special arrangements for the safety of the people of Makkah by making its land *Ḥaram*, a sacred inviolable precinct. All the tribes of Arabia, despite their mutual feuds and their disbelief, were unanimous that killing and feuding were strictly prohibited on the land of Makkah. If the killer of a man's father met the son inside the Ḥaram, then despite extremely strong feelings of revenge he could not raise his hand against him. It was simply not possible for anyone to kill or harm his enemy on that ground. So, Maʿārif concludes, it was not at all a convincing excuse: how could the Creator of everything let them die as believers when He had arranged their safety in the Ḥaram even while they were disbelievers? Maʿārif notes that the Qur'an gives three answers to this lame excuse, and dwells on this first one at length.

Maʿārif also relays **Yahya Ibn Sallam's** explanation of the ayah, as cited by Qurtubi, which turns their logic inside out: *You were safe and secure because of the Ḥaram, and you were enjoying the sustenance I provided in plenty — and still you used to worship others instead of Me. You did not get worried over that situation of yours; on the contrary, you got worried over believing in Me.*

## "Fruits of all kinds — a provision from Ourselves"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that two qualities of the Ḥaram are described in this ayah: that it is a place of peace, and that fruits from different parts of the world were brought there.

On the second, Ibn Kathir explains simply: all kinds of fruits came from the surrounding regions, from At-Ta'if and elsewhere, and likewise the people of Makkah engaged in trade, with other goods coming into their city.

Maʿārif draws attention to an odd choice of words. Fruits are the product of trees, so it would have seemed apt to say *thamarātu kulli shajar* — "the fruits of every **tree**." Instead the Qur'an says *thamarātu kulli shay'* — "the fruits of every **thing**." It is quite likely, Maʿārif suggests, that "everything" here encompasses produce and products of all kinds, including agricultural produce: the output of an industrial factory is also, in this sense, its "fruit." The promise, then, is not merely food but all sorts of things of human need.

And Maʿārif points out how improbable this is in that place. Allah chose Makkah Mukarramah, out of the whole world, to establish the Ka'bah and the Ḥaram — a region whose environment and geography are such that, under normal circumstances, hardly any economic or commercial goods and activity should have existed there. Even basic staples like wheat, rice, gram and sundry cereals were not cultivated before on any significant scale, let alone a variety of vegetables (though in recent years, Maʿārif notes, the Saudi Government has put some emphasis on their cultivation). Yet everything is available there in such abundance that one is amazed. During hajj some two million people are drawn from all over the world and stay for an average of a month; it has never been heard that any scarcity of food was experienced there. On the contrary, cooked and prepared food catering to all types of races and peoples is readily available at all times. Anyone visiting Makkah for hajj or 'umrah can confirm that everything produced anywhere in the world is readily available there.

Set that against the excuse and the argument collapses. The Lord who was so kind to them that He made all the bounties of the world available in their city, despite the fact that they are not produced there, and who made that city completely free of risk and danger — Maʿārif calls it *the worst kind of ignorance* to presume of Him that He would deprive them of these benefits if they believed in Him.

## "But most of them know not"

The passage ends where it began, with knowledge. Ibn Kathir's comment on the closing words is a single sentence, and it explains everything that came before: *this is why they said what they said.* They spoke as they did because they did not know **whose** provision they were living on. Had they recognised the hand behind the safety and the fruit, the fear that stopped them believing would have had nothing to stand on.

## Living it

**Carry the message, not the outcome.** Ibn Kathir sums up the Messenger's ﷺ own brief: all that you have to do is convey the Message, and Allah will guide whom He wills. If the one who loved Abu Talib was not given the power to put faith in his heart, then that was never our part of the work either. Speak, teach, show the path — and hand the result back to Allah.

**Do not let love become despair, or resentment.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that this ayah came in response to the Prophet's ﷺ great desire that his uncle accept faith: he was told that placing faith in a heart was not in his control. And follow the adab that Maʿārif relays from *Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī*: abstain from needless argument and judgment about where other people end up.

**Name your real excuse.** The Makkans believed his teachings were based on truth and still refused, on grounds of cost — they feared all of Arabia turning against them and being driven from their land. That admission is instructive, because the modern versions rhyme: *I would lose my position, my circle, my standing.* The Qur'an's reply is not to deny that the fear feels real; it is to point at the sanctuary and the fruit and ask who has been holding them up all along — for it is, in the ayah's own words, "a provision from Ourselves."

passages.title: Ruined towns and fleeting worldly enjoyment
passages.tafsir:
This passage answers an excuse with two long views: a look backwards over ruined towns, and a look forwards to the Day when two kinds of men are set side by side. What binds ayat 58–61 together is a single argument about *what is actually worth fearing* and *what is actually worth having* — and it ends by asking the reader, quite bluntly, whether he is using his mind.

## The shape of the argument

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads these ayat as a sequence of replies to an excuse the Makkans had offered. It does not spell out the wording of that excuse, but the replies themselves show what is being answered.

**Ayah 58 is the second reply.** They should recall the plight of other disbelieving peoples of the world — how their habitations, their strong forts and all the means of their protection were destroyed, and destroyed because of their disbelief and rejection of the truth. What deserves their fear, then, is *disbelief and associating others with Allah*, since that is the real cause of destruction. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the irony sharply: how foolish and ill-informed they were, that they feared faith and did not fear the denial of truth.

**Ayah 60 is the third reply.** Just in case they did get involved in some sort of trouble as a result of accepting faith, it would last only a few days. Just as worldly wealth and comfort are temporary, so worldly troubles are transient and short-lived. Wisdom therefore lies in seeking and caring for the comfort that lasts; and if one has to suffer trouble for a short time for the sake of permanent and everlasting comfort, it is well worth it.

That is the spine of the passage. Everything else fills it in.

## Ayah 58: the town that grew insolent over its living

*"And how many a town have We destroyed, which was thankless for its means of livelihood!"*

Ibn Kathir notes that Allah is here **referring to the people of Makkah**, and explains the phrase **بَطِرَتْ مَعِيشَتَهَا** — of a people who *"were arrogant transgressors who denied Allah's blessing of giving them ample provision."* Notice the shape of the sin: not poverty but plenty badly handled. The very abundance that should have produced gratitude produced arrogance instead. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the same phrase as being *over-proud of their means of living*.

Ibn Kathir links it to the parable in Sūrah al-Naḥl: *"And Allah puts forward the example of a township, that dwelt secure and well-content: its provision coming to it in abundance from every place"* — running to *"So the torment overtook them while they were wrongdoers"* (16:112–113). Security, contentment, provision arriving from every direction: the description is of a place any of us would want to live. And the last word on them is *wrongdoers*.

**"And those are their dwellings, which have not been inhabited after them except a little."** Ibn Kathir: *"Their land became empty and desolate, and you can see nothing but their dwellings."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same of them: the habitations of the earlier peoples, destroyed by the divine torment, still lie uninhabited, with the exception of a few. The Qurʼān says *those* — pointing, as one points at something that can be seen.

### Two readings of "except a little"

The scholars differed over what the exception is measuring, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives both:

- **Zajjāj** takes the exception to be about the *places*: those places could never get inhabited, except a few that are inhabited.
- **Sayyidunā Ibn ʿAbbās** takes the exception to be about *time*, not the place and houses. Even if someone does live there, it is for a short time, like travellers, who cannot be regarded as permanent residents.

Both readings leave the same aftertaste. A house outlives the household; the dwellings stand and the people are gone.

**"And verily, We have been the heirs."** Ibn Kathir: *"Their towns became ruins, with none remaining."* An heir is the one left holding the property once the owner is gone — and here it is Allah alone who remains after every proud proprietor has been taken away.

## Ayah 59: Allah does not destroy before establishing proof

Ibn Kathir marks the turn precisely: *"Then Allah tells us of His justice and that He does not destroy anyone unjustly; on the contrary, He destroys those whom He destroys after establishing proof against them."*

So the ruins of ayah 58 are not arbitrary. Ayah 59 supplies the rule behind them: no town is destroyed *"until He sends to their mother town a Messenger reciting to them Our Ayat,"* and none is destroyed *unless the people thereof are wrongdoers*. Two conditions, both of them protections: the warning must arrive first, and the wrongdoing must be real. Ibn Kathir cites the parallel from Sūrah al-Isrāʼ: *"And We never punish until We have sent a Messenger"* (17:15).

### "Mother of the towns"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the word **أُمّ (umm)**. Its popular meaning is *mother*; and since the mother is the very basis of human creation, the word is also used extensively for *origin, base and foundation*. The pronoun in *ummihā* refers back to the towns, so *"the mother of the towns"* means the **central town**. The meaning of the ayah: Allah does not destroy a people unless He has sent His message through His messengers in their main cities. When the invitation to truth has reached them and they still do not accept it, only then does the torment come.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why messengers are generally sent to big cities rather than smaller towns: such towns are normally under the influence of the big cities, both for their economic and their educational needs. If something is known in a big city, it becomes known automatically in the smaller towns around it. So when a prophet is sent to a big city and begins his call, the message spreads to the surrounding towns in no time, and Allah's message reaches all and sundry.

Ibn Kathir identifies the mother town here as **Makkah**, and reads the ayah as indicating that *"the Unlettered Prophet, Muhammad ﷺ was sent from the Mother of Cities as a Messenger to all cities and towns, Arab and non-Arab alike."* He stacks the supporting ayat: *"so that you may warn the Mother of Towns and all those around it"* (6:92); *"Say: O mankind! Verily, I am sent to you all as the Messenger of Allah"* (7:158); *"That I may therewith warn you and whomsoever it may reach"* (6:19); and the warning that *"those of the sects that reject it, the Fire will be their promised meeting place"* (11:17). Because the Prophet ﷺ was sent to the Mother of Cities — *"their source to which they all return"* — he was thereby sent to all the towns, that is, to all mankind.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir notes that it was recorded in the Two Sahihs that the Prophet ﷺ said: *"I have been sent to the red and the black."* And he draws out what follows from that universality: *"Prophethood ended with him, and there is no Prophet or Messenger to come after him, but his way will remain as long as night and day remain, until the Day of Resurrection."*

Ibn Kathir also reads the ayah alongside 17:58 — *"And there is not a town but We shall destroy it before the Day of Resurrection, or punish it with a severe torment"* — telling us that Allah will destroy every town before the Day of Resurrection.

### A ruling the scholars drew from this ayah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes a legal principle that follows from the city–village relationship: as the smaller habitations depend on the cities for their needs, so when a law or order is promulgated in the city it automatically becomes effective in the surrounding towns and villages, and *"the excuse of having no knowledge of the law is not acceptable."*

The jurists declared the same principle applicable to the sighting of the moon for Ramadan and the two ʿĪds (Shawwāl and Dhū al-Ḥijjah): if the evidence of witnesses in the city establishes the sighting, the people of the towns and villages around it have to follow the same. In the case of *other* cities, however, it applies only when the Qāḍī of that city accepts the evidence and makes the announcement. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites *Al-Fatāwā al-Ghayāthiyyah*.)

## Ayah 60: the small size of everything you own

*"And whatever you have been given is an enjoyment of the life of the world and its adornment, and that which is with Allah is better and will remain forever."*

Ibn Kathir says the ayah tells us *"about the insignificance of this world and its contemptible adornments which are nothing in comparison to the great and lasting delights which Allah prepared for His righteous servants in the Hereafter."*

Note the sweep of *"whatever you have been given"*: not some narrow category of pleasures, but the whole inventory, everything handed to you. And note the measure being applied — not size but duration and worth *in comparison* to what is with Allah.

Ibn Kathir gathers the ayat that say the same thing from different angles: *"Whatever is with you, will be exhausted, and whatever is with Allah will remain"* (16:96); *"and that which is with Allah is the best for the most righteous"* (3:198); *"whereas the life of this world as compared with the Hereafter is but a brief passing enjoyment"* (13:26); and the diagnosis of what actually goes wrong in a person — *"Nay, you prefer the life of this world. Although the Hereafter is better and more lasting"* (87:16–17).

He then relates that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"By Allah, the life of this world in comparison to the Hereafter is as if one of you were to dip his finger in the sea; let him see what comes back to him."* Sit with the image rather than skimming it. The finger comes out wet, and the wetness is real. But hold that film of water against the sea it came out of, and you have the comparison between the two abodes.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the conclusion plainly: mundane wealth and comforts are all mortal, while the recompense one receives in the Hereafter for good deeds done in the world is much superior and everlasting; the best comforts of this world are no match for the bounties of the Hereafter; and *"there is no doubt that anyone having some sense would prefer the better comforts and the ones that will last forever, rather than the short-lived temporary ones."*

**"Have you then no sense?"** Ibn Kathir explains: *do those who prefer this world to the Hereafter have no sense?* The rebuke is aimed at the intellect, not the emotions. Preferring a smaller, briefer good over a greater, permanent one is not merely a sin here; it is a miscalculation.

### Who counts as wise

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān follows this with a striking legal illustration under the heading that the sign of prudence is that one does not involve himself too much in worldly matters and cares more for the Hereafter. **Imām Shāfiʿī** said that if a person bequeaths his wealth and property to be given to *the wisest men*, the beneficiaries of such a will are those busy in worshipping and obeying Allah — because what they are doing is the demand of wisdom, and no doubt they are the wisest among worldly people. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that this ruling is also mentioned in *Ad-Durr al-Mukhtār*, the famous book of the Ḥanafī school, in its chapter on *waṣiyyah* (bequests). The Qurʼān's *"have you then no sense?"* is thus taken so seriously that it shapes how a man's will is read.

## Ayah 61: two men, one comparison

*"Is he whom We have promised an excellent promise — which he will find true — like him whom We have made to enjoy the luxuries of the life of the world, then on the Day of Resurrection, he will be among those brought up?"*

Ibn Kathir unpacks the question: *"Is the one who believes in the reward which Allah has promised in return for righteous deeds, which he will undoubtedly attain, like one who disbelieves in the meeting with Allah and in His promises and threats? He is only enjoying a few days in this life."*

Look at how the two lives are described. The first man has a **promise** — nothing in hand yet — but the Qurʼān adds *"which he will find true"*, guaranteeing the delivery before the story ends. The second man has been given actual enjoyment now, and the sentence about him does not stop there: *"then on the Day of Resurrection, he will be among those brought up."* The clause that ruins him is the one that comes *after* the pleasure.

**"Those brought up" (al-muḥḍarūn).** **Mujāhid and Qatādah** said: *"He will be among those who are punished."* Ibn Kathir shows how the Qurʼān uses the word elsewhere — the believer in Paradise looking out at his companion who is in Hell and saying, *"Had it not been for the grace of my Lord, I would certainly have been among those brought forth (to Hell)"* (37:57), and *"but the Jinn know well that they have indeed to appear (before Him)"* (37:158).

**Who was meant?** Ibn Kathir reports that it was said this was revealed concerning the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and Abū Jahl, or that it was revealed concerning Ḥamzah and ʿAlī, and Abū Jahl — both views narrated from Mujāhid. His own judgement is that *"the apparent meaning is that it is more general than that."* The named men are specimens of a permanent contrast, not the limits of it.

## No excuse on the Day

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, commenting here, describes the scene the disbelievers are heading toward: the very first question the disbelievers will be asked at the Tumultuous Place (*maḥshar*) will be about *shirk* (associating someone else with Allah) — where are those they used to associate with Allah, and can they provide any help today? They will respond that it was not a fault of theirs, that it was Shayṭān who deluded them. The devils, asked what they have in their defence, will accept their role of deceit but plead that they only misled them and did not force them: alongside their misleading, the prophets and their deputies were guiding these people towards the right path with sound arguments, making the truth crystal clear to them. They rejected the truth the prophets brought and listened to us using their own free will and discretion.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the conclusion: if someone chooses of his own free will to follow those who wish to put him on the wrong path, despite having before him clear-cut arguments against them and the righteous way to follow, then he has no excuse to offer.

## Living it

- **Fear the right thing.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's charge against the Makkans is that they feared faith and did not fear the denial of truth. Ask of any decision not only "what will faith cost me?" but "what does refusing cost me?"
- **Watch what plenty does to you.** The town of ayah 58 was *over-proud of its means of living* — provision received without gratitude, curdling, in Ibn Kathir's words, into arrogant transgression. Prosperity is the test in this passage, not poverty.
- **Price your hardships correctly.** If following the truth brings trouble, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the trouble is as short-lived as the comforts. Both ends of this life are temporary.
- **Use your reason.** *"Have you then no sense?"* — the passage treats preferring the passing over the permanent as a failure of intelligence. Take one thing you are chasing and hold it against the image of the finger and the sea.
- **Warning always precedes ruin.** Ayah 59 shows Allah's justice: no town is destroyed until a Messenger has recited His ayat to them and they are wrongdoers. For anyone who has received the Qurʼān, the warning has already arrived.

passages.title: The Day He calls: where are My partners?
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat put us at the Gathering and let us hear Allah question those who worshipped others alongside Him. Two calls hold the passage together — in ayah 62, *"Where are My (so-called) partners whom you used to assert?"*, and in ayah 65, *"What answer gave you to the Messengers?"* — and between and after them we watch every support a person leaned on fall away, until ayah 67 opens the one door that is still open today.

## Two calls, one Day

Ayat 62 and 65 open with the same words — *wa yawma yunādīhim fa-yaqūlu*, "and the Day He will call to them, and say." Ibn Kathir introduces the passage by telling us what kind of scene this is: Allah is informing us "of how He will rebuke the idolators on the Day of Resurrection, when He will call them."

Of the two calls, Ibn Kathir says that "the first call will be concerning the issue of **Tawhid**" — the oneness of Allah, that He alone deserves worship — and he adds that this issue "includes evidences of the prophethood." The second call is then given its plain sense: *"What was your response to the Messengers who were sent to you? How did you deal with them?"*

Ibn Kathir also draws a line between this and something nearer to us. These, he says, are like the questions which will be asked of a person in his grave: *who is your Lord? who is your Prophet? and what is your religion?* The believer will testify that there is no god except Allah and that Muhammad ﷺ is His servant and Messenger; the disbelievers will say, "Oh, oh, I do not know." (Ibn Kathir gives this comparison without naming any collection, so we take the teaching exactly as he gives it and add no attribution of our own.)

## Ayah 62: a question that is not asking for information

*"Where are My (so-called) partners whom you used to assert?"* Ibn Kathir gives the meaning: *"where are the gods which you used to worship in the world, the idols and rivals — can they help you or save you?"* And he tells us the register of the question: **"This is said in the nature of a rebuke and warning."** It is not a request for information. It is a claim being made to stand up in public.

Notice too the parenthesis Ibn Kathir puts into his own rendering — *"My (so-called) partners."* The partners are named as *Mine* only because that is where the claimants had assigned them; the words are quoted back to the people who said them.

Ibn Kathir sets alongside this the ayah in Surah al-Anʿam where the same emptiness is described: they come to Allah alone, as they were first created, having left behind everything they were given, and *"We see not with you your intercessors whom you claimed to be partners with Allah. Now all relations between you and them have been cut off, and all that you used to claim has vanished from you"* (6:94). The dreaded answer to *"Where are they?"* is that there is nowhere to point.

## Ayah 63: the leaders turn state's evidence

*"Those about whom the Word will have been fulfilled will say…"* Ibn Kathir identifies them: **the Shayatin and evil Jinn, and those who used to advocate disbelief** — *Shayatin* meaning the devils, the rebellious creatures who call human beings away from Allah.

Their speech does something worth reading slowly. Ibn Kathir summarises it in two movements: **"They will testify against them and say that they led them astray, then they will declare their innocence of their worship."**

First they testify against their followers: *"Our Lord! These are they whom we led astray."* Then, in the same breath, they place themselves inside the same ruin: *"We led them astray, as we were astray ourselves."* Whatever they had to offer was never guidance; it was an overflow of their own straying. Then they cut the rope: *"We declare our innocence before You"* — and finally, *"It was not us they worshipped."* The alliance that looked so solid in the world does not survive one question.

Ibn Kathir gathers the Qur'an's other witnesses to this collapse, and the pattern is unmistakable:

- They took gods besides Allah, "that they might give them honor, power and glory" — *"Nay, but they will deny their worship of them, and become opponents to them"* (19:81–82).
- No one is more astray than one who calls besides Allah upon what will not answer him till the Day of Resurrection and is unaware of his call; and when mankind are gathered, *"they will become their enemies and will deny their worshipping"* (46:5–6).
- Ibrahim Al-Khalil, peace be upon him, said it to his own people: *"The love between you is only in the life of this world, but on the Day of Resurrection, you shall disown each other, and curse each other"* (29:25).
- And in Surah al-Baqarah: when those who were followed disown those who followed, and they see the torment, *"then all their relations will be cut off from them" … "And they will never get out of the Fire"* (2:166–167).

Read together, as Ibn Kathir places them, these ayat say the same thing from four directions: a bond built on anything other than the truth belongs only to "the life of this world."

## The argument in full: who is to blame?

Maarif ul Quran lays out the exchange as a courtroom scene, and this is where the passage speaks hardest to the reader.

The very first question the disbelievers will be asked at the **Tumultuous Place (mahshar)** — the place where all creation is gathered on that Day — will be about **shirk**, associating someone else with Allah: *where are those you used to associate with Us? Can they provide you any help today?*

Their defence is the oldest one there is: *it was not a fault of ours; we did not associate them with Allah on our own — it was the Shaitan who deluded us.* So Allah, may He be exalted, then asks the Shaitans whether they have anything to say in their defence. And they **accept their role of deceit** — yes, we misled them — but they add one devastating clause: *we only misled them; we did not force them to act upon it.*

Maarif ul Quran then completes their argument. At the very same time as we were leading them astray, **the prophets and their deputies were also guiding them towards the Right Path with sound arguments, making the Truth crystal clear to them.** They heard both. *"They rejected the Truth presented by the prophets and instead listened to us using their free will and discretion. So, how could they be free from the blame?"*

The conclusion is stated plainly: if someone chooses of his own good will to follow those who wish to put him on the wrong path, "despite the fact that he has before him clear cut arguments against them and the righteous way to follow, then he has no excuse to offer."

That principle — that being misled is not the same as being forced, and does not transfer the blame — is the heart of what these ayat establish.

## Ayah 64: "Call upon your partners" — and the silence

*"Call upon your partners."* Ibn Kathir explains what is being invited: call them **"to save you from the predicament you are in, as you hoped that they would do in this world."** They are being told to do, one last time and in the open, exactly what they did all their lives.

*"And they will call upon them, but they will give no answer to them."* Nothing comes back. And then: *"and they will see the torment"* — which Ibn Kathir explains means **"they will realize for sure that they are inevitably destined for the Fire."**

*"If only they had been guided!"* Ibn Kathir takes this as their own wish at the moment the punishment is before their eyes: **"when they see the punishment with their own eyes, they will wish that they had been among the guided in this world."** The regret is complete, and it arrives when it can no longer be acted on.

The parallel Ibn Kathir cites is from Surah al-Kahf: *"Call those partners of Mine whom you claimed." Then they will cry unto them, but they will not answer them, and We shall put a Mawbiq* — Ibn Kathir glosses it: a barrier — *between them. And the criminals shall see the Fire and apprehend that they have to fall in it. And they will find no way of escape from there* (18:52–53).

## Ayat 65–66: the second call, and the answer that will not come

*"What answer gave you to the Messengers?"* Ibn Kathir unpacks it as: *"What was your response to the Messengers who were sent to you? How did you deal with them?"* Not only what did you believe — what did you *do* with the people who brought you the truth?

And there is no answer. Ibn Kathir states it directly: **"he will have no answer on the Day of Resurrection except to remain silent, because whoever is blind in this world (i.e., does not see Allah's signs and believes not in Him), will be blind in the Hereafter, and more astray."**

Ayah 66 names the effect: *"Then the news of a good answer will be obscured to them on that Day, and they will not be able to ask one another."* Here Ibn Kathir brings the word of **Mujahid**, one of the early authorities in tafsir: **"The proof will be obscured from them."** Every argument they were once so fluent in is simply not there when they reach for it.

Then the last resource fails. Ibn Kathir's comment on the closing words is that **they will not be able to ask one another for help by virtue of their blood ties.** Even kinship is not a channel on that Day.

Notice the sequence across the whole passage. The false gods are asked for and cannot be produced (62). Those who led disown those who followed (63). The call for rescue returns nothing (64). There is no answer to give but silence (65). The proof is obscured (66). Even blood ties cannot be appealed to (66). Layer by layer, everything a person might stand on is removed.

## Ayah 67: the door that is still open

After all of that, the passage does not close on the Fire. It turns: *"But as for him who repented, believed, and did righteous deeds…"*

Ibn Kathir marks the timing of both halves, and much of the mercy of the ayah is in that marking. The repenting, believing and doing righteous deeds are **"in this world."** The being among the successful is **"on the Day of Resurrection."** The passage has just shown us a Day on which nothing can be done — and then names three things that can still be done now, before the calling-out.

Then comes the word that reads like a hesitation and is anything but. *"Then **perhaps** he will be among those who are successful."* Ibn Kathir gives the rule that governs it: **the word "perhaps" (*ʿAsa*), when used in reference to Allah, may He be exalted, implies that the thing described will inevitably come to pass, and this will undoubtedly happen by the grace and mercy of Allah.**

What sounds like a maybe on human lips is, on His, a certainty — and Ibn Kathir is careful to say where that certainty comes from: not from the worth of the deed, but from the grace and mercy of Allah.

## Taking it to heart

What follows is reflection rather than commentary, drawn from what the sources above have already established.

Ibn Kathir has told us that these two calls resemble the questions of the grave — *who is your Lord? who is your Prophet? and what is your religion?* — and that the believer answers while the disbeliever can only say, "Oh, oh, I do not know." That is worth sitting with as a question addressed to oneself.

And Maarif ul Quran has told us the principle that decides the case: being led is not being forced, and a person who chooses his misleaders while the clear arguments and the righteous way stand in front of him "has no excuse to offer." Every one of the ayat Ibn Kathir gathered — 19:81–82, 46:5–6, 29:25, 2:166–167 — shows the same ending for those alliances: they are disowned, and the relations are cut off.

Which leaves ayah 67 as the passage's own answer, and it is an answer we can still act on: repent, believe, do righteous deeds — in this world, now — and the "perhaps" of Allah is not a maybe at all.

passages.title: Your Lord creates, chooses, and knows all
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat close the surah's long argument with a declaration about Allah Himself: He alone creates, He alone chooses, He alone knows the inside of a chest as plainly as the outside — and therefore He alone is worshipped, praised, obeyed and returned to. What holds them together is a single phrase repeated at the head of two consecutive ayat: **"and your Lord"** (*wa rabbuka*) in ayah 68 and again in ayah 69. The Prophet ﷺ is being addressed directly: this is *your* Lord — the One whose choices are being questioned by the people rejecting you.

## What the passage is answering

Ibn Kathir opens his comment with the heading that sums up the whole unit: *Allah Alone is the One Who has the Power of Creation, Knowledge and Choice*. He explains that Allah "is the only One Who has the power to create and make decisions, and there is no one who can dispute with Him in that or reverse His judgement."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the human scene behind that abstraction. Imam Baghawi, in his commentary, understood ayah 68 as the reply to a specific complaint of the Makkan idolaters, the one the Qur'an records elsewhere: *"Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon some man of moment in the two cities?"* (43:31). Their reasoning was that if Allah had wished to reveal this Qur'an, He should have revealed it to some dignitary of Makkah or Ṭāʼif — someone who already commanded respect and reverence. What wisdom, they asked, could there be in revealing it to a poor orphan?

Ayah 68 is the answer, and it does not argue with them on their own terms. It removes their standing to ask. It is the prerogative of the Lord of the universe, who created all the creatures without any help or partner, to select any one of His creatures for the special favours He wishes to confer. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it: it is not for you to suggest whom He should or should not select, nor is He bound to listen to your suggestions.

Once you see that, the passage stops reading as three general statements about Allah and starts reading as a closing argument. *He creates* — so the material is His. *And He chooses* — so the honour is His to place. *He knows what your chests conceal* — so nothing about the objection is hidden from Him. *There is no god but He* — so there is no second authority to appeal to. *His is the decision* — so the case is closed. *And to Him you will be returned* — so the verdict will be delivered.

## "And He chooses" — two readings

The verb *yakhtār* ("He chooses") is the hinge of the passage, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that the commentators took it in two directions.

**First**, that the choice referred to here is Allah's choice with regard to the divine commands. Just as Allah is unique in the creation of the universe and no one is His partner, so is He in the issuance of His commands: He can give out any command to His creatures.

**Second**, the reading adopted by Imam Baghawi in his commentary and by ʿAllāmah Ibn al-Qayyim in the preface of *Zād al-Maʿād*: that the choosing spoken of here relates to the prerogative by which Allah selects any one of His creatures for His favours. This is the reading that connects directly to the Makkan objection above.

The source presents these as two interpretations of the ayah rather than as one settled meaning, and that is how they are best left — attributed, not collapsed into each other.

Ibn Kathir draws out the first clause of the ayah: *He creates whatsoever He wills* means "whatever He wills, for what He wills, happens; and what He does not will, does not happen." Then he adds the sentence that gives the believer somewhere to stand: **"All things, good and bad alike, are in His Hands and will return to Him."** That is affirmed exactly as Allah revealed it and as Ibn Kathir wrote it — without likening it to anything in creation, and without explaining it away. What it settles for the believer is this: nothing at all falls outside it — not the things you would have chosen differently, not the ones that hurt.

## "No choice have they"

The words *mā kāna lahumu al-khiyara* can be read in more than one way, and Ibn Kathir states plainly where he stands: **it is a negation, according to the correct view.** That is, the phrase does not grant people a share in the choosing; it denies them one. He supports this by placing beside it the verse:

> *"It is not for a believer, man or woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decreed a matter, that they should have any option in their decision."* (33:36)

Ibn Kathir sets the two verses side by side and leaves them there. The pairing is worth sitting with as he gives it: the denial of "choice" in ayah 68 is illustrated by a believer's position once Allah and His Messenger ﷺ have decreed a matter.

Ayah 68 then closes with the phrase Ibn Kathir carries in his rendering of the verse: **"Glorified is Allah, and exalted above all that they associate."** Declaring Him far removed from every defect is the fitting response to people assigning partners to the One who has no partner in creating and no partner in choosing.

## Ibn al-Qayyim's rule of preference

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that Ḥāfiẓ Ibn al-Qayyim drew an outstanding rule out of this very ayah, under the heading: *giving preference to one thing over the other or to one person over the other, and determination of correct standard of preference, are all Divine prerogatives.*

His point is that the preferences we see distributed across creation were not achieved by things through their own efforts or deeds. They are the result of the direct selection and prerogative of the Creator of the universe. Ibn al-Qayyim walks it down the whole ladder:

- Allah created seven skies, and gave the highest preference over the others — **though the material of all is the same.**
- He gave preference to Jannat al-Firdaws over all other parts of the Jannah.
- Among the angels, He preferred Jibrāʾīl, Mīkāʾīl, Isrāfīl and their like.
- Among human beings, He placed the prophets on the highest pedestal.
- Among the prophets, He gave preference to the more resolute ones over all others.
- Among the resolute, He gave preference to His *khalīl* — the Arabic word means an intimate, close friend — Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him), and His beloved Muhammad ﷺ, over all other resolute prophets.
- Then the progeny of Ismāʿīl (peace be upon him) over all other people of the world; Quraysh among the progeny of Ismāʿīl; Banū Hāshim over all the Quraysh; and finally Sayyidnā Muhammad Muṣṭafā ﷺ over the entire Banū Hāshim.

The preference given to the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ and to the other elders of this Ummah falls under the same principle — it is all under the control and prerogative of Allah, and the result of His selection. So too with places, and with days and nights: many are preferred over ordinary ones. In short, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, the original standard of preference in the entire universe is His prerogative and His selection.

The detail about the skies is the one to sit with. Same material, different rank. Preference is not something the honoured thing generated out of itself; it is conferred.

## The second kind of preference — the one within reach

The discussion does not end in fatalism, and this is where it becomes practical. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān continues: **at times, human acts may also become a cause of preference** — in the sense that those performing righteous acts are preferred over others, and the places where such people live or perform virtuous acts may also acquire preference over other places. This kind of preference *can* be gained, by sincerity of effort and righteous deeds.

So the basis of preference in this world rests on two things:

1. **What is beyond one's control** — resting entirely on the selection of Allah.
2. **What is within human ability** — achieved through righteous deeds and superior morals.

That distinction is worth memorising. It answers two diseases at once: envy of what Allah gave someone else (category one — never yours to allocate, and no insult to you) and complacency about your own standing (category two — genuinely open, and genuinely your responsibility).

Ibn al-Qayyim, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, deliberated on this subject in great detail and concluded that the four Rightly Guided Caliphs have precedence over all other Companions of the Prophet ﷺ; that Sayyidnā Abū Bakr has preference over the other three; then Sayyidnā ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb over the remaining two; and Sayyidnā ʿUthmān over Sayyidnā ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with them all) — and he established that sequence with the help of the two standards just described. The author of Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that Shah ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz Dehlawi also wrote a booklet on this subject in Persian, and that he himself translated that booklet into Urdu and Arabic — the Arabic translation being included in his own *Aḥkām al-Qurʼān*, under Sūrah al-Qaṣaṣ. He describes it as a research work that would be of interest to scholars.

## Ayah 69: the Lord who knows what the chest conceals

*And your Lord knows what their breasts conceal, and what they reveal.*

Ibn Kathir's gloss is compact: "He knows what is hidden in their hearts, just as He knows what they do openly." The Arabic sets the two halves side by side — *mā tukinnu ṣudūruhum* (what their chests keep covered) against *mā yuʿlinūn* (what they announce). Ibn Kathir supports it with:

> *"It is the same whether any of you conceals his speech or declares it openly, whether he be hid by night or goes forth freely by day."* (13:10)

Placed where it is, this ayah does two things at once. To the objectors of ayah 68 it says: what you said aloud about which man deserved revelation is not the whole of what is in your chests, and your Lord knows both. And to every reader since, it says: the same knowledge covers you. It is a mercy as much as a warning — nobody who worships Allah in secret is unseen, and no grief carried silently is unnoticed by *your Lord*.

## Ayah 70: four exclusive rights, in one breath

The final ayah gathers everything the passage has established into a statement of pure tawhid — the oneness of Allah.

**"And He is Allah; there is no god but He."** Ibn Kathir: He is unique in His divinity, for none is to be worshipped besides Him — and then the line that stitches the ayah back to ayah 68 — **"and there is no lord who can create what he wills and chooses besides Him."** The argument is complete: the One who alone creates and alone chooses is the only One who may rightly be worshipped. Tawhid is not merely asserted here; it is concluded.

**"His is the praise in the first and in the last."** Praise belongs to Him in this world and in the Hereafter, and Ibn Kathir gives the reason: in all that He does, He is to be praised for His justice and wisdom. Which is to say — the choices the objectors could not understand in ayah 68 are among the things He is praised for.

**"And His is the decision."** *Al-ḥukm* — the judgement, the final say. Ibn Kathir: it is a decision "that none can put back, because of His might, power, wisdom and mercy." Notice the four qualities he lists. A decree that cannot be reversed would be terrifying if it issued from power alone; it issues from power *and* wisdom *and* mercy.

**"And to Him you will be returned."** Ibn Kathir: all of you, on the Day of Resurrection, and everyone will be rewarded or punished according to his deeds, good and evil alike, "and absolutely none of their deeds will be concealed from Him." That last clause loops straight back to ayah 69 — the One who knew what the chests concealed is the One before whom the record is opened.

## Living it

Read as one unit, the passage asks three concrete things of a believer.

**Stop auditing Allah's choices.** The Makkans' error was not simply denying a Creator; it was assuming they were entitled to say who deserved His favour — and the ayah answers that it is not for them to suggest whom He should or should not select. Whenever we feel that a blessing landed on the wrong person, or that our own life was assigned the wrong portion, we are standing where they stood. Ayah 68 answers with *mā kāna lahumu al-khiyara* — no choice have they.

**Compete only where competition is open.** Since Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies one kind of preference as resting entirely on Allah's selection and another as attainable through sincerity of effort and righteous deeds, put your whole effort into the second and leave the first alone entirely. Envy targets a category that was never up for negotiation.

**Work on the inside.** Ayah 69 places what the chest conceals alongside what is announced, both equally known to your Lord, so the reputation you manage in public is the smaller half of your life. And since ayah 70 ends with the return and the reckoning where absolutely no deed stays concealed from Him, the private half is the half that will be read out.

And when a decree lands that you cannot undo, hold Ibn Kathir's two comments together: *"His is the decision, that none can put back, because of His might, power, wisdom and mercy,"* and *"all things, good and bad alike, are in His Hands and will return to Him."* Hence the praise in ayah 70 is *fī al-ūlā wa al-ākhirah* — in the first life and in the last. Not praise once the outcome is finally explained, but praise now, on the strength of who is doing the choosing.

passages.title: Night and day, and the partners that vanish
passages.tafsir:
This passage takes the argument for Allah's oneness out of the realm of debate and places it in something no one can avoid: the turning of night into day, every single day, for every single person. Ayat 71–73 put a question to the listener that he cannot answer — *if Allah made the night unending, or the day unending, which god besides Allah could undo it?* — and then name what the alternation actually is: mercy. Ayat 74–75 move to the Day of Resurrection, where a question is asked again in its final form: *where are these partners of Mine you kept claiming?* The thread holding the five ayat together is a single argument in two settings: the "partners" cannot supply you anything in this world, and on that Day they will not even be able to show up.

## The two thought experiments (ayat 71–72)

Both ayat open with the same command: **قُلْ أَرَأَيْتُمْ** — "Say: Tell me…" What follows is not a request for information but a scenario, laid out for the listener to think through for himself: *if Allah makes the night continuing upon you forever up to the Day of Judgment…*

The word describing that unending state is **سَرْمَدًا** (*sarmadan*), rendered in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān as "continuing upon you forever upto the Day of Judgment," and by Ibn Kathir as "continuous for you till the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is reminding His servants of His favours by subjugating for them the night and the day, "without which they could not survive." He then unpacks each half of the scenario:

- **If the night never ended** — this "would be harmful for them and would cause boredom and stress." The question that follows, *which god besides Allah could bring you light?*, means, in Ibn Kathir's words, light "with which you could see things and which would bring you relief."
- **If the day never ended** — this "would also be harmful for them and their bodies would get tired from so much movement and activity." Hence the question *which god besides Allah could bring you night wherein you rest?* — Ibn Kathir glosses: "to rest from your work and activity."

Read together, the two ayat cover the whole of human need. Unending darkness brings boredom and distress; unending daylight wears the body out. You need both halves, and you receive both halves, and you did not arrange either one.

The force of the challenge lies in **مَنْ إِلَٰهٌ غَيْرُ اللَّهِ** — *which god besides Allah?* The question is not an abstract one about whether anything divine exists; it asks the listener to name the one, besides Allah, who could actually do this particular job — bring back the light, or bring back the night. No such name is offered in reply. This is why Ibn Kathir titles the section *Night and Day are among the Blessings of Allah and are Signs of Tawhid* — tawḥīd being the affirmation of Allah's oneness. The same fact is simultaneously a gift to be thankful for and a sign to be convinced by.

## Why the night's benefit is named and the day's is not

There is a fine asymmetry here that Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Maẓharī, draws attention to. When ayah 72 speaks of night, it names its benefit: **بِلَيْلٍ تَسْكُنُونَ فِيهِ** — "a night *in which you may have comfort*." But when ayah 71 speaks of light, no benefit is attached to it at all. It just says "light."

Maʿārif explains that the reason for the omission "is but obvious." Daylight is superior in its very entity to darkness, and its benefits "are so numerous and well known that their repetition was not prudent." The darkness of night, by contrast, "does not have any other benefit except that it provides rest to everything" — its usefulness is based on the rest it gives people, and so that one benefit is the one mentioned. Night's single benefit is stated, because otherwise you might not think it had one; day's countless benefits are left unstated, because you already live inside them.

## Two different closing questions: hearing and seeing

Each ayah ends with a rebuke, but not the same rebuke. Ayah 71 closes with **أَفَلَا تَسْمَعُونَ** — "Then do you not *listen*?" Ayah 72 closes with **أَفَلَا تُبْصِرُونَ** — "Then do you not *see*?"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, again citing Maẓharī, offers this as a possible allusion: the benefits of the day are so numerous that they cannot be *seen*, but can only be *heard about*. Indeed, the knowledge and understanding human beings have acquired "has mainly come through hearing and listening, and very little by way of seeing." So the ayah about light closes with "do you not listen?" The benefits of the night are far fewer by comparison, and they *can* be seen. So that ayah closes with "do you not see?"

It is offered as a subtlety, not a certainty — Maʿārif itself introduces it with "it may have the allusion." But it is worth sitting with, because it flatters neither of our senses: most of what we know we did not witness, we were told. Which is precisely the position of anyone hearing revelation.

## Mercy is the word for it (ayah 73)

Ayah 73 does not add a new argument. It renames what has already been described: **وَمِنْ رَحْمَتِهِ** — "It is out of His mercy." Ibn Kathir stops here to say simply: mercy "towards you." Everything in ayat 71–72 that could have been framed as raw power is instead framed as mercy.

Then the ayah lays out the two halves of a human life with their two purposes, and Ibn Kathir maps them precisely:

- **جَعَلَ لَكُمُ اللَّيْلَ وَالنَّهَارَ** — "that He has made for you the night and the day": He created both.
- **لِتَسْكُنُوا فِيهِ** — "that you may rest therein": this is during the night.
- **وَلِتَبْتَغُوا مِنْ فَضْلِهِ** — "and that you may seek of His bounty": this is during the day, "by traveling, moving about and working."

Notice how the Qur'an describes earning a living. It is not called seeking *your* provision but **seeking of His bounty** — *faḍl*, the word rendered here as "bounty." The commute, the trade, the labour: the ayah dignifies all of it — travelling, moving about and working — and at the same time keeps its source honest. You go out and work; what you come home with is His bounty.

**وَلَعَلَّكُمْ تَشْكُرُونَ** — "and in order that you may be grateful." Ibn Kathir explains what that gratitude looks like in practice: "that you may give thanks to Allah by performing all kinds of acts of worship at night and during the day." Gratitude here is not merely a feeling; it is the use you make of the two containers you have been given.

And then he adds a mercy inside the mercy: **whoever misses something during the night can make it up during the day, and vice versa.** The alternation is not only rest and work — it is a standing second chance. He notes that this is like the ayah:

> "And He it is Who has put the night and the day in succession, for such who desires to remember or desires to show his gratitude." (25:62)

The word rendered "in succession" there is *khilfah*. Ibn Kathir adds that there are many similar ayat. The night that just ended without your prayer is not a closed door; the day is walking in behind it.

## The Day the question is asked back (ayah 74)

Ayah 74 shifts the scene without changing the subject. **وَيَوْمَ يُنَادِيهِمْ** — "And the Day when He will call to them."

Ibn Kathir describes this as "another call by way of rebuke for those who worshipped other gods besides Allah." The Lord, may He be exalted, will call to them "before all the witnesses," and will say:

**أَيْنَ شُرَكَائِيَ الَّذِينَ كُنْتُمْ تَزْعُمُونَ** — "Where are My (so-called) partners, whom you used to assert?" — and Ibn Kathir adds the crucial two words: *in this world*.

Everything painful in this ayah is in its wording. The question is **أَيْنَ** — *where?* — and a question of location demands that the thing be produced. In ayat 71–72 the challenge was *which* god could bring you light; here it is *where* is he now.
