And the partners are called **شُرَكَائِي** — "*My* partners," which Ibn Kathir's rendering carefully marks as "so-called," since, as he says at ayah 75, "there is no god besides Him." And the claim belonged to *this world* — something said among people who could not check it, now put to the One it was said about.

## Witnesses, and a demand for evidence (ayah 75)

**وَنَزَعْنَا مِنْ كُلِّ أُمَّةٍ شَهِيدًا** — "And We shall take out from every nation a witness." On the identity of that witness, Ibn Kathir reports the explanation of Mujāhid: "This means a Messenger."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān connects this to what came earlier in the sūrah: a question was already mentioned that will be asked of the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment, to repeat what they had replied to the prophets when they were invited to the truth. Here in ayah 75 we are told that the prophets themselves would testify about the reply that was given. So no one is convicted on hearsay. Every community is confronted by the witness taken out from it.

Then comes the demand: **فَقُلْنَا هَاتُوا بُرْهَانَكُمْ** — "and We shall say: Bring your proof." Ibn Kathir specifies what is being demanded: proof "of the truth of your claim that Allah had any partners." The whole case for shirk — associating partners with Allah — is asked, once, to produce a single piece of evidence for itself.

**فَعَلِمُوا أَنَّ الْحَقَّ لِلَّهِ** — "Then they shall know that the truth is with Allah." Ibn Kathir explains: "that there is no god besides Him. Then they will not speak and they will not be able to find any answer." Observe that the ayah says they will *know*. This is not a knowledge they are refused; it is a knowledge that arrives when there is nothing left to say. The very oneness of Allah they argued against in the world becomes, on that Day, something they simply know.

**وَضَلَّ عَنْهُمْ مَا كَانُوا يَفْتَرُونَ** — "and the lies which they invented will disappear from them." Ibn Kathir: "they will vanish and will be of no benefit to them." Everything a person built his life on, and could not produce when he was asked for it.

## Living it

**Let the sky argue for you.** The passage does not ask for a philosophical proof of Allah's oneness; it asks you to notice that you have never once arranged sunrise, and neither has anything you might rely on besides Him. Ibn Kathir's heading says it plainly: night and day are blessings *and* signs of tawḥīd. The evidence is scheduled twice a day.

**Use the two containers as they were designed.** The night was given so you would *rest in it* — Ibn Kathir says the rest is "from your work and activity," so actual rest is part of the design, not a failure of ambition. The day was given so you would go out and *seek of His bounty*: travelling, moving about, working. Both are named as mercy in ayah 73, so treating either one as wasted time misreads the ayah.

**Take the second chance.** Ibn Kathir's note is worth keeping close: whoever misses something during the night can make it up during the day, and vice versa. That is the practical shape of the alternation — a believer who missed his portion of worship last night has not lost the round.

**Turn the question on yourself now.** Ayah 74 asks *where* the claimed partners are, and Ibn Kathir points out the claim was made "in this world." The mercy of hearing that question today is that there is still time to check what, other than Allah, you are quietly counting on to bring you light — and to answer the question before it is put to you.

passages.title: Korah's treasures and his boast of knowledge
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat open the story of Qarun — a man from Musa's own people whom Allah loaded with wealth, and who let that wealth turn his head. Ayah 76 introduces him and the treasure so vast its very keys were a burden; the righteous among his people then counsel him in ayat 76–77 with a short, complete philosophy of how a believer holds money; and in ayah 78 he answers them with the sentence that ruins him: *"I have been granted all this because of some knowledge I have."* What binds the passage together is that single exchange — a warning offered in kindness, and a boast returned in place of gratitude.

## Where this story sits in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that from the beginning of Sūrah al-Qasas up to this point the subject has been Musa (peace be upon him) with Pharaoh and his people. Here the Qur'an turns to a second story — this time a man from *inside* the community, one of Musa's own fraternity. The link back is deliberate. An earlier ayah of this same surah had said, *"And whatever thing you are given is the enjoyment of the worldly life"* (28:60). Qarun is what happens when a man is handed that enjoyment and forgets the caution attached to it: he grew intoxicated by it, displayed ingratitude, refused to fulfil what he owed to Allah out of what Allah had given him — and, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the story goes on to relate, was sunk into the ground along with his treasure.

## Who Qarun was

The name itself is non-Arabic, perhaps from Hebrew (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān). What the Qur'an itself establishes is his lineage in one phrase: *he was of the people of Musa* — a man of Banī Isrāʼīl, not an outsider like Pharaoh.

As for his exact relationship to Musa (peace be upon him), Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says frankly that there are different versions. Ibn Kathir records from Ibn ʿAbbās that he was "the son of his paternal uncle" — Musa's cousin. That view is also reported from Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī, ʿAbdullāh bin al-Ḥārith bin Nawfal, Sammāk bin Ḥarb, Qatādah, Mālik bin Dīnār and Ibn Jurayj, among others. Ibn Jurayj gives the genealogy: "He was Qārūn bin Yashar bin Qāhith, and Musa was the son of ʿImrān bin Qāhith" — two grandsons of one man. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports this same cousin narration from Ibn ʿAbbās and adds that other versions exist besides it (citing Qurtubi and Rūḥ). The Qur'an settles the point that matters and leaves the rest open: he was one of them.

A narration of Muhammad Ibn Isḥāq, reproduced in Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī and cited by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, sharpens the tragedy: Qarun **remembered the Torah more than any other Israelite**, yet turned out a hypocrite like Sāmirī. The stated cause of that hypocrisy was his misplaced love and greed for worldly wealth and status. Leadership of the whole of Banī Isrāʼīl had been conferred on Musa and his brother Hārūn (peace be upon them), Hārūn being his assistant and partner in prophethood. Qarun grew jealous — he too was a cousin, so why no share in the leadership? He made a complaint to that effect before Musa, who replied that the matter was entirely from Allah and that he had no power in it. Qarun was not convinced by that reply, and the jealousy against Musa stayed.

Hold that portrait in mind as you read: not an ignorant man, but one who knew the Torah better than anyone; not a stranger, but a relative; and a man so fixed on the one thing he was not given that the enormous wealth he *was* given could not settle him.

## "He behaved arrogantly" — the word *baghā*

*Fa-baghā ʿalayhim* (ayah 76). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the word *baghā* carries quite a few meanings, and two are brought forward here:

- **Cruelty.** This is the more popular meaning, and it fits: intoxicated by his wealth, he began perpetrating cruelty on people. Yaḥyā Ibn Sallām and Saʿīd Ibn al-Musayyab, as cited via Qurtubi, state that Qarun was a wealthy man who had been appointed by Pharaoh to keep vigilance over Banī Isrāʼīl — and that, taking advantage of this position, he started harassing them. Authority over his own people, turned against his own people.
- **Conceit and arrogance.** Many commentators have adopted this meaning: intoxicated by his wealth, he became conceited and looked down upon Banī Isrāʼīl.

The two readings are not rivals so much as two ends of one rope. Contempt for people in the heart is what makes cruelty to them easy in the hand. Notice also the preposition: he transgressed *ʿalayhim* — "against **them**", his own people. The first casualty of his wealth was the community that shared his blood.

## The keys that bent strong men

*Kunūz* (ayah 76) is the plural of *kanz*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that it means **buried treasure**, and that in the commonly used religious sense *kanz* is that treasure on which zakah is not paid. The word chosen for his wealth already says something about how he held it. Sayyidnā ʿAṭāʼ narrated, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from Rūḥ, that he got hold of a magnificent buried treasure of Yūsuf (peace be upon him).

Then the image: *mā inna mafātiḥahu la-tanūʼu bi'l-ʿuṣbati ulī'l-quwwah*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the two key words: *nāʼa* means **to bend down under a weight**, and *ʿuṣbah* means **a group**. The sense of the sentence is that his treasures were so many, and their keys in such large number, that a group of strong people trying to lift them would bend under the weight. Normally keys are light things — but their sheer number multiplied that weight until even a band of strong men could not lift them all (Rūḥ, via Maʿārif ul Qurʼān). Ibn Kathir puts it the same way: groups of strong men would not have been able to carry them because they were so many. Al-Aʿmash narrated from Khaythamah that the keys of Qarun's treasure were made of leather, each key like a finger, each key for a separate storeroom, and that when he rode anywhere the keys would be carried on sixty mules with white blazes on their foreheads and white feet. Ibn Kathir adds that other views were also given, "and Allah knows best" — a reminder to hold such details loosely.

The rhetorical craft here is worth pausing on. The ayah does not describe the treasure at all. It describes the *keys* — and lets you calculate backwards. And it describes them not as glorious but as **heavy**: the first thing we are told about Qarun's wealth is that it was a load which bent strong backs.

## "Do not exult" — the counsel begins

*Idh qāla lahu qawmuhu lā tafraḥ* (ayah 76). Ibn Kathir specifies who is speaking: **the righteous ones among his people** exhorted him, by way of sincere advice and guidance. This is not envy talking; it is naṣīḥah — the loving correction of a man heading for a cliff.

"Do not exult in what you have" means, says Ibn Kathir, *do not be arrogant and proud of your wealth*. On *"Allah likes not those who exult,"* Ibn ʿAbbās said it means **those who rejoice and gloat**; Mujāhid said it means **those who are insolent and reckless, and do not thank Allah for what He has given them**.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word *faraḥ* itself: literally, the happiness one gets as a result of an instant pleasure. And it resolves an apparent tension in the Qur'an. Several ayat declare *faraḥ* contemptible — this one, and *"nor rejoice in what has come to you"* (57:23), and *"and they are happy with the worldly life"* (13:26). Yet in some ayat it is allowed, and in a way declared desirable — *"and on that day the believers will rejoice"* (30:4), and *"with these they should rejoice"* (10:58).

Put together, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the guideline: **joy is contemptible and not allowed when it reaches the level of arrogance and boasting — when a man regards the pleasure he has attained as his own personal achievement, and not a gift and favour from Allah.** Below that line it is not disallowed; rather, in a way it is desirable, because in such a situation the happiness itself is an expression of gratitude to Allah.

That is a liberating distinction. Islam is not asking you to be joyless about a blessing. It is asking you never to forget Who handed it to you.

## The four counsels of ayah 77

Ayah 77 is the heart of the passage: four short commands that together form a complete ethic of wealth. Ibn Kathir glosses each:

**1. Seek, with what Allah has bestowed on you, the home of the Hereafter.** Meaning: use this great wealth and immense blessing Allah has given you to worship your Lord and draw closer to Him by doing a variety of good deeds which will earn you reward in this world and the Hereafter. The wealth, on this reading, is not the obstacle — it is the instrument. And notice whose gift the ayah says it is: *what **Allah** has given you* — the very thing Qarun is about to deny in the next ayah.

**2. And forget not your portion of lawful enjoyment in this world.** Ibn Kathir: that which Allah has permitted of food, drink, clothing, dwelling places and women. Then the balance is spelled out — *your Lord has rights over you, your self has rights over you, your family has rights over you, and your visitors have rights over you; so give each of them their due.*

**3. And be generous as Allah has been generous to you.** Ibn Kathir: be generous to His creatures, as He has been generous to you. The measure of your giving is set by the memory of His giving. *Aḥsin kamā aḥsana'llāhu ilayk* — you are being asked to imitate, on your small scale, a kindness you have already received on a vast one.

**4. And seek not mischief in the land.** Ibn Kathir: do not let your aim be to spread corruption on earth and do harm to Allah's creation. The ayah closes, *"Verily, Allah likes not the mischief-makers."*

Notice the two closing refrains that frame the counsel: Allah **likes not** those who exult (ayah 76), and Allah **likes not** the mischief-makers (ayah 77). The men advising him are not threatening him with loss of money. They are warning him about standing outside Allah's love — which tells you what they thought was actually at stake.

## "Your portion of this world" — two readings

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that commentators explain *"do not neglect your share from this world"* in two ways, and both are worth carrying:

- **Your portion is what you send ahead.** Many commentators — and Ibn ʿAbbās favoured this explanation, as Qurtubi reports — take it to mean his life in this world and the deeds that may help him in the Hereafter, which include charity and all other righteous deeds. On this reading the second sentence is an emphasised repetition of the first: make use of all that has been gifted — life, wealth, health, strength — to collect what will help you in the Hereafter. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it with real force: **that portion of worldly possessions is the one that is truly one's own; the rest belongs to one's heirs.**
- **Your portion is your legitimate needs.** Other commentators explain it as: whatever Allah has given you, use it for the Hereafter without losing sight of your needs in this world — do not become a pauper by giving everything away in charity; retain something for your own needs as well.

The first guards against hoarding; the second guards against a reckless self-stripping that harms yourself and those who depend on you. Read alongside Ibn Kathir's list of rights — your Lord's, your own, your family's, your visitors' — the ayah is asking for proportion, not renunciation.

## Ayah 78: the boast

*Qāla innamā ūtītuhu ʿalā ʿilmin ʿindī* — "He said: This has been given to me only because of the knowledge I possess."

Ibn Kathir first tells us what this is: Allah informing us how Qarun responded to the exhortations of his people when they sought to guide him to what is good. And the sense of his answer: *I have no need of your advice; Allah has only given me this wealth because He knows that I deserve it and because He loves me* — He gave it to me because He knows I am fit for this. Ibn Kathir compares two other ayat where the same self-crediting reflex appears: *"then when We have changed it into a favour from Us, he says: Only because of knowledge I obtained it"* (39:49), and *"if We give him a taste of mercy from Us, after some adversity has touched him, he is sure to say: This is from me"* (41:50) — meaning, *I deserved it*.

Ibn Kathir also notes an alternative interpretation of the phrase: "only because of what **Allah** knows about me did I obtain this favour." He says Imam ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam explained the ayah very well, putting it this way: *were it not for the fact that Allah is pleased with me and knows my virtue, He would not have given me this wealth.* Either way the sickness is the same — the blessing is read as a certificate of merit.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a second layer on *"knowledge"*:

- Some commentators hold that the knowledge meant is **his understanding of the Torah**. As reported in some narrations, Qarun remembered the Torah by heart and was an authority on it, and was one of the seventy scholars whom Musa (peace be upon him) had selected for the *mīqāt* — the appointed time and place for conversation with Allah. But he became conceited over that knowledge and regarded it as his personal achievement, so that his statement meant: this wealth is the direct result of my own skill and intelligence, mine by right, with nobody's favour in it.
- More plausible in the context, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, is that the knowledge he meant was **the understanding and skill of managing trade and industry**, which brings in wealth. On this reading he is saying his fortune came to him as a result of his personal skill and efforts, with no favour of Allah involved in it.

And then the quiet demolition: **what the foolish conceited man ignored was that his skill, understanding and experience were themselves the gift of Allah.** He could not have gained them on his own. Grant him his premise entirely — grant that he earned every coin by his own brilliance — and the question simply moves back one step: who gave you the brilliance?

## The Qur'an's reply

*Awalam yaʿlam anna'llāha qad ahlaka min qablihi mina'l-qurūni man huwa ashaddu minhu quwwatan wa aktharu jamʿā* — "Did he not know that Allah had destroyed before him generations, men who were stronger than him in might and greater in the amount they had collected?"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the strategy of this response. The real answer to Qarun's assertion is the one just given — even if we accept for a moment that he acquired his wealth by his personal skill and knowledge, that knowledge and experience were themselves Allah's gift. But to bring home the more important aspect of the subject, the Qur'an states that **abundance of wealth is of no avail and is devoid of merit, nor does it help in distress.** As proof, the example of the wealthy from earlier generations is quoted: when they disobeyed and rejected the truth, they were suddenly caught by the torment of Allah.

Ibn Kathir turns the same ayah on the onlookers rather than only on Qarun: *this is what those who have little knowledge say when they see a person whom Allah has granted a lot of wealth — they say that if he did not deserve it, Allah would not have given it to him.* The mistake is not confined to the rich man. It lives in everyone who watches him and quietly concludes that fortune is evidence of favour.

The ayah then closes, *"But the criminals will not be questioned of their sins."*

## Living it

The passage is unusually practical, and its demands are concrete.

**Read your blessings backwards to their Giver.** The whole difference between the counsel of ayah 77 and the boast of ayah 78 is one phrase: *fīmā ātāka'llāh* — what Allah has given you. Say that about your income, your health, your intelligence, your opportunities, and the fourfold ethic follows naturally. Say instead *ʿilmin ʿindī*, "knowledge I possess," and everything unravels.

**Do not read wealth as a verdict.** Neither in yourself nor in others. Ibn Kathir names this as the error of those who have little knowledge, and the ayah answers it with the ruins of stronger, richer generations.

**Spend, enjoy, and keep proportion.** Aim the wealth at the Hereafter; take the lawful enjoyment Allah has permitted you; give each rightful claimant — your Lord, your self, your family, your visitors — their due; be generous in the measure that Allah has been generous with you; and never let your aim on this earth be corruption.

**And let your joy be gratitude.** *Faraḥ* is not forbidden. Only the kind that rises into arrogance and boasting is — the joy that says *I achieved this*, instead of *He gave me this*.

passages.title: Korah swallowed by the earth
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are the ending of the story of Qarun: a parade, two reactions to it, a sudden collapse, and the crowd's changed mind the next morning. What holds them together is a single question asked twice — *what is wealth actually worth?* — first answered by the eye, then answered by the earth.

## The parade (ayah 79)

Ayah 79 opens with a public spectacle. Ibn Kathir describes it as Allah telling us how Qarun went forth one day before his people with his magnificent regalia: his fine clothes, his fine horses, his servants and his retinue. This is not a man quietly enjoying what he has. It is a display staged for an audience — he "came out **before his people**," and everything about the scene is arranged to be looked at.

What makes the parade meaningful is that the Qur'an does not describe the finery in detail. It describes instead **who was watching, and what the watching did to them.**

**Two crowds, one street.** The Qur'an splits the onlookers by what they *want*, not by what they own. The first group is named "those who desire the life of this world" — desire is their defining trait. Seeing his adornments and splendour, they said: *"Ah, would that we had the like of what Qarun has been given! Verily, he is the owner of a great fortune."* Ibn Kathir glosses the last phrase — *dhū ḥaẓẓin ʿaẓīm* — as meaning "he is very lucky and has a great share in this world."

Notice how honest and how ordinary that reaction is. They do not praise his character or claim he earned it. They simply say: *lucky man.* That is the whole theology of the crowd — outcomes are luck, and luck is what you want. And notice the wording they use: *what Qarun has been **given***. Even in their envy they half-admit the wealth was granted, not generated.

That is the very admission Qarun himself had refused to make. In the ayah just before, he had said his wealth came to him "because of knowledge I have" (28:78). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān mentions that commentators differed over what "knowledge" he meant, and finds it more plausible in context that he meant his understanding and skill in managing trade and industry — the know-how that brings wealth in. Either way, his sentence claims the wealth as his own doing, with no favour owed to anyone. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names the flaw in it: what the foolish, conceited man ignored was that **his skill, understanding and experience were themselves a gift of Allah.** He could not have gained them on his own. That is the mind behind the parade — and the self-made man is a man who has forgotten one step back in the chain.

## The second voice (ayah 80)

Into this street of admiring faces, ayah 80 introduces a different group: **"those who were given knowledge."** Their first word is a rebuke — *waylakum*, rendered "Woe to you!" and "Shame on you!" It is not a gentle correction. Something is at stake urgent enough to warrant an outcry: they can see that a crowd is being reshaped by a wish.

Their answer is not "wealth is bad." It is a comparison: **"The reward of Allah is better for those who believe and do righteous deeds."** Ibn Kathir explains the sense as: *Allah's reward to His believing, righteous servants in the Hereafter is better than what you see.* The last three words carry it. The crowd's whole case rests on what is visible — the horses, the retinue, the clothes going past. The scholars are not denying that it looks good. They are saying you are comparing a visible thing to a thing you have not been shown.

**Beyond seeing.** Ibn Kathir supports this with a hadith he describes as authentic (he does not name the collection), in which Allah Most High says that He has prepared for His righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what the heart of a human cannot comprehend — and he invites the reader to recite, if he wishes, *"No person knows what is kept hidden for them of joy as a reward for what they used to do"* (32:17).

Set that against the parade. Qarun's splendour was arranged to be seen, and seeing was the only instrument the crowd was using. The reward the scholars point to is, by the terms of that report, beyond the reach of every instrument the crowd had.

**Who these knowledgeable people are.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the fact that the Qur'an sets "those who were given knowledge" directly opposite "those who desire the life of this world." That contrast, it says, clearly indicates that it is not the trait of knowledgeable people to aspire to accumulate wealth and make it the object of life. Their eyes stay on the lasting benefits of the Hereafter; of worldly wealth they take what meets their day-to-day needs, and remain content with that.

Read that carefully, because it is a description of *appetite*, not of income. The dividing line in ayat 79–80 is not rich versus poor — the crowd wishing for Qarun's wealth had none of it. The line is between people whose life is organised around the goal of having, and people who use what they have and keep their gaze somewhere else.

**"None shall attain it except the patient."** The ayah closes with a clause that the early scholars discussed. As-Suddi said: "None shall reach Paradise except the patient" — reading the clause as the completion of the statement made by the people of knowledge. Ibn Jarir said it applies specifically to those who patiently forsake the love of this world, seeking the Hereafter; and he noted that it seems to be part of what the people of knowledge said, yet it is placed as part of the Words of Allah, stating this fact.

That second reading is worth feeling. The words begin as human advice shouted in a street and end as Allah's own verdict on the matter — the sentence rises from testimony to truth. And the *ṣabr* Ibn Jarir describes is a very specific kind: patiently letting go of the love of this world for the sake of the Hereafter. In the setting of these ayat, that means holding your ground when nothing has gone wrong for you, except that something has gone very right for somebody else.

## The earth opens (ayah 81)

Then, with no argument, no warning and no transition, ayah 81: *"We caused the earth to swallow him up, along with his home."* Ibn Kathir frames it as the sequel to Qarun's conceit, his pride in his adornments, his arrogance towards his people and his transgression against them.

One detail deserves attention: **"and his home."** It was not only the man who went down but his dwelling place with him. The splendour the crowd had been coveting the day before disappeared in the same instant as its owner.

**Then he had no group to help him.** The ayah's second half itemises the failure with something close to irony: *"he had no group to help him against Allah, nor was he one of those who could save themselves."* Ibn Kathir explains: his wealth, his group, his servants and his retinue were of no avail to him; they could not protect him from the wrath and vengeance of Allah, nor could he help or save himself. There was no one to help him — neither himself nor anybody else.

Look at that list beside the parade in ayah 79. The servants and the retinue that made him impressive in the street are the same servants and retinue now counted among the things that could not save him. What he had displayed as proof of his standing became, at the decisive moment, a crowd of bystanders.

## From the Sunnah: arrogance and the ground under it

Ibn Kathir attaches to this ayah reports about how the Prophet ﷺ spoke of this kind of end.

- Al-Bukhārī records in the *Ṣaḥīḥ*, from Sālim, who said that his father told him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"While a man was dragging his lower garment, he was swallowed up, and he will remain sinking down into the earth until the Day of Resurrection."** Ibn Kathir notes that he also recorded something similar from Sālim from Abū Hurayrah from the Prophet ﷺ.
- Imām Aḥmad records from Abū Saʿīd that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"When a man among the people who came before you went out wearing two green garments, walking proudly and arrogantly, Allah commanded the earth to swallow him up, and he will remain sinking down into it until the Day of Resurrection."** Ibn Kathir notes that this version was recorded only by Aḥmad, and that its chain of narration is *ḥasan* (sound).

Two things in these reports illuminate ayah 81 directly. The trigger in both is not wealth but the *manner of walking* — a garment trailing, a swagger in fine clothes. That is Qarun "coming out before his people in his glamour" reduced to its essence. And the punishment is not described as over: the man keeps sinking until the Day of Resurrection. The earth closing over Qarun was not the end of the account, only the moment it left public view.

## The morning after (ayah 82)

Ayah 82 returns to the same street and the same people: these are the ones "who had craved his position **the previous day**." One day earlier they had said *would that we had the like of what Qarun has been given*; now the same mouths say the opposite.

Their new words open with the exclamation *wayka'anna*, which Ibn Kathir renders as **"Know you not that…"** — the sound of a person catching himself mid-error.

**First realisation: provision is not a verdict.** *"Allah expands the provision for whom He wills of His servants, and restricts it."* Ibn Kathir's comment is the theological heart of the whole passage: **wealth does not indicate that Allah is pleased with its owner**, for Allah gives and withholds, allows times of difficulty and times of ease, raises and lowers; His is the most complete wisdom and the most convincing proof.

This corrects the crowd's original sentence exactly. Yesterday they said Qarun had "a great share" — treating the size of his portion as a score. Now they see that expansion and restriction are both acts of a Lord distributing according to a wisdom that is not a scoreboard.

Ibn Kathir cites here a narration from Ibn Masʿūd (he does not name a collection for it): **"Allah has allotted your character among you just as He has allotted your provision. Allah gives wealth to those whom He loves and to those whom He does not love, but He gives faith only to those whom He loves."** That single sentence resolves the parade. Wealth is distributed across both categories of people, so it proves nothing about where you stand; faith is distributed only to the beloved. The crowd had spent a day envying the wrong column.

**Second realisation: the wish was the danger.** *"Had Allah not been gracious to us, He could have caused the earth to swallow us up!"* Ibn Kathir explains their meaning: were it not for the kindness and grace of Allah towards us, we could have been swallowed up by the earth just as he was swallowed up — **because we wanted to be like him.**

This is the sharpest line in the passage. They were not swallowed for owning anything; they owned nothing. By their own account, what put them near that fate was a *wish* — and what kept them out of it was the kindness and grace of Allah, nothing they had done.

**Third realisation: he was never successful.** *"Know you not that the disbelievers will never be successful."* Ibn Kathir states it plainly: he was a disbeliever, and the disbelievers will never be successful before Allah, in this world or in the Hereafter. Yesterday's crowd had used the language of "great fortune" about him. The correction is not that his success ended — it is that what they were looking at was never success at all.

## Living it

- **Watch what a display does to your wish, not just to your opinion.** The crowd in ayah 79 did not endorse Qarun's arrogance. They just wanted his life. That was enough to put them, by their own later admission, in danger.
- **Judge by the standard the scholars used in ayah 80.** Their argument was a comparison of two rewards, not a condemnation of wealth. The honest question before any envy is: better *than what*, and for *how long*?
- **Take Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's portrait of the people of knowledge as a measure.** Not "how much do I have," but: is having the object of my life, or do I take what meets my needs and stay content while my eyes rest elsewhere?
- **Do not read someone's provision as Allah's verdict on them** — in either direction. Ibn Kathir's principle cuts both ways: wealth is no proof of pleasure, and the narration from Ibn Masʿūd places wealth in the hands of those Allah loves and those He does not, while reserving faith for the beloved.
- **Thank Allah for the ruin you were kept out of.** The people of ayah 82 credited nothing but His kindness and grace for the fact that the earth did not take them too, though they had wanted to be like him.
- **Mind the walk, not only the wealth.** The reports from al-Bukhārī and from Aḥmad fix the danger on the trailing garment and the proud stride — the small theatre of self-display that anyone at any income can afford.

passages.title: The Home for those who seek no arrogance
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat name who the everlasting Home actually belongs to. Ayah 83 gives the qualification — no desire to exalt oneself in the land, no desire for corruption, and a good end reserved for *al-muttaqīn*, those who have **taqwā** (the reverent awareness that keeps a person obedient to Allah and afraid to disobey Him). Ayah 84 then gives the accounting that follows: good is repaid with better, evil is repaid with no more than itself.

## "That Home of the Hereafter"

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is telling us He has made **the home of the Hereafter, and its eternal delights which will never change or fade away**, for His believing, humble servants. That description is the heart of the promise: not simply that the Home is pleasant, but that its delights *never change or fade away*.

And Allah says **"We shall assign it"** — *najʿaluhā*. The Home is placed by Allah where He chooses to place it, and in the very same breath He tells us the kind of servant He assigns it to: the believing and humble, "who do not rebel against the truth with pride and oppression in the land."

## What "ʿuluww" means here

The commentators define the word closely:

- **ʿIkrimah** said the phrase refers to haughtiness and arrogance.
- **Ibn Jurayj** said *lā yurīdūna ʿuluwwan fi'l-arḍ* ("those who do not want to exalt themselves in the land") means "arrogance and tyranny," and *wa lā fasādā* ("nor cause corruption") means "committing sins."
- **Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** defines **ʿuluww** (عُلُوّ) as pride or conceit — "to present oneself as superior before others, and to look down upon others and treat them in an insulting manner." For *fasād* (mischief or corruption) it cites **Sufyān ath-Thawrī**: here it means oppression.

Maʿārif also records the observation of some commentators that **every sin is a "mischief in the world,"** because the nuisance of the sin curtails the blessings of the world. On that reading the two words together sweep up the whole of a corrupt life: ʿuluww is what a person does with his *self* — inflating it — and fasād is what that inflated self does to *everything around him*. Maʿārif's conclusion is blunt: those who intend cruelty and feel proud, or who commit sin, have no share in the Hereafter.

Ibn Kathir joins the two in one description: these are servants "who do not rebel against the truth with pride and oppression in the land. They do not exalt themselves above the creatures of Allah, arrogantly oppressing them and spreading corruption among them." Two relationships are named there — how a person stands *before the truth*, and how he treats *people*. The ayah asks about both.

## The most searching word: "who do not WANT"

The ayah does not say the Home is for those who do not *do* ʿuluww. It says it is for those who **do not want** it. Maʿārif renders the phrase "those who intend neither haughtiness on earth nor mischief," and says plainly that only those will achieve salvation and success in the Hereafter **who do not intend** any mischief and are not indulging in ʿuluww. The verdict is passed on the appetite itself, before it ever becomes an act.

This is why **ʿAlī**'s comment, recorded by **Ibn Jarīr** and quoted by Ibn Kathir, is so arresting: *"If a man wants the straps of his sandals to be better than the straps of his companion's sandals, then he is one of those referred to in the Ayah."*

Sandal straps. Not armies, not palaces — a strip of leather. The point is that what is being measured is not the size of the thing you want to be ahead in; it is the *wanting to be ahead*. What Ibn Jurayj called "arrogance and tyranny" can live, in seed form, inside a man comparing his footwear.

Ibn Kathir then draws the line precisely: **this is understood to mean that if his intention is to show off and appear better than others, then that is to be condemned.** The problem is not the sandal. It is the intention riding on it.

He supports this with a hadith which he reports as coming from the Ṣaḥīḥ, in which the Prophet ﷺ said:

> "It has been revealed to me that you should be humble to the extent that none of you boasts to others or mistreats others."

Read that standard carefully. It is not merely "do not oppress." It is humility *so complete* that boasting has nowhere left to stand. And once again the two evils of ayah 83 appear side by side in the Prophet's ﷺ words: *boasting* and *mistreating*.

## But this is not a religion of shabbiness

Having set that bar, both sources immediately guard against a misreading — because a sincere person hearing "do not want to be above others" can slide into thinking that anything good, clean or beautiful is spiritually suspect.

Ibn Kathir says plainly: **if a person simply likes to look good, then there is nothing wrong with that.** He reports that a man said, "O Messenger of Allah, I like to have my garment looking good and my shoes looking good — is this a kind of arrogance?" The Prophet ﷺ answered:

> "No, for Allah is beautiful and loves beauty."

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** makes the same point, citing a hadith in **Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim** as its basis: the arrogance and conceit condemned in this ayah "is the behavior in which one shows off as being superior, and looks down upon others. Otherwise to strive for oneself a good dress, a good house, and good food, when it is not intended to show off, is no sin."

So the dividing line does not run between plain and fine. It runs between *this pleases me and Allah loves beauty* and *this puts me above him*. Two men can wear the identical garment, and one of them is inside this ayah and the other is not — the difference is invisible to everyone except the One who assigns the Home.

## Intending a sin is itself a sin

Because ayah 83 turns on *wanting*, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a broader principle from it, citing **Rūḥ**: since the verse makes clear that the intention for mischief and pride debars a person from a share in the Hereafter, it follows that **the firm intention of a sin is as much a sin.**

It then qualifies this carefully, citing **Ghazzālī**:

- If a person **changes his mind for fear of Allah**, a reward is noted in his record instead of a sin.
- But if he **held the firm intention and only failed to act on it for reasons beyond his control**, the sin stays against his name and is recorded as such.

That distinction is worth sitting with. What redeems the abandoned sin is not the failure to commit it; it is the *fear of Allah* that made you abandon it. A person prevented by circumstance was, in his heart, already set on it. A person stopped by fear of Allah has actually turned toward Him.

## "And the good end is for those who have taqwā"

Ayah 83 does not stop at the two negations. It ends: **wa'l-ʿāqibatu li'l-muttaqīn** — rendered by Ibn Kathir as "And the good end is for those who have Taqwa," and by Maʿārif as "And the (best) end is for those mindful of Allah."

Maʿārif reads this closing clause as deliberately completing the picture: **it is not enough to abstain from mischief and pride** in order to get the share of the Hereafter, "but following the righteous path is as much a requirement. To follow all the religious obligations is also essential for the salvation in the Hereafter."

So the passage asks for both halves. Empty yourself of the desire to tower over people — and then fill that space with obedience. A person who harms nobody but obeys nobody has met one condition of the ayah and not the other. The best end, Allah tells us, belongs to those mindful of Him.

## Ayah 84: two ledgers, kept differently

Having named who gets the Home, Allah now shows how the reckoning that leads there is conducted — and the two halves of ayah 84 are deliberately unequal.

**"Whosoever brings good, he shall have the better thereof."** Ibn Kathir explains *man jāʼa bi'l-ḥasanah* ("whosoever brings good") as meaning **on the Day of Resurrection** — the deed is *brought*, carried in and presented. And *fa-lahu khayrun minhā* ("he shall have the better thereof"): "the reward of Allah is better than the good deeds of His servant — how can it not be, when Allah has multiplied it many times over?" Ibn Kathir calls this **the position of generosity**.

**"And whosoever brings evil, then those who do evil deeds will only be requited for what they used to do."** Here there is no multiplication. The requital is exactly what was done — no more. Ibn Kathir points to the parallel ayah, where those who bring an evil deed are cast down on their faces in the Fire and told: *"Are you being recompensed anything except what you used to do?"* (27:90).

Ibn Kathir's summary of ayah 84 is that it is **the position of generosity and justice** together: generosity in how good is repaid, justice in how evil is. Nobody in the Fire will have a grievance — they receive exactly what they brought. Everybody in the Home will have received better than they brought.

## Living it

- **Audit the wanting, not just the doing.** The ayah screens for an intention. Before the deed there is a wish to appear better than someone; Maʿārif says that intention alone is what debars a person from a share in the Hereafter.
- **Watch the small comparisons.** ʿAlī's example was sandal straps. Ours might be the phone, the car, the job title, the child's school, even the reputation for piety. The scale of the item tells you nothing; the impulse tells you everything.
- **Do not confuse humility with self-neglect.** Allah is beautiful and loves beauty. Good dress, a good house, good food are no sin — showing off with them is.
- **When you turn away from a sin, turn away *for Allah*.** By Ghazzālī's principle in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, that is the difference between a reward noted in your record and a sin left standing against your name.
- **Add obedience to abstention.** Maʿārif is explicit: abstaining from pride and mischief is not enough — following the righteous path and the religious obligations is required too. Harming no one is the floor, not the ceiling.
- **Bring something on that Day.** Ibn Kathir reads "whosoever brings good" as meaning on the Day of Resurrection. Whatever good you bring, Allah will return better than it — and whatever evil you bring, you will be requited with no more than what you used to do.

This is where the passage lands: the everlasting Home, whose delights never change or fade away, is assigned by Allah to the servant who was never trying to get above anyone.

passages.title: A sure return, and all perishes but His Face
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat close Sūrat al-Qasas, and they are addressed directly to the Prophet ﷺ at the hardest point of his mission: a promise that he will be brought back, instructions on how to carry himself until then, and a final sentence about what alone survives when everything else is gone. They move as one piece — from *your* return, to *your* task in the meantime, to *everyone's* return to the One who never perishes.

## Why the surah ends this way

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that these verses were revealed at the close of the surah to console the Prophet ﷺ and to make him firm in his mission as a messenger. They connect to everything that came before. This surah has narrated at length the story of Sayyidnā Mūsā (peace be upon him) with Pharaoh — Pharaoh's enmity toward the Children of Israel, their fear of him, and how in the end Allah overpowered Pharaoh's people. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ faced a strikingly similar situation: he was harassed, plans were made to kill him, and the lives of the Muslims in Makkah were made miserable. But, in the words of Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, "following His (Allah) old tradition, Allah graced them with victory over all of them," and finally gifted the Muslims possession of Makkah — the very city they had been made to vacate.

So the long story of Mūsā was never simply history. The surah ends by turning it around on the listener's own present: what happened to Mūsā is happening to you, and it will end the same way.

## The promise given at Juhfah

**"Surely the One who has enjoined the Qurʼān upon you will surely bring you back to a place of return."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān preserves a narration from Muqātil, whom it calls "the Imam of tafsir," that places this ayah in one of the most poignant moments of the Prophet's ﷺ life. During the Hijrah from Makkah to Madinah, he ﷺ came out of the cave of Thawr at night. Because enemies were pursuing him, he did not take the conventional route but trod unfamiliar paths. When he reached Juhfah — a well-known place on the way to Madinah, near Rābigh, where the conventional route to Madinah separates from that of Makkah — he glanced back toward the route of Makkah and remembered his hometown.

At that moment Jibrīl (peace be upon him) descended with this ayah, giving him the good tiding that the separation from Makkah was temporary and that he would return there soon. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this was, in fact, advance news of the victory of Makkah. It adds, on the authority of Qurtubi, that it is against this background that Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) observed in a narration that this verse was revealed at Juhfah, and that it is neither Makki nor Madani.

Feel the placement of it. He is a hunted man at a fork in the road, allowed one backward look at the home that had thrown him out. And the reassurance that comes is not "you will be safe" or "they will be punished." It is: *you are going back.*

## "A place of return": one word, several horizons

The Arabic word is **maʿād**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that it lexically means simply "a place of return" — and the early authorities read that open word in more than one way.

- **Makkah.** Al-Bukhārī, in the Tafsir of his Sahih, recorded Ibn ʿAbbās's comment on "will surely bring you back to the return": *"To Makkah."* Ibn Kathir notes this was also recorded by an-Nasāʼī in the Tafsir in his Sunan, and by Ibn Jarīr. In a report from al-ʿAwfī, Ibn ʿAbbās said it means "will surely bring you back to Makkah as He brought you out of it." Muhammad bin Ishāq recorded that Mujāhid said: "Back to your place of birth in Makkah." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān follows this reading, citing Ibn ʿAbbās as reported in Sahih al-Bukhari, and draws out the sense: though the Prophet ﷺ had to leave his hometown — and especially the Haram — for a short while, he would be brought back to Makkah by Allah, the One who had revealed the Qurʼān to him and made it obligatory to act upon it.
- **The Day of Resurrection.** This is the reading Ibn Kathir leads with. Allah is commanding His Messenger ﷺ to convey the message and recite the Qurʼān to people, and telling him that he will be brought back to the return — the Day of Resurrection — where he will be asked about the prophethood he was entrusted with. Ibn Kathir supports this with three other ayat: *"Then surely, We shall question those to whom it was sent and verily, We shall question the Messengers"* (7:6); *"On the Day when Allah will gather the Messengers together and say to them: 'What was the response you received?'"* (5:109); and *"and the Prophets and the witnesses will be brought forward"* (39:69).
- **Death**, and **Paradise.** Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn ʿAbbās is also said to have interpreted the word variously as death, as the Day of Resurrection which comes after death, and as Paradise — which will be the Prophet's ﷺ reward and his destiny for putting the message of Allah into practice and conveying it to humans and jinn, and because he is the most perfect, most eloquent and most noble of all the creation of Allah.

These are layers of one promise. The exile returns to his city; the mortal returns to his Lord; the messenger returns to be asked about his trust; and the beloved returns to the Garden.

## Why Allah names Himself this way

Notice how Allah identifies Himself in the ayah. Not "the One who created you" or "the One who protects you," but **"the One who has enjoined the Qurʼān upon you."** The verb is *faraḍa* — to make binding, obligatory. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks it as: the Lord of the universe who has made it obligatory upon you to recite it, to teach it, and to act upon it. Ibn Kathir gives the same sense: "the One Who has commanded you to put it into practice among mankind."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why that particular name is chosen here: the promise of return and victory is attached to it as a hint that recitation of the Qurʼān and acting on its injunctions would actually be the cause of the divine help and the manifest victory. The Book was not merely the reason he had to leave; it was the means by which he would come back.

## What he is told to say — and what he is told not to become

The rest of the passage is a single set of instructions for the road: one thing to say, and three things not to let happen to him.

**What to say.** *"Say: 'My Lord is Aware of him who brings guidance, and of him who is in manifest error.'"* Ibn Kathir renders the sense: say, O Muhammad, to those among your people who oppose you and disbelieve you, among the idolaters and those who follow them in their disbelief — my Lord knows best which of us, you or I, is rightly guided; and you will come to know for which of us will be the happy end in the Hereafter, and for which of us a good end and victory in this world and the Hereafter. It is a deliberately restrained answer. He is not told to argue his own case or to curse them. He is told to hand the verdict to the One who knows, and to let the outcome make the argument.

**What he was given, unasked.** *"You never expected this Book to be revealed to you, but it is a mercy from your Lord."* Ibn Kathir explains: before the revelation was sent down to you, you did not expect that revelation would be sent down to you. And "a mercy from your Lord" means revelation was sent down to you from Allah as a mercy to you, and as a mercy to mankind because of you. Ibn Kathir places this as a reminder of the numerous blessings Allah granted him and mankind by virtue of sending him to them — and it is the reminder of a gift that grounds the command which follows.

**Do not lend your weight to those who reject it.** *"So never be a supporter of the disbelievers."* The word Ibn Kathir glosses is *ẓahīr* — "i.e., a helper," one who backs another up. Rather, Ibn Kathir says, separate from them, express your hostility toward them, and oppose them. A man who has been handed a mercy he never asked for does not then lend his weight to those who reject it.

**Do not let their pressure wear you down.** *"And let them not turn you away from the ayat of Allah after they have been sent down to you."* Ibn Kathir catches the emotional reality here. The danger is not that the Prophet ﷺ would abandon the revelation; it is that sustained opposition wears a person down. So the meaning is: do not let their opposition to you affect you or put people off from following your way; do not worry about that or pay any attention to it — for Allah will make your word supreme, will support your religion, and will make the message with which He has sent you prevail over all other religions.

**And keep calling.** *"And invite to your Lord, and be not of the idolaters."* Ibn Kathir: to worship your Lord alone, with no partners or associates. The answer to being pushed back from the message is not defensiveness. It is to keep inviting.

## The last word of the surah

**"And do not invoke any other god with Allah. There is no god but He."** Ibn Kathir: it is not appropriate to worship anything or anybody except Him, and divinity does not befit any except His glory. The whole surah — Pharaoh and his power, the Prophet's ﷺ exile and promised return — resolves into this one sentence.

**"Everything will perish save His Face."** Ibn Kathir reads this as a statement about Allah Himself: here Allah is telling us that He is Eternal, Ever Lasting, Ever Living, Self-Sustaining — although His creation dies, He will never die. He pairs it with *"Whatsoever is on it will perish. And the Face of your Lord, full of majesty and honour, will remain forever"* (55:26–27), and states that Allah used the word "Face" to refer to Himself; so "everything will perish save His Face" means everything except Him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same: the word "His Face" in this verse means the very Being of Allah, and the meaning of the verse is that except for Allah everything is mortal, will get destroyed, and will vanish.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then records a second interpretation, with attribution: some commentators have taken the phrase "His Face" to mean the good deeds performed by human beings exclusively for Allah. On that reading, the meaning of the verse would be that those actions performed exclusively for Allah will not be destroyed, while all other things will perish. The first is the reading Ibn Kathir gives and the one Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states first; the second adds a searching practical edge — of everything you are accumulating, only what was done for His sake survives the general ruin.

**The truest line a poet ever said.** Ibn Kathir reports here that it was recorded in the Sahih, via Abu Salamah, that Abu Hurayrah said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"The truest word of a poet was the saying of Labīd — indeed everything except Allah is false."* A poet stumbled onto the one true sentence about reality, and the Prophet ﷺ acknowledged it. The ayah says what Labīd said — but as certainty rather than intuition.

**"His is the decision, and to Him you shall be returned."** Ibn Kathir: *lahu al-hukm* means dominion and control — there is none who can reverse His judgement or His decision. And "to Him you shall be returned" means the Day when you will be brought back, and He will reward or punish you according to your deeds: if they are good, then you will be rewarded, and if they are bad, then you will be punished.

Notice what happens to the address in that last phrase. The passage has been speaking to one man throughout — the Arabic keeps saying *ʿalayka*, *laraddukka*, *ilayka*: upon **you**, back to **you**, sent down to **you**, all singular. The closing word, *turjaʿūn*, is plural: to Him **you all** shall be returned. The promise of a return that was given personally to the Prophet ﷺ at Juhfah closes as a fact about every human being reading it.

## Living it

The passage asks for three things, in order, and they are the same three whether you are a prophet on a mountain road or an ordinary believer.

- **Hold on to the Book that was made binding on you.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's point is not decorative: recitation of the Qurʼān and acting on its injunctions is presented here as the cause of Allah's help and manifest victory, not merely as a reward for it.
- **Do not lend your weight to what opposes it, and do not let opposition steer you.** The passage names both failure modes: becoming a helper of those who reject the message, and being turned away from it by their pressure. The instruction for the second is remarkably simple — do not pay it any attention; keep inviting.
- **Measure everything against the closing ayah.** If everything perishes except Him, then nothing you could call on beside Him is worth calling on, and no verdict but His will stand.

## A closing note from the commentator

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān finishes its commentary on this surah with a personal note, and it is worth reading as an unintended illustration of the ayah it had just explained. The commentary records that it was concluded on Dhū al-Qaʿdah 9, 1391 AH (September 1971), at a time when — as it describes — Pakistan was attacked, Karachi was bombarded daily for fourteen days, the city was severely damaged, hundreds of Muslims were martyred and many houses demolished, and the fourteen-day war finished on the sad note that East Pakistan was cut off and about ninety thousand troops surrendered there. "Every Muslim is stuck with grief and bewilderment," it says. It signs off with the words of the very truth it had just been explaining: *innā lillāhi wa innā ilayhi rājiʿūn* — "Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we return."

Cities fall, states break, and the man writing the commentary was watching it happen as he wrote the words "everything will perish save His Face." That is the passage's own claim, tested in real time — and the same claim that had once been given as consolation to a man looking back toward the route of Makkah from the road at Juhfah.
